title: Preface
content:
Preface Number Systems: From 
N to 
R ended with the real numbers as a complete ordered field. Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 built the complex numbers on those real numbers. This volume starts with the arithmetic of the integers, divisibility and congruences, then takes these results and builds the algebra that linear algebra and the algebra volumes assume on their first page. It studies fields as objects of their own, introduces groups through permutations, makes polynomials into formal objects, and proves that polynomials over a field have the arithmetic of the integers. It ends with the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra: every non-constant complex polynomial has a root. Who it is for. The reader we have in mind has worked through Logic and Proof, Sets and Functions and the main line of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, and has read the complex numbers of Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1, or has their habits from elsewhere. That means running an induction, checking that an operation on classes is well defined, and proving a statement about every element of a ring from the ring axioms alone. The chapters point back to those volumes wherever they use a definition or a result, with a link, so a reader who is unsure of a step can look it up. Much of the material is familiar in outline from school or from a first linear algebra course; what is new is that every rule is proved, and that nothing is used before it is proved. What it covers. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Chapter Title What it does ----------------------- -------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 1 Divisibility and Congruences Bézout’s theorem and the Euclidean algorithm, Euclid’s lemma and unique prime factorization, ideals and quotient rings, 
Z/n
Z as a commutative ring, units, 
Z/p
Z a field, and the Chinese remainder theorem (moved from Number Systems; in revision) 2 Fields The field axioms and their consequences; the finite fields 
F_p; subfields and the subfield test; field homomorphisms; the characteristic and the prime subfield; the binomial theorem, the Frobenius map and Fermat’s little theorem 3 Groups, Subgroups, and Homomorphisms Groups, products of many factors and integer powers; subgroups and the subgroups of 
Z; homomorphisms, kernels and isomorphisms; permutations, cycle notation and the disjoint cycle decomposition; transpositions generate the symmetric group 4 Formal Polynomials A polynomial as a sequence of coefficients; the ring R[x] over a commutative ring; degree and integral domains; evaluation and substitution as ring homomorphisms, and why a polynomial is not its function; the formal derivative 5 Polynomials over a Field Division with remainder, the greatest common divisor and the Euclidean algorithm in F[x]; irreducible polynomials and unique factorization; roots, multiplicity and repeated roots; interpolation, the rings F[x]/\langle m angle and the Chinese remainder theorem; the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra and the factorization of real polynomials -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The complex numbers of Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 are the volume’s most important example, and Chapter 2 names what they have in common with 
Q, 
R and 
Z/p
Z. Chapter 3 uses the complex numbers and Chapter 2 only in examples, remarks and one review exercise. Chapters 4 and 5 form a pair. Chapter 4 builds polynomials over any commutative ring and asks only what can be done without dividing; Chapter 5 takes the coefficients in a field and runs again, with the degree in place of size, the arithmetic that Chapter 1 ran in 
Z. How to read it. Read the chapters in order; each uses the ones before it. Every section has Quick checks with folded answers; answer each one before you unfold it. The exercises of a section come in three groups, A to check understanding, B for practice and C to go deeper, and the last section of each chapter adds R items that reach back to earlier chapters. A chapter’s opening page lists what it needs, with links, and the time it takes. Second-reading folds hold edge cases and longer justifications. They can stay closed on a first reading, but they are not optional, since later proofs may use what they contain. No borrowed fact. Every result of this volume is proved from the earlier volumes. The complex numbers come from Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1, which assumes five facts about cosine and sine for polar form and the roots of unity; this volume uses those only in examples and remarks, and Chapter 5 proves the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra from the square roots of Analytic Preliminaries, Section 1.4 and the completeness of 
R alone. Nothing in the volume depends on Analysis on the Real Line. Time. The chapter openings add up to about 130 hours on the core track and about 185 hours for everything. What comes next. The linear algebra volumes, beginning with Spaces and Maps, take their scalars from a field and use the complex numbers, polynomials and their roots throughout: Chapter 2’s fields and subfields, Chapter 4’s evaluation of a polynomial, Chapter 5’s division with remainder and the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra, and Chapter 3’s permutations, which Determinants and the Structure of Operators needs for the determinant. The algebra volumes start where this one stops. Groups continues Chapter 3 with cyclic groups, the sign of a permutation, cosets and Lagrange’s theorem; Rings and Fields continues Chapters 2, 4 and 5 with fraction fields, polynomials over the integers, Gauss’s lemma and field extensions. Many of their first definitions are the ones proved here, under the same names.

title: Divisibility and Congruences
content:
Divisibility and Congruences Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2 built 
Z out of pairs of natural numbers and proved it an ordered ring, but it said nothing about which integers divide which. Sets and Functions, Section 3.2 did, for the school integers: it proved division with remainder, showed that every integer from 2 on has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of prime factorization aside as a fact it neither proved nor used. This chapter proves that arithmetic again for the constructed 
Z, and goes further, using the ordered-ring axioms and two properties of the order of 
Z: there is no integer strictly between 0 and 1 (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), and a non-empty set of integers with a lower bound has a least element (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element); the field 
Q enters chiefly for the integer part  loor{a/n} and for lowest terms. The second property gives division with remainder at once. Then one move does most of the work. In a set of integers closed under sums and under multiplication by any integer, the least positive element divides every element, and dividing by it with remainder is how one sees this. Applied to the combinations ax + by, it makes the greatest common divisor a combination of a and b (Bézout’s theorem), and the Euclidean algorithm computes it. Multiplying that combination by a third integer gives Euclid’s lemma, that a prime dividing a product divides one of the factors, and with it the uniqueness of prime factorization and the lowest terms of a rational number. The second half returns to the clock of Sets and Functions, Section 5.2. There, and again for 
Z and 
Q in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3, each sum and product of classes was checked separately to be well defined. Section 1.3 makes the check once, for the quotient of any commutative ring by an ideal, and 
Z/n
Z becomes a commutative ring with n elements on which, for n \ge 2, no order fits. In it the classes that can be divided by are exactly the classes of the integers coprime to n. So 
Z/p
Z is a field with p elements for every prime p, and two congruences with coprime moduli have exactly one class of solutions modulo the product of the moduli, the Chinese remainder theorem. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5 builds 
R in the same shape, as classes of rational Cauchy sequences whose difference is null (the null sequences play the part of the ideal), though it checks its operations directly; Chapter 5 of this volume runs division with remainder, gcd and unique factorization again for polynomials over a field. Two integers, one theory. Sets and Functions, Chapters 1 and 3 proved its facts about divisibility for the school integers, from school facts such as the closure of 
Z under +, - and \cdot (@fd2:prp-integers-closed). This chapter keeps their definitions of divisibility, prime and congruence (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime, @fd2:def-congruence), read word for word on the ring of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2, and proves the results again; no proof in it cites a result of Sets and Functions about integers. Each such result has a twin here: transitivity of divisibility (@fd2:prp-divides-transitive) and even or odd (@fd2:thm-even-or-odd), from its Chapter 1, are @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b) and @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a); the others are named in the section that proves them: division with remainder (@fd2:thm-division-algorithm) and the antisymmetry of divisibility on 
N (@fd2:prp-divides-partial-order) in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5; a prime factor of every n \ge 2 (@fd2:thm-prime-factor) and lowest terms (@fd2:lem-lowest-terms) in Section 1.2; and the arithmetic of congruence classes (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic) in Section 1.3. Nothing earlier was circular: the earlier chapters used these facts about the school integers as stated facts, and this chapter proves them for the constructed ones. What you need. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 1–3, chiefly Sections 2.3–2.5, and Sets and Functions, Chapters 1–5, chiefly Sections 1.1, 3.2 and 5.2. From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3: the commutative ring 
Z and its algebra (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra), its order, its positive elements, the rules for inequalities and discreteness (@fd3:prp-order-from-positives, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules, @fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring), the least element of a set of integers bounded below (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element), the copy of 
N inside 
Z (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers), the lemma that a rule on classes is a function when equivalent inputs give equivalent outputs (@fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes), the two-element field that cannot be ordered (@fd3:exm-finite-ring-not-orderable), and the field 
Q with 
Z inside it, its order, reciprocals and integer part (@fd3:def-rational-operations, @fd3:thm-rationals-field, @fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals, @fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field, @fd3:prp-reciprocal-order, @fd3:prp-rational-integer-part); and from its Section 2.5, division with remainder, the rules for divisibility and parity (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd). From its Chapter 1, the citing rule of its Section 1.4 (@fd3:cor-omega-identification), by which induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and the recursion theorem (@fd2:thm-recursion, @fd3:thm-omega-recursion) apply to 
N; and powers and parity on 
N (@fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity), used in review exercise R2. From Sets and Functions, Section 1.1, the definitions of divisibility and prime (@fd2:def-divides, @fd2:def-prime); from its Section 3.3, finite products (@fd2:def-sum-product), used in Section 1.2 as a pattern for products of lists; from its Section 5.2, equivalence relations, classes and quotient sets (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:thm-classes-partition) and congruence (@fd2:def-congruence); from its Section 5.3, suprema and the divisibility order (@fd2:def-order-supremum, @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm), in a remark of Section 1.1 and in Section 1.2’s B2. From Sets and Functions, Chapters 1 and 2: products, equality of functions and bijections (@fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-bijective); and from its Section 4.1, finite sets and equinumerous sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-equinumerous-properties), to count 
Z/n
Z, with more on finite sets (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique, @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy, @fd2:exr-finite-sets-c2, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets) in Section 1.4’s B3 and C2. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 8, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), for Section 1.2’s B1 and C2 and Section 1.4’s C2. A few results are compared with and not used: the twins listed above; Euclid’s argument in Logic and Proof, Section 8.1’s C1 (@fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1) in Section 1.2’s C3; a rule on classes that is not a function (@fd2:exm-ill-defined-class-map) in Section 1.3’s C1; lowest terms in Sets and Functions, Section 3.2’s C2 (@fd2:exr-induction-in-practice-c2) in Section 1.2; and, in the review exercises, the countable product of Sets and Functions, Section 4.2 (@fd2:exr-countable-sets-b2, @fd2:thm-product-countable) in R2, the two proofs that \sqrt 2 is not rational (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational, @fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two) in R3. Review exercise R1 also returns to the integers as classes of pairs (@fd3:def-integers-as-classes). Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 30 hours for everything. Roadmap - The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm. The combinations a
Z + b
Z and the multiples n
Z, the greatest common divisor with \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0, Bézout’s theorem (the least positive combination is the gcd, and every combination is a multiple of it), coprime integers, and the Euclidean algorithm as a recursion that keeps the set of combinations fixed, with back-substitution for the coefficients. - Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Euclid’s lemma from the Bézout identity, a prime dividing a product of primes equal to one of them, coprime divisors, the least divisor above 1 as a prime, existence and uniqueness of non-decreasing prime factorizations by comparing the largest primes, a monoid in which factorization is not unique, and lowest terms in 
Q. - Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n. Ideals as the subsets that a quotient needs, the quotient ring R/I of a commutative ring by an ideal, the failure for 
Z \subseteq 
Q, the ideals of 
Z as the sets n
Z, and 
Z/n
Z as a commutative ring with n elements that no order fits when n \ge 2. - Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Units of a commutative ring, the units of 
Z/n
Z as the classes coprime to n with inverses from back-substitution, 
Z/n
Z a field exactly when n is prime, and the Chinese remainder theorem for two coprime moduli, with the failures when the moduli share a factor; the review exercises reach back to Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 1–3, Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, and Sets and Functions, Chapter 4. Named moves - Least positive element, then divide. Take the least positive element d of a set of integers closed under integer combinations; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than d, so it is 0. This proves Bézout’s theorem in Section 1.1 and the description of the ideals of 
Z in Section 1.3, and Section 1.2’s B2 and Section 1.3’s C2 use it for common multiples and for sets closed under subtraction. - Multiply the Bézout identity. From 1 = ax + by, multiply by c: c = acx + bcy, and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about common divisors into an equation, and it gives Euclid’s lemma in Section 1.2; in Section 1.4 the same identity, read modulo n, gives inverses, and read modulo m and modulo n at once, the Chinese remainder theorem. - Compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. An operation on classes a + I is well defined because a change of representative is an element of I, and multiplying it by the other argument keeps it in I. This is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2’s check one argument at a time, now made once for every commutative ring and every ideal.

title: 1.1 The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content:
The Greatest Common Divisor, Bézout, and the Euclidean Algorithm Number Systems, Section 2.5 gave the constructed integers a relation a \mid b and a division with remainder (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder). This section asks what two integers have in common. Here is a concrete version. A machine accepts only coins worth 12 and 42 units, and gives change in the same coins. Which amounts can be paid exactly? Paying x coins of the first kind and y of the second, with negative numbers for coins received as change, pays 12x + 42y. So 42 - 3 \cdot 12 = 6 can be paid, and hence every multiple of 6; and since 6 divides both 12 and 42, nothing else can. Why 6, and why exactly the multiples of 6? The answer is a theorem about every pair of integers, and its proof is the main move of this chapter. Integer combinations The amounts 12x + 42y form a set that deserves a name. Integer Combinations Let a, b, n \in 
Z. The set of integer combinations of a and b is a
Z + b
Z \coloneqq \{ ax + by : x, y \in 
Z \} , and the set of multiples of n is n
Z \coloneqq \{ kn : k \in 
Z \}. So n
Z is the set of m \in 
Z with n \mid m (@fd2:def-divides), and a
Z + b
Z is written as one symbol: it is defined directly, not as a sum of two sets. Three closure properties hold for every a, b \in 
Z. For x, y, x', y', m \in 
Z, the ring laws of @fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) give  egin{aligned} (ax + by) + (ax' + by') &= a(x + x') + b(y + y'), \ -(ax + by) &= a(-x) + b(-y), \ m(ax + by) &= a(mx) + b(my), \end{aligned} so a
Z + b
Z is closed under +, under -, and under multiplication by any integer. It contains 0 = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 0, a = a \cdot 1 + b \cdot 0 and b = a \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1. Taking b = 0 gives n
Z + 0
Z = \{ nx + 0y \} = \{ xn : x \in 
Z \} = n
Z, by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) and (F6); so n
Z has the same three properties. Examples: - 12
Z + 42
Z contains 12, 42, 30 = 42 - 12 and 6 = 12 \cdot (-3) + 42 \cdot 1, so it contains every multiple of 6, by the third closure property. - 2
Z + 3

Z: it contains 1 = 2 \cdot (-1) + 3 \cdot 1, and with it m \cdot 1 = m for every m \in 
Z. - The degenerate case: 0
Z + 0
Z = \{0\} (the case n = 0 above, since 0
Z = \{ k \cdot 0 : k \in 
Z \} = \{0\} by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). It is the only case in which a
Z + b
Z has no positive element (if a 
e 0, one of a, -a is a positive element, by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h); likewise for b), and the theorem below must exclude it. Non-example by minimal change. Allow only paying, with no change given: \{ 12x + 42y : x, y \in 
N \}. It contains 12 and 42 and is closed under +, but not under -: it contains no negative integer, since x, y \ge 0 give 12x + 42y \ge 0. Nor does it contain 6: a non-zero element has x \ge 1 or y \ge 1, so it is at least 12. The coefficients must range over all of 
Z. The greatest common divisor An integer d is a common divisor of a and b if d \mid a and d \mid b. Every pair has the common divisor 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). For the coins, 6 is a common divisor of 12 and 42, and the question was why it is the one that matters. The greatest common divisor is the largest integer that divides both. [Greatest Common Divisor] Let a, b \in 
Z. If (a, b) 
e (0, 0), the greatest common divisor \gcd(a, b) is the greatest element, for \le, of the set of common divisors of a and b. We set \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0. In words: among all integers dividing both a and b, take the largest. The definition says “the greatest element”, so it owes us a proof that there is one. Well-definedness. Let (a, b) 
e (0, 0), and let D be the set of common divisors of a and b. It is non-empty, since 1 \in D. Say a 
e 0 (otherwise b 
e 0, and the same argument runs with b). By @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h), one of a, -a is positive; call it c. Every d \in D satisfies d \le c: if d > 0, then d \mid c by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d), and d \le c by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e); if d \le 0, then d \le 0 < c. So D is bounded above, and by @fd3:prp-integer-least-element it has a greatest element. Since 1 \in D, that element is at least 1. Hence \gcd(a, b) \ge 1 whenever (a, b) 
e (0, 0), and \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a), since the condition “d \mid a and d \mid b” is symmetric in a and b. Examples: - \gcd(4, 6) = 2. A positive common divisor d satisfies d \le 4, by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), and d \ge 1, so d \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\} by discreteness (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)), applied repeatedly. Now 4 
mid 6 and 3 
mid 4, because 6 = 1 \cdot 4 + 2 and 4 = 1 \cdot 3 + 1 have non-zero remainders (the divisibility test after @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder), while 2 divides both. So the greatest common divisor is 2. - \gcd(-5, 5) = 5: the common divisors of -5 and 5 are the divisors of 5 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), and the greatest is 5, by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e). - \gcd(1, b) = 1 for every b \in 
Z: a common divisor d divides 1, so d = \pm 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), and the greater is 1. Why the convention for (0, 0). Every integer divides 0, so 0 and 0 have no greatest common divisor for \le, and some value has to be chosen. The value 0 is the one that keeps clauses (c) and (e) of the theorem below true for (0, 0), as the remark after it shows. It also matches @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm of Sets and Functions, Section 5.3, where 0 is the top of (
N, \mid), divisible by everything. Listing divisors one by one, as in the first example, is slow. The Euclidean algorithm below replaces the list by one division per step, and Bézout’s theorem is what makes it work. Bézout’s theorem Here is the answer to the coin question for every pair of integers: the payable amounts are exactly the multiples of the greatest common divisor, and the greatest common divisor is itself payable. Bézout’s Theorem Let a, b \in 
Z, not both 0, and let S \coloneqq (a
Z + b
Z) \cap 
Z_{>0}. 1. S has a least element d, and d = ax_0 + by_0 for some x_0, y_0 \in 
Z. 2. d \mid a and d \mid b. 3. Every common divisor of a and b divides d. 4. d = \gcd(a, b). In particular, \gcd(a, b) = ax + by for some x, y \in 
Z. 5. a
Z + b
Z = d
Z. Try it first (ten minutes): for a = 12 and b = 42, list the positive numbers 12x + 42y you can reach. Which is the least, and why should the least one divide 12? The obvious plan starts from the greatest common divisor and tries to write it as ax + by. It stalls: the definition of \gcd(a, b) says nothing about combinations, so there is nothing to build x and y from. The attempt on 12 and 42 suggests starting at the other end. The positive combinations 12, 42, 30, 18, 6, \dots have a least element, and it was found as a combination. Why should it divide 12? Divide 12 by it. The remainder is 12 minus a multiple of a combination, so it is again a combination, and it is smaller than the least positive one. So it cannot be positive: it is 0. Once the least positive combination d is known to divide a and b, the rest is bookkeeping: every common divisor divides the combination d, so none exceeds it. Before reading on: where is the minimality of d used, and where its positivity? (a) Suppose a 
e 0; if a = 0, then b 
e 0, and the argument is the same with b in place of a. Both a = a \cdot 1 + b \cdot 0 and -a = a \cdot (-1) + b \cdot 0 lie in a
Z + b
Z, and by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h) one of them is positive. So S 
e \emptyset. Every element of S is positive, so 0 is a lower bound, and by @fd3:prp-integer-least-element S has a least element d. Since d \in a
Z + b
Z, there are x_0, y_0 \in 
Z with d = ax_0 + by_0. (b) Since d \in 
Z_{>0}, @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a) gives q, r \in 
Z with a = qd + r and 0 \le r < d. Then r = a - qd = a - q(ax_0 + by_0) = a(1 - qx_0) + b(-qy_0) , so r \in a
Z + b
Z. If r > 0, then r \in S and r < d, contradicting the minimality of d. Hence r = 0, and a = qd, that is, d \mid a. Dividing b by d in the same way gives d \mid b. (c) Let c \mid a and c \mid b. By @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c), c \mid ax_0 + by_0 = d. (d) By (b), d is a common divisor of a and b. Let c be any common divisor. If c > 0, then c \mid d by (c), and c \le d by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), since d > 0. If c \le 0, then c \le 0 < d. So d is the greatest common divisor: d = \gcd(a, b) by @def-integer-gcd, and \gcd(a, b) = ax_0 + by_0. (e) (\supseteq) Let k \in 
Z. Then kd = k(ax_0 + by_0) = a(kx_0) + b(ky_0) \in a
Z + b
Z. (\subseteq) Let x, y \in 
Z. By (b), d \mid a and d \mid b, so d \mid ax + by by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c), that is, ax + by \in d
Z. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt: the minimality of d is used once, in (b), to force the remainder r to be 0. The positivity of d is used twice: to divide by d at all (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder needs a positive divisor), and in (d), where c \le d for positive c comes from @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) and for the other c from 0 < d. (The step r \in S uses the positivity of r, not of d, which is why the case r = 0 is split off.) The proof of (b) is the move this chapter is built on, and we give it a name: least positive element, then divide. Take the least positive element d of a set closed under integer combinations; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than d, so it is 0. Section 1.2 uses the move again for common multiples, and Section 1.3 for sets closed under subtraction. For the coins, the theorem says: the payable amounts form 12
Z + 42
Z = d
Z, where d is the least positive payable amount, and d = \gcd(12, 42). The Try-it-first list finds d = 6 = 12 \cdot (-3) + 42 \cdot 1. Clause (c) says that \gcd(a, b) is greatest also for divisibility, not only for \le. For a, b \in 
N, not both 0, it is the infimum of \{a, b\} in (
N, \mid) (@fd2:def-order-supremum): it divides both, and every c \in 
N dividing both divides it. This is the mirror image of @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm, where the supremum is the least common multiple. For general a, b \in 
Z, let a' be the one of a, -a that lies in 
N, and likewise b' (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (h), with a' = 0 if a = 0). Since a and -a have the same divisors (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (d) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)), \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(a', b'). With the convention \gcd(0, 0) = 0, clauses (c) and (e) also hold for (0, 0) when d is read as 0: every integer divides 0, and 0
Z + 0
Z = \{0\} = 0
Z. So 0, the top of (
N, \mid), is also the infimum of \{0, 0\} = \{0\}. Pairs whose greatest common divisor is 1 get a name of their own. [Coprime Integers] Integers a, b \in 
Z are coprime if \gcd(a, b) = 1. For instance, 2 and 3 are coprime, and so are 1 and any b; but 4 and 6 are not, since \gcd(4, 6) = 2, and neither are 0 and 0, since \gcd(0, 0) = 0. For coprime integers, (d) of the theorem produces 1 as a combination, and conversely: [Coprime Means 1 Is a Combination] Let a, b \in 
Z. Then a and b are coprime if and only if ax + by = 1 for some x, y \in 
Z. (\Rightarrow) If \gcd(a, b) = 1, then (a, b)

title: 1.2 Euclid's Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
content:
Euclid’s Lemma and the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic Section 1.1 gave every pair of integers, not both zero, a greatest common divisor, and wrote it as a combination ax + by (@thm-integers-bezout). This section spends that identity. Take 60. It splits as 2 \cdot 30, as 6 \cdot 10, as 4 \cdot 15, and every way of splitting it further, until no factor splits again, ends with the same primes 2, 2, 3, 5. Sets and Functions, Section 3.2 proved, for the school integers, that every integer at least 2 has a prime factor, and set the uniqueness of the full splitting aside. Here we prove both, for the integers of Number Systems, Chapter 2. The key is a property of primes that the definition (“no positive divisors except 1 and itself”) does not obviously give: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. As in Number Systems, Section 2.5, numerals are the natural numbers of those names, and their sums and products may be computed in 
N (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers (a)). Euclid’s lemma The definition of a prime p speaks about the divisors of p. The property we want speaks about the numbers that p divides. Something has to connect the two, and the connection is the Bézout identity of Section 1.1. We first prove a version for any divisor that shares no factor with one of the two numbers multiplied. Euclid’s Lemma Let a, b, c \in 
Z. If a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1, then a \mid c. The hypothesis \gcd(a, b) = 1 is a statement about common divisors, which is hard to use directly. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination it is the same as an equation 1 = ax + by, and an equation can be multiplied. Multiplying it by c writes c as acx + bcy. The first term is a multiple of a on sight, and the second is one because bc is. Suppose a \mid bc and \gcd(a, b) = 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination there are x, y \in 
Z with ax + by = 1. Since a \mid bc, there is k \in 
Z with bc = ka (@fd2:def-divides). Multiplying the identity by c, with (F7), (F9), (F5) and (F6), c = c(ax + by) = a(cx) + (bc)y = a(cx) + a(ky) = a(cx + ky) . Since cx + ky \in 
Z, this shows a \mid c. We call the move of this proof multiply the Bézout identity: from 1 = ax + by, multiply by c and read off what divides c. It turns a statement about divisors into an equation, which is where the work can be done. Each hypothesis has a job. Without \gcd(a, b) = 1 the conclusion fails: 4 \mid 2 \cdot 6 = 12, but 4 
mid 6, since 6 = 1 \cdot 4 + 2 leaves a non-zero remainder (uniqueness in @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a)); here \gcd(4, 2) = 2. The common factor 2 of 4 and 2 let 4 divide the product without dividing 6. Lists, products and prime factorizations To say that a factorization is unique, we must first say what a factorization is. The products 2 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 and 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 5 \cdot 2 are equal and use the same primes, and we want to count them as one. We do so by writing the primes in order, smallest first. A factorization also has a length, and the length may be 0: the number 1 is the product of no primes at all. Products of lists are defined by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product. That definition was made for sequences of real numbers, and we use it as a pattern, as group (iii) of the citing rule of Number Systems, Section 1.4 allows, with the ordered field 
Q (@fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field) in place of 
R. A product of integers is an integer (@fd3:prp-integers-embed-rationals), so the products of lists below lie in 
Z; the paragraph “Why the product exists” below checks directly that the recursion runs in 
Z. Small primes Later arguments need to know that a few small integers are prime in the constructed 
Z. Sets and Functions, Section 1.1 checked some of these after @fd2:def-prime, for the school integers; that check is not a proof about the ring of Number Systems, Chapter 2, so we redo it here. The small-primes remark. The integers 2, 3, 5 and 7 are prime in 
Z. Let p \in \{2, 3, 5, 7\}. Then p \ge 2. Let d be a positive divisor of p. Then 1 \le d by discreteness (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)) and d \le p by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), so d is one of 1, 2, \dots, p: applying discreteness repeatedly (if d 
e 1 then 2 \le d; if d 
e 2 then 3 \le d; and so on up to p) leaves no other value. For a prime a it is @cor-prime-divides-product (b), which is proved from this lemma, so citing it here is circular. For a general integer a the line is the lemma itself in a weaker form, so citing it is circular again; only special cases are available (for a = \pm 1, a \mid b by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a), with (d) for -1), and the proof must work for every a. Either way the line uses what has not been established, which is (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The distractor (iii′) divides in 
Z, where there is no division: a may be 0 (\gcd(0, 1) = 1), and then the line divides by 0; for a 
e 0, 1/a is not an integer unless a = \pm 1. Divisibility is defined by multiplication (@fd2:def-divides), not by fractions. [B2: The least common multiple] Let a, b \in 
Z_{>0}, and let M \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z_{>0} : a \mid m 	ext{ and } b \mid m \}. Prove that M has a least element L, and that L \mid c for every c \in 
Z with a \mid c and b \mid c. The first part of a proof is given. ab > 0 by (O4), and a \mid ab, b \mid ab, so ab \in M; and 0 is a lower bound of M. By @fd3:prp-integer-least-element, M has a least element L. Let c \in 
Z with a \mid c and b \mid c. By @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a), c = qL + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < L. Since r = c + (-q)L, and a divides c and L, a \mid r (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)); likewise b \mid r. The last step is blank. Name the move, then complete it. The move is least positive element, then divide: the remainder lies in the set and is smaller than its least positive element, so it is not positive. Completion: if r > 0, then r \in 
Z_{>0} is a common multiple of a and b, so r \in M, and r < L, against the choice of L. Hence r = 0 (as r \ge 0), and c = qL, that is, L \mid c. The same argument proved @thm-integers-bezout (b), with the set of positive combinations in place of M. This is the twin of @fd2:exm-divisibility-lcm, now on the constructed 
Z. [B3: Two factorizations and a gcd] Find the prime factorizations of 1001 and of 2^{10} - 1, proving that each entry is prime. Then show that \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 in two ways. First, use the factorizations to write 1001 = 11 \cdot 91 and 1023 = 11 \cdot 93: show \gcd(91, 93) = 1, and deduce \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 from a Bézout identity for 91 and 93 (@cor-coprime-iff-combination). Second, use the Euclidean algorithm. Hint: the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime shortens each primality check. Do not use the school rule “the gcd is the product of the shared primes”: this chapter does not prove it. Factorizations. 1001 = 7 \cdot 143 = 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13, and 2^{10} - 1 = 1024 - 1 = 1023 = 3 \cdot 341 = 3 \cdot 11 \cdot 31. So the prime factorizations are (7, 11, 13) and (3, 11, 31), both non-decreasing, once the entries are known to be prime. The primes 3 and 7 are covered by the small-primes remark above. For 11, 13 and 31 we use the remark after @lem-least-divisor-prime: it suffices that no d \ge 2 with d \cdot d \le p divides p. - p = 11 and p = 13: d \in \{2, 3\}, since d \ge 4 gives d \cdot d \ge 16. The divisions 11 = 5 \cdot 2 + 1 = 3 \cdot 3 + 2 and 13 = 6 \cdot 2 + 1 = 4 \cdot 3 + 1 leave non-zero remainders. - p = 31: d \in \{2, 3, 4, 5\}, since d \ge 6 gives d \cdot d \ge 36. The divisions 31 = 15 \cdot 2 + 1 = 10 \cdot 3 + 1 = 7 \cdot 4 + 3 = 6 \cdot 5 + 1 leave non-zero remainders. A non-zero remainder means d 
mid p, by the uniqueness in @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder (a). By @thm-fundamental-arithmetic these are the only prime factorizations. The gcd from the factorizations. We do not use a rule “the gcd is the product of the shared primes”, which this chapter does not prove. We have 1001 = 11 \cdot 91 and 1023 = 11 \cdot 93. First, \gcd(91, 93) = 1: a common divisor of 91 and 93 divides 93 - 91 = 2 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), so a positive one is 1 or 2 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e) and discreteness), and 2 
mid 91 = 45 \cdot 2 + 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination, 91x + 93y = 1 for some x, y \in 
Z; indeed 91 \cdot 46 - 93 \cdot 45 = 4186 - 4185 = 1. Multiplying by 11, 1001 \cdot 46 - 1023 \cdot 45 = 11 . So every common divisor of 1001 and 1023 divides 11 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), and a positive one is at most 11 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). Since 11 is itself a common divisor, \gcd(1001, 1023) = 11 (@def-integer-gcd). The gcd by the algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers): 1023 = 1 \cdot 1001 + 22, 1001 = 45 \cdot 22 + 11, 22 = 2 \cdot 11 + 0. The last non-zero remainder is 11. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: unique factorization] Prove that two prime factorizations of the same positive integer are equal: the uniqueness half of @thm-fundamental-arithmetic. You may cite @thm-euclid-lemma-integers and @cor-prime-divides-product. The proof of uniqueness in @thm-fundamental-arithmetic is a complete answer. Its steps, in order: set up P(k) for non-decreasing lists of primes of length k and arbitrary length l, with equal products; base case k = 0, where a non-empty list of primes cannot have product 1; in the step, l \ge 1, then p_{k+1} = q_j \le q_l and q_l = p_i \le p_{k+1} by @cor-prime-divides-product (c) (proved from Euclid’s lemma by induction on the length of the product) and the order of the lists; so p_{k+1} = q_l; cancel this non-zero factor (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)); apply P(k) to the shortened lists. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: sets up an induction on the length of one list (or a least counterexample), with the statement quantified over all lengths of the other list, and proves the base case. - 3: shows that the largest (or any chosen) prime of one list divides the other product, and identifies it with an entry of the other list by Euclid’s lemma for products of several factors (cited as @cor-prime-divides-product (c), or proved by induction from Euclid’s lemma). - 2: uses the symmetric step and the non-decreasing order to get equality of the two chosen extreme entries (both largest, or both smallest). - 1: justifies the cancellation by the absence of zero divisors. - 2: applies the induction hypothesis (or minimality) to the shortened lists and concludes equality of length and entries. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using the uniqueness of the factorization of a smaller number without an induction or a least counterexample set up; applying Euclid’s lemma for two factors to a product of many with no induction. Canceling a prime without noting that it is non-zero costs 1 point and is not fatal. A least-counterexample proof on n (the least positive integer with two different factorizations) maps to the same points: its set-up and the case n = 1 take the first 2, and “the cofactor m in n = m p_k has only one factorization” takes the last 2. A proof that compares the smallest entries p_1 = q_1 earns the same points, provided it proves (for example by induction on the length) that a product equals its first entry times the product of the re-indexed list (p_2, \dots, p_{k+1}), and states the re-indexing of the shortened lists (p_2, \dots, p_{k+1}) and (q_2, \dots, q_l) before applying the induction hypothesis; asserting that identity without proof costs the 1 cancellation point. [C2: Find the error] Here is a statement and an argument for it. Claim. Let m, n, c \in 
Z. If m \mid c, n \mid c and \gcd(m, n) = 1, then mn \mid c. Argument. (1) Write c = mk and c = nl with k, l \in 
Z. (2) Then c^2 = c \cdot c = (mk)(nl) = mn \cdot kl. (3) So mn \mid c^2. (4) Hence mn \mid c. Is the claim true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, explain why, and give a counterexample to the step. The claim is true: it is @prp-coprime-divisors-product. The argument does not prove it. Lines (1)–(3) are correct. The failing line is (4). It rests on a general “fact”: x \mid c^2 implies x \mid c. That has not been proved, and it is false, so the line cites nothing: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. A counterexample to the step: x = 4, c = 2, with 4 \mid 4 = c^2 and 4 
mid 2 (a positive divisor of 2 is at most 2, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e)). There is no counterexample to the conclusion, which is true. A sign that something is wrong: the argument never uses \gcd(m, n) = 1, and without that hypothesis the claim is false (4 \mid 12, 6 \mid 12, 24 
mid 12). The repair is the proof of @prp-coprime-divisors-product, which spends the coprimality in Euclid’s lemma. [C3: There is no last prime] Prove that no finite list contains every prime: for every list of primes (p_1, \dots, p_k), with k \in 
N, there is a prime that is not an entry of the list. [Hint 1] Consider N \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i + 1, and ask which primes can divide it. [Hint 2] First prove, by induction on k, that every entry of a list of primes divides its product, and that the product is at least 1. A lemma on products. For a list of primes (p_1, \dots, p_k), write P_j \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{j} p_i for j \le k. We prove, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) on j, the statement “if j \le k, then P_j \ge 1 and p_i \mid P_j for every i \le j”. Base j = 0: P_0 = 1 (the recursion of @def-prime-factorization), and there are no entries to check. Step: let j + 1 \le k; then j \le k, so the statement holds for j, and P_{j+1} = P_j p_{j+1} by the recursion. Each p_i with i \le j divides P_j, which divides P_{j+1}, so p_i \mid P_{j+1} (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (b)); and p_{j+1} \mid P_{j+1} by @fd2:def-divides. Since P_j \ge 1 > 0 and p_{j+1} \ge 2 > 0, P_{j+1} > 0 \cdot p_{j+1} = 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (c), @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so P_{j+1} \ge 1 by discreteness (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (c)). The new prime. Let N \coloneqq P_k + 1. Then N \ge 2, so its least divisor q \ge 2 is prime (@lem-least-divisor-prime), and q \mid N. If q = p_i for some i, then q \mid P_k by the lemma, so q divides N - P_k = 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c)), and q = \pm 1 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g)), against q \ge 2. So q is a prime that is not an entry of the list. For the empty list, N = 2 and q = 2. For (2, 3, 5, 7), N = 211, which happens to be prime; for (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13), N = 30031 = 59 \cdot 509 is not, and the new prime is 59. The proof promises a new prime factor of N, not that N itself is prime. This is the direct proof asked for in part (c) of @fd1:exr-connective-rhetoric-c1, now on the constructed 
Z and including the empty list. Its two school facts are replaced by @lem-least-divisor-prime and @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (c). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines N as the product plus 1 and shows N \ge 2, with a reason that the product is positive. - 2: shows that each p_i divides the product, by an induction or a cited result. - 2: produces a prime factor q of N, citing @lem-least-divisor-prime or an equivalent. - 3: shows q is not any p_i, since it would divide 1. - 1: concludes with the quantifiers in order: for every list there is a prime outside it. Fatal errors (0 for the step): claiming that N is prime; assuming “the set of primes is finite” and taking its product without a list (no list, no product).

title: 1.3 Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n
content:
Ideals, Quotient Rings, and the Integers Modulo n Sets and Functions, Section 5.2 turned the school integers into a clock, 
Z/n, and checked by hand that its sum and product are well defined (@fd2:prp-congruence-arithmetic). Number Systems, Chapters 2 and 3 made the same kind of check twice more, for 
Z and for 
Q, each time through @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes and a computation special to the formula. This section makes the check once, for every commutative ring and every subset of the right kind, called an ideal. The integers modulo n, now a ring, are the first example. Number Systems, Chapter 5 builds 
R in the same shape, from classes of Cauchy sequences of rationals that differ by a null sequence, and checks its operations there directly; Chapter 5 runs division with remainder, gcd and unique factorization again for polynomials over a field. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), with a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). What a quotient needs Let I \subseteq R, and call a and b related when they differ by an element of I: a \sim_I b \quad :\Longleftrightarrow \quad a - b \in I . For R = 
Z and I the multiples of n, this is congruence modulo n. We want two things: \sim_I should be an equivalence relation, and the sum and product of classes should be computable on representatives. Each wish makes a demand on I. - Reflexivity, a - a \in I, needs 0 \in I. - Symmetry: b - a = -(a - b), so it needs I to be closed under negatives. - Transitivity: a - c = (a - b) + (b - c), so it needs I to be closed under sums. - The sum on classes. Changing a to a' changes a + b to a' + b, and the difference is a - a' again: no new demand. - The product on classes. Changing a to a' changes ab to a'b, and the difference is (a - a')b: an element of I multiplied by an arbitrary element of R. So I must swallow such products. The last demand contains the second: -x = (-1)x. Three clauses remain, and they get a name. An ideal is a set of allowed errors: it contains 0, it is closed under adding errors, and an error multiplied by anything is still an error. [Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring. A subset I \subseteq R is an ideal of R if 1. 0 \in I; 2. for all a, b \in I, a + b \in I; 3. for all a \in I and all r \in R, ra \in I. In words: (I1) and (I2) say that I contains 0 and is closed under addition; (I3), absorption, says that multiplying an element of I by any element of the ring, inside I or not, lands in I. The ring element r in (I3) ranges over all of R, and that is what separates (I3) from mere closure under multiplication, where r would have to lie in I. Two consequences are used constantly. First, an ideal is closed under negatives and differences: for a \in I, -a = (-1)a \in I by (I3), since (-1)a = -(1 \cdot a) = -a by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) and (F7) with (F6); then a - b = a + (-b) \in I for a, b \in I, by (I2). Second, if 1 \in I, then I = R, since every r = r \cdot 1 \in I by (I3). Examples. - The degenerate cases: \{0\} and R itself are ideals of R. For \{0\}: 0 + 0 = 0 and r \cdot 0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). For R, every clause asks for an element of R. They are the two extremes: “no error allowed” and “everything allowed”. - For n \in 
Z, the multiples n
Z = \{ kn : k \in 
Z \} form an ideal of 
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations): 0 = 0 \cdot n; kn + ln = (k + l)n; r(kn) = (rk)n. In particular the even integers 2
Z form an ideal. - For a, b \in 
Z, the combinations a
Z + b
Z form an ideal of 
Z, by the closure properties in @def-integer-linear-combinations; @thm-integer-ideals-principal below records this. Non-examples by minimal change. 
N \subseteq 
Z satisfies (I1) and (I2), but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = -1: (-1) \cdot 1 = -1 
otin 
N, since -1 < 0 (1 > 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), as 1 
e 0 in 
Z by @fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring, then (a)) while 
N = \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring (b)). And 
Z \subseteq 
Q satisfies (I1), (I2) and is even closed under negatives and products, but (I3) fails at a = 1, r = 1/2: (1/2) \cdot 1 = 1/2 
otin 
Z. (If 1/2 = m \in 
Z, then 2m = 1, but 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 is odd and so not of the form 2m, by @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a).) In both cases the ring element r comes from outside the subset, which is exactly what (I3) allows. Why these clauses. Each clause was forced by one of the five wishes above, and dropping one loses its wish: without (I1) or (I2), \sim_I is not reflexive or not transitive; without (I3), the product on classes can fail, as the warning after the next theorem shows for 
Z \subseteq 
Q. The quotient ring The payoff is a single theorem that builds a ring of classes from any ideal. We write [a], or [a]_I when the ideal must be named, for the class of a under \sim_I, and R/I for the quotient set R/{\sim_I} (@fd2:def-quotient-set). [Quotient Ring by an Ideal] Let R be a commutative ring and I an ideal of R. 1. Setting a \sim_I b \iff a - b \in I defines an equivalence relation \sim_I on R, and the class of a is [a] = a + I \coloneqq \{ a + x : x \in I \}. 2. The rules [a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b], [a] \cdot [b] \coloneqq [ab] and -[a] \coloneqq [-a] are well defined on R/I \coloneqq R/{\sim_I}. 3. R/I, with these operations, is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The quotient map \pi \colon R 	o R/I, \pi(a) \coloneqq [a], satisfies \pi(a + b) = \pi(a) + \pi(b), \pi(ab) = \pi(a) \pi(b) and \pi(1) = [1]. 4. [a] = [0] if and only if a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] if and only if I = R. In words: (a) and (b) say that classes modulo an ideal can be added, multiplied and negated through any representatives; (c) says that the result obeys every ring law, and that passing to classes respects the operations; (d) says that the elements of I are exactly those that become 0, and that the quotient collapses to the zero ring exactly when I is everything. A change of representative is an element of I. The equivalence-relation clauses ask that such changes can be reversed and chained, which is closure under negatives and sums. The operations ask that a change in one argument produce a change in the output: for the sum the change is the same element of I, and for the product it is that element multiplied by the other argument, which (I3) keeps in I. The ring laws are then laws of R read on classes. Before reading on: where is “ra \in I for every r \in R” used, and why does closure under + not suffice for the product? (a) Let a, b, c \in R. (Eq1): a - a = 0 \in I, by (F4) and (I1). (Eq2): if a - b \in I, then b - a = -(a - b) \in I, since I is closed under negatives; here (a - b) + (b - a) = 0 by (F1)–(F4), so b - a = -(a - b) by the uniqueness of negatives (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). (Eq3): if a - b \in I and b - c \in I, then a - c = (a - b) + (b - c) \in I, by (F2)–(F4) and (I2). So \sim_I is an equivalence relation (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation). For the class: if x \sim_I a, then x - a \in I and x = a + (x - a) \in a + I; conversely, for y \in I, (a + y) - a = y \in I, so a + y \sim_I a. Hence [a] = a + I. (b) We check the hypotheses of @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes (b), with X = R and the relation \sim_I, for the maps (a, b) \mapsto a + b and (a, b) \mapsto ab. Let a \sim_I a', so a - a' \in I, and let b \in R. Then  egin{aligned} (a + b) - (a' + b) &= a - a' \in I , \ ab - a'b &= (a - a')b = b(a - a') \in I , \end{aligned} by (F1)–(F4) in the first line, and by (F9), (F6) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c) in the second, where the membership is (I3) with r = b: the ideal absorbs b. This is the first hypothesis. Since a + b = b + a and ab = ba ((F1), (F6)), the second hypothesis is the first with the two arguments exchanged. For the negative we check the hypothesis of @fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes (a) for a \mapsto -a: (-a) - (-a') = -(a - a') \in I, by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a) and closure under negatives. Hence the three rules define functions. (c) Every element of R/I is a class [a] (@fd2:def-quotient-set). Each axiom of @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field other than (F8) is an equation, and by (b) both of its sides, read on classes, are the classes of the two sides of the same equation in R. For example, for (F9), [a] igl([b] + [c] igr) = [a][b + c] = [a(b + c)] = [ab + ac] = [ab] + [ac] = [a][b] + [a][c] , using (F9) in R in the middle; for (F3), [a] + [0] = [a + 0] = [a]; for (F4), [a] + (-[a]) = [a] + [-a] = [a + (-a)] = [0]; for (F7), [a][1] = [a \cdot 1] = [a]. The laws (F1), (F2), (F5) and (F6) go the same way. So R/I is a commutative ring with zero [0] and one [1]. The equations for \pi are the definitions in (b) read from right to left, and \pi(1) = [1] by definition of \pi. (d) [a] = [0] holds if and only if a \sim_I 0 (@fd2:thm-classes-partition (b)), that is, a - 0 \in I; and a - 0 = a + 0 = a, since -0 = 0 (0 + 0 = 0 and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a)). So [a] = [0] \iff a \in I. In particular [1] = [0] \iff 1 \in I. If 1 \in I, then I = R, since r = r \cdot 1 \in I for every r \in R by (I3); and if I = R, then 1 \in I. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Absorption with an arbitrary r \in R, the full force of (I3), is used exactly once in the proof of (a) and (b): in the product, at ab - a'b = (a - a')b, where the change of representative a - a' \in I is multiplied by an arbitrary b \in R. Elsewhere (I3) enters only with r = -1, through closure under negatives (-x = (-1)x), and otherwise the proof uses (I1) and (I2). Closure under + does not suffice for the product because b need not lie in I: the product changes by a multiple of the error, not by a sum of errors. We call this move compute on representatives; the ideal absorbs the change. It is the move of Number Systems, Chapter 2’s “one argument at a time”, now with the change of representative recorded as one element of I. Closure under + and - is not enough for the product. 
Z \subseteq 
Q contains 0 and is closed under sums and negatives, and these are all that the proof of (a) and of the sum and negative in (b) used. So “x - y \in 
Z” relates rationals by an equivalence relation, and [x] + [y] \coloneqq [x + y] is well defined on its classes. But [x][y] \coloneqq [xy] is not: [1/2] = [3/2], since 3/2 - 1/2 = 1 \in 
Z, while 	frac12 \cdot 	frac12 = 	frac14 , \qquad 	frac32 \cdot 	frac12 = 	frac34 , \qquad 	frac34 - 	frac14 = 	frac12 
otin 
Z . One class, two products in different classes. The missing clause is (I3): 
Z is not an ideal of 
Q. The ideals of the integers In 
Z every ideal is as simple as possible: the multiples of one number. The proof is the move that gave the gcd in Section 1.1. [Ideals of the Integers] 1. For all a, b \in 
Z, a
Z + b

Z. 2. Every ideal I of

N: n = 0 if I = \{0\}, and otherwise n is the least positive element of I. For (b), take the least positive element n of I. Its multiples lie in I by absorption. Conversely, divide any a \in I by n: the remainder a - qn lies in I and is smaller than n, so it is not positive, and it is 0. This is least positive element, then divide once more. Z_{>0}. The ring 
Z/n

Z (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal, @thm-integer-ideals-principal (a)). Its relation is congruence modulo n of @fd2:def-congruence, read on the constructed

title: 1.4 Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem

Units, Prime Moduli, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem Section 1.3 made 
Z/n
Z a commutative ring, and @exm-integers-mod-six put two of these rings side by side. In 
Z/5
Z every non-zero class has a partner whose product with it is [1], so we may divide by it. In 
Z/6
Z the class [2] has no such partner: the products [2][x] are only [0], [2], [4]. Which classes can be divided by, and for which moduli can all non-zero classes? This section answers both questions with the gcd of Section 1.1, and finds a field with p elements for every prime p. It then solves two congruences at once, the Chinese remainder theorem, by the move of Section 1.2, multiply the Bézout identity: write 1 as a combination and multiply. Throughout, n \in 
Z_{>0} and classes are taken in 
Z/n
Z unless another modulus is named. Two classes are equal exactly when their representatives are congruent: [u] = [v] \iff u - v \in n
Z \iff n \mid u - v . The first equivalence is @fd2:thm-classes-partition (b) for the relation of @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (a); the second is the definition of n
Z (@def-integer-linear-combinations) read with @fd2:def-divides. We call it the class test. Products of classes are computed on representatives, [u][v] = [uv] (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (b)). Units of a commutative ring In 
Z/6
Z the equation [2][x] = [1] has no solution, while [5][x] = [1] has the solution [x] = [5]. The elements that can be divided by are the ones that solve “u times something is 1”, and they deserve a name in every commutative ring at once. A unit is an element that has a multiplicative inverse in the ring itself. [Unit of a Commutative Ring] Let R be a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field). An element u \in R is a unit of R if there exists v \in R with uv = 1. The set of units of R is written R^{	imes}. For a unit u, the element v is unique; it is written u^{-1} and called the inverse of u. In words: u is a unit when the equation ux = 1 can be solved inside R. The definition asks for one solution; it does not ask u to be non-zero. Well-definedness of u^{-1}. Let uv = 1 and uv' = 1. Then, by (F7), (F5) and (F6), v = v \cdot 1 = v(uv') = (vu)v' = (uv)v' = 1 \cdot v' = v' . So the inverse is unique, and the notation u^{-1} names one element. Closure. The element 1 is a unit, since 1 \cdot 1 = 1. If u is a unit, so is u^{-1}, with (u^{-1})^{-1} = u, because u^{-1} u = u u^{-1} = 1 by (F6). If u and w are units, then (uw)(u^{-1} w^{-1}) = (u u^{-1})(w w^{-1}) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 , reordering the four factors by (F5) and (F6); so uw is a unit and (uw)^{-1} = u^{-1} w^{-1}, by uniqueness. A unit is not a zero divisor. If u is a unit and ux = 0, then x = (u^{-1} u) x = u^{-1}(ux) = u^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0 , by u^{-1} u = 1 (above) and 1 \cdot x = x \cdot 1 = x ((F6), (F7)) in the first equality, (F5) in the second, and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) in the third. So a unit times a non-zero element is never 0. Examples. - The integers. 
Z^{	imes} = \{ 1, -1 \}. Indeed 1 \cdot 1 = 1 and (-1)(-1) = 1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (c)). Conversely, uv = 1 says u \mid 1, so u = 1 or u = -1 by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (g). - The rationals. 
Q^{	imes} = 
Q \setminus \{0\}: every non-zero rational has an inverse by (F8) (@fd3:thm-rationals-field), and 0 is not a unit, since 0 \cdot v = 0 
e 1 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). - The integers modulo six. By the multiplication table of @exm-integers-mod-six, the units of 
Z/6
Z are [1] and [5], and [5]^{-1} = [5]. - The zero ring \{0\} of Number Systems, Section 2.3, where 1 = 0. Here 0 \cdot 0 = 0 = 1, so 0 is a unit and R^{	imes} = R. This degenerate case is why “every non-zero element is a unit” is not by itself the definition of a field. A non-example by minimal change. Change 5 to 2 in the third example. The class [2] \in 
Z/6
Z is non-zero, like [5], but [2][3] = [6] = [0]: it is a zero divisor, so by the paragraph above it is not a unit. Concretely, the clause “there exists v with uv = 1” fails: the products [2][x] for x = 0, \dots, 5 are [0], [2], [4], [0], [2], [4], and [1] is not among them. Why this definition. With units, the field axiom (F8) reads: every non-zero element is a unit. So a field (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field) is exactly a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 in which R^{	imes} = R \setminus \{0\}; when 1 
e 0, the element 0 is never a unit, since 0 \cdot v = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)). The definition asks for an inverse in R, not in some bigger ring: 2 \in 
Z has the inverse 1/2 in 
Q, and it is still not a unit of 
Z. “Non-zero and not a zero divisor” does not make an element a unit. In 
Z there are no zero divisors at all (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f)), yet 2 is not a unit, since 2 
mid 1. The paragraph above proves only one direction: a unit is never a zero divisor. So “not a unit” must be checked against the definition, or, in 
Z/n
Z, by the next theorem. The units of a commutative ring are closed under products and inverses and contain 1: they form what Chapter 3 calls a group. Here we only need to find them in 
Z/n
Z. Which classes are units In 
Z/6
Z the units [1] and [5] are the classes of the integers coprime to 6, and the non-units [0], [2], [3], [4] share a factor with 6. The equation [a][x] = [1] says n \mid ax - 1, that is, ax + ny = 1 for some integer y: a Bézout identity. So the question is answered by Section 1.1. [Units Modulo n] Let n \in 
Z_{>0} and a \in 
Z. Then [a] is a unit of 
Z/n
Z if and only if \gcd(a, n) = 1. In that case, for any x, y \in 
Z with ax + ny = 1, [a]^{-1} = [x]. Both directions translate between one equation in 
Z/n
Z and one equation in 
Z. A solution of [a][x] = [1] is an integer combination ax + ny = 1, and @cor-coprime-iff-combination says that such a combination exists exactly when \gcd(a, n) = 1. The class test does the translation. (\Leftarrow) Suppose \gcd(a, n) = 1. By @cor-coprime-iff-combination there are x, y \in 
Z with ax + ny = 1. Let x, y be any such pair. Then ax - 1 = -ny = (-y)n, so n \mid ax - 1, and by the class test [ax] = [1]. Hence [a][x] = [ax] = [1], where the first equality is the definition of the product on classes (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal (b)). So [a] is a unit, and [x] is its inverse, which is unique (@def-ring-unit); thus [a]^{-1} = [x] for every such pair. (\Rightarrow) Suppose [a] is a unit. Every element of 
Z/n
Z is the class of an integer (@fd2:def-quotient-set), so [a][x] = [1] for some x \in 
Z. Then [ax] = [1], so n \mid ax - 1 by the class test: ax - 1 = yn for some y \in 
Z. Hence ax + n(-y) = 1, and \gcd(a, n) = 1 by @cor-coprime-iff-combination. This proves the theorem. The theorem turns “is [a] invertible?” into a gcd, and the Euclidean algorithm (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers) computes the gcd. Back-substitution, as in @exm-euclidean-algorithm-run, then produces the x with ax + ny = 1, and with it the inverse. Whether \gcd(a, n) = 1 depends only on the class [a], since by the theorem it is equivalent to a statement about [a]; so any representative may be used. [Inverting a class modulo sixty] Decide whether [17] and [12] are units of 
Z/60
Z, and find the inverse of each one that is. The class [17]. Run the Euclidean algorithm on (60, 17):  egin{aligned} 60 &= 3 \cdot 17 + 9 , & 17 &= 1 \cdot 9 + 8 , \ 9 &= 1 \cdot 8 + 1 , & 8 &= 8 \cdot 1 + 0 . \end{aligned} The last non-zero remainder is 1, so \gcd(60, 17) = 1 (@thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers (c)), and [17] is a unit by @thm-units-mod-n.
