R, Chapter 6’s @fd3:prp-cof-map-fixes-rationals. The uniqueness half of the theorem is a rigidity statement. It says that a homomorphism has no choice on the prime subfield, and the next corollary spells this out. [Homomorphisms Respect the Prime Subfield] 1. Let \varphi \colon F 	o L be a homomorphism. Then \varphi \circ \iota_F = \iota_L, and \varphi maps the prime subfield of F onto the prime subfield of L. 2. The identity is the only homomorphism 
Q 	o 
Q, and the only homomorphism 
F_p 	o 
F_p for each prime p. In particular the only automorphism of 
Q, and of 
F_p, is the identity. 3. Every automorphism of a field F fixes each element of the prime subfield of F. (a) By @prp-characteristic-invariant (b), \operatorname{char} F = \operatorname{char} L, so \iota_F and \iota_L have the same domain D, which is 
Q or 
F_p by @thm-prime-subfield. The composite \varphi \circ \iota_F \colon D 	o L is a homomorphism (@prp-field-homomorphism-properties (e)), so it equals \iota_L by the uniqueness clause of @thm-prime-subfield. Hence \varphi(\iota_F(D)) = \iota_L(D), and by @thm-prime-subfield these images are the prime subfields of F and of L. (b) The identity \id_{
Q} is a homomorphism (@prp-field-homomorphism-properties (e)), and \operatorname{char} 
Q = 0 (@exm-characteristics), so by the uniqueness clause of @thm-prime-subfield (b) with F = 
Q, every homomorphism 
Q 	o 
Q equals \id_{
Q}. Likewise for 
F_p, using \operatorname{char} 
F_p = p and part (a) of the theorem. An automorphism is a homomorphism, so it is the identity. (c) Let \sigma be an automorphism of F. By (a) with L = F, \sigma \circ \iota_F = \iota_F, so \sigma(x) = x for every x = \iota_F(d) in the image of \iota_F, which is the prime subfield. This proves the corollary. For instance, complex conjugation fixes every rational number, and the automorphisms of 
Q(\sqrt 2) and of 
Q(i) in Section 2.4 had no choice on 
Q; only the images of \sqrt 2 and of i were free. Finite fields are the case that matters most for computation, and for them the characteristic cannot be 0. [A Finite Field Has Prime Characteristic] Let F be a finite field. 1. \operatorname{char} F is a prime p. 2. F contains a subfield isomorphic to 
F_p, namely its prime subfield. 3. p \cdot a = 0 for every a \in F. (a) Say F has N elements (@fd2:def-finite). Suppose \operatorname{char} F = 0, and consider f \colon \{1, \dots, N + 1\} 	o F, f(k) \coloneqq k \cdot 1. If k \cdot 1 = k' \cdot 1, then (k - k') \cdot 1 = 0 (@lem-integer-multiples (d)), so 0 \mid k - k' by @prp-characteristic-divides (a), hence k - k' = 0 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)) and k = k'. So f is an injection from a set with N + 1 elements into a set with N elements, which @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) forbids. Hence \operatorname{char} F 
e 0, and \operatorname{char} F is a prime by @thm-characteristic-prime. (b) is @thm-prime-subfield (a). (c) By @lem-integer-multiples (c), p \cdot a = (p \cdot 1) a = 0 \cdot a = 0, using @thm-field-basic-properties (d). This proves the corollary. A finite field therefore contains one of the fields 
F_p of Section 2.2. One can show that it has p^n elements for some n \ge 1; that needs the vector spaces of the linear-algebra volumes, and nothing in this volume uses it. Can a field with 6 elements contain a copy of 
F_2 and also a copy of 
F_3? No. A copy of 
F_2 is a subfield K with \operatorname{char} K = 2, and a copy of 
F_3 a subfield with characteristic 3 (@exm-characteristics, @prp-characteristic-invariant (b) for the isomorphisms). By @prp-characteristic-invariant (a) both characteristics equal \operatorname{char} F, and 2 
e 3. (In fact no field has 6 elements, but that is the p^n fact just mentioned, which we do not prove.) Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about the proof of @thm-prime-subfield. 1. In the proof of part (b), where is the hypothesis \operatorname{char} F = 0 used, and where is it not needed? 2. Try to define 
Q 	o 
F_5 by m/n \mapsto [m][n]^{-1} (n > 0). Name a rational number that has no image, and explain why the rule also fails to be well defined. 3. What are \iota_{
R} and \iota_{
C}? Justify your answer from the uniqueness clause. 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. (a) Only in the step “the formula makes sense”: n \cdot 1 
e 0 for n > 0 (@prp-characteristic-divides (a)), so (n \cdot 1)^{-1} exists. Well-definedness, the homomorphism property, the image and uniqueness are computations in an arbitrary field once these inverses exist. (b) 1/5: its image would be [1][5]^{-1}, and [5] = [0] has no inverse. The rule is not even well defined on the rationals where it seems to make sense: 1 = 1/1 = 5/5, and the representative (5, 5) gives [5][5]^{-1}, which does not exist, while (1, 1) gives [1]. (c) Both are inclusions. 
Q is a subfield of 
R and 
R of 
C (@exm-subfields-gaussian (iii)), so 
Q is a subfield of 
C, and the inclusion of a subfield is a homomorphism (@exm-complex-conjugation-automorphism (ii)). By the uniqueness clause of @thm-prime-subfield (b) (both fields have characteristic 0, @exm-characteristics), \iota_{
R} and \iota_{
C} are these inclusions, q \mapsto q. (d) A homomorphism out of 
Q or 
F_p is forced by 1 \mapsto 1 to send m/n to (m \cdot 1)(n \cdot 1)^{-1} (or [n] to n \cdot 1), so there is at most one, and its image lies in every subfield. The characteristic decides whether this forced formula makes sense, and when it does, the fraction rules show it is a homomorphism, whose image is then the prime subfield. B. Practice [B1: Reducing multiples] Let F be a field of characteristic p > 0 and a \in F. 1. Show that (p - 1) \cdot a = -a. 2. Show that (kp + r) \cdot a = r \cdot a for all k, r \in 
Z. 3. In 
F_7, compute 100 \cdot [3] directly, and again using (b). (a) By @lem-integer-multiples (d) and (c), (p - 1) \cdot a + a = (p - 1) \cdot a + 1 \cdot a = p \cdot a = (p \cdot 1) a = 0 \cdot a = 0, using @thm-field-basic-properties (d). By uniqueness of negatives (@thm-field-basic-properties (c)), (p - 1) \cdot a = -a. (b) By @lem-integer-multiples (d), (kp + r) \cdot a = (kp) \cdot a + r \cdot a = k \cdot (p \cdot a) + r \cdot a. Now p \cdot a = 0 as in (a), and k \cdot 0 = (k \cdot 1) 0 = 0 by @lem-integer-multiples (c) with (d) and @thm-field-basic-properties (d). So (kp + r) \cdot a = 0 + r \cdot a = r \cdot a. (c) Directly: 100 \cdot [3] = (100 \cdot [1])[3] = [100][3] = [300] (@lem-integer-multiples (c), @thm-integers-mod-n-ring (d)), and 300 = 42 \cdot 7 + 6, so 100 \cdot [3] = [6]. By (b): 100 = 14 \cdot 7 + 2, so 100 \cdot [3] = 2 \cdot [3] = [6]. The two agree. [B2: Completing the square] Let F be a field with \operatorname{char} F 
e 2, and write 2 \coloneqq 2 \cdot 1, 4 \coloneqq 4 \cdot 1. 1. Show that x = -x implies x = 0, for x \in F. 2. Let b, c \in F. Show that the equation x^2 + bx + c = 0 has a solution x \in F if and only if b^2 - 4c = s^2 for some s \in F, and that then its solutions are exactly x = (-b + s)/2 and x = (-b - s)/2. 3. Use (b) to solve x^2 + x + 1 = 0 in 
F_7. 4. Explain why (b) says nothing in 
F_2, and show that its conclusion is in fact false there. By @prp-characteristic-divides (b), 2 
e 0, so 2 is invertible; and 4 = (2 \cdot 2) \cdot 1 = 2 \cdot 2 
e 0 by @lem-integer-multiples (b) and @thm-field-basic-properties (f). For u \in F, 2u = (2 \cdot 1)u = u + u by @lem-integer-multiples (c). (a) If x = -x, then 2x = x + x = x + (-x) = 0. Since 2 
e 0, x = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f). (b) Since 4 
e 0, x^2 + bx + c = 0 if and only if 4(x^2 + bx + c) = 0 (one direction by @thm-field-basic-properties (d) and (F6), the other by (f)). By @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d), (2x + b)^2 = (2x)^2 + 2(2x)b + b^2 = 4x^2 + 4bx + b^2, the products of the multiples regrouped by @lem-integer-multiples (b), (F5) and (F6). Hence, with D \coloneqq b^2 - 4c, 4(x^2 + bx + c) = (2x + b)^2 - D , and the equation is equivalent to (2x + b)^2 = D. (Multiplying this identity by 4^{-1} gives the familiar x^2 + bx + c = (x + b/2)^2 - D/4.) If x is a solution, s \coloneqq 2x + b has s^2 = D. Conversely, if s^2 = D, then by @cor-field-squares-equal, (2x + b)^2 = s^2 if and only if 2x + b = s or 2x + b = -s, and by @prp-field-linear-equation (a) (with 2 
e 0) these say x = (-b + s)/2 or x = (-b - s)/2. (c) Here b = c = 1 and D = 1 - 4 = -3 = 4 = 2^2 in 
F_7, so s = 2; and 2^{-1} = 4, since 2 \cdot 4 = 8 = 1. The solutions are x = 4(-1 + 2) = 4 and x = 4(-1 - 2) = -12 = 2. Check: 4^2 + 4 + 1 = 21 = 0 and 2^2 + 2 + 1 = 7 = 0 in 
F_7. This agrees with @exr-finite-fields-from-modular-arithmetic-c3, found there by trying all seven elements. (d) In 
F_2, 2 = 0 and 4 = 0, so the first step, “x^2 + bx + c = 0 iff 4(\dots) = 0”, fails, and /2 has no meaning. The conclusion of (b) is false there: for x^2 + x + 1 = 0, D = 1 - 0 = 1 = 1^2 is a square, yet the equation has no solution, since x = 0 and x = 1 both give 1. [B3: When the integers embed] Let F be a field. 1. Show that for n, n' \in 
Z, n \cdot 1 = n' \cdot 1 if and only if \operatorname{char} F \mid n - n'. 2. Deduce that the map 
Z 	o F, n \mapsto n \cdot 1, is injective if \operatorname{char} F = 0, and is not injective if \operatorname{char} F = p > 0. (a) By @lem-integer-multiples (d), n \cdot 1 - n' \cdot 1 = (n - n') \cdot 1. So n \cdot 1 = n' \cdot 1 iff (n - n') \cdot 1 = 0, iff \operatorname{char} F \mid n - n' by @prp-characteristic-divides (a). (b) If \operatorname{char} F = 0 and n \cdot 1 = n' \cdot 1, then 0 \mid n - n' by (a), so n - n' = 0 (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)) and n = n'. If \operatorname{char} F = p > 0, then p \cdot 1 = 0 = 0 \cdot 1 with p 
e 0, so the map is not injective. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the characteristic] Using only @def-characteristic, @lem-integer-multiples, division with remainder in 
Z, @fd2:def-prime and the rules for divisibility in 
Z (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers), and the field axioms with @thm-field-basic-properties, prove: 1. for a field F and n \in 
Z, n \cdot 1 = 0 if and only if \operatorname{char} F \mid n; 2. \operatorname{char} F is 0 or a prime. (a) Let c \coloneqq \operatorname{char} F. Case c = 0. No positive n has n \cdot 1 = 0, by @def-characteristic. For n < 0, n \cdot 1 = -((-n) \cdot 1), and (-n) \cdot 1 
e 0; since -x = 0 implies x = -(-x) = 0, also n \cdot 1 
e 0. And 0 \cdot 1 = 0. So n \cdot 1 = 0 iff n = 0, iff 0 \mid n (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a)). Case c > 0. Divide: n = qc + r with q, r \in 
Z, 0 \le r < c (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder). By @lem-integer-multiples (d), (qc) \cdot 1 = (q \cdot 1)(c \cdot 1) = (q \cdot 1) 0 = 0 and n \cdot 1 = (qc) \cdot 1 + r \cdot 1 = r \cdot 1. If c \mid n, then r = 0 by uniqueness of the remainder, so n \cdot 1 = 0 \cdot 1 = 0. If n \cdot 1 = 0, then r \cdot 1 = 0 with 0 \le r < c; r > 0 would contradict the minimality of c, so r = 0 and c \mid n. (b) Let c > 0. As 1 \cdot 1 = 1 
e 0, c \ge 2. If c were not prime, by @fd2:def-prime it would have a positive divisor r 
otin \{1, c\}; write c = rs. Then s > 0, r, s \le c by @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (e), and s 
otin \{1, c\}, since s = 1 gives r = c and s = c gives r = 1 (cancel c 
e 0). So 1 < r, s < c, and (r \cdot 1)(s \cdot 1) = (rs) \cdot 1 = 0 by @lem-integer-multiples (b), so r \cdot 1 = 0 or s \cdot 1 = 0 (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)), contradicting the minimality of c. So c is prime. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the case c = 0, including negative n (a negative multiple is the negative of a non-zero element, hence non-zero). - 3: division of n by c with remainder, and n \cdot 1 = r \cdot 1 justified by the rules for multiples and c \cdot 1 = 0. - 2: minimality of c forces r = 0; the converse c \mid n \Rightarrow n \cdot 1 = 0. - 1: c 
e 1 from 1 
e 0. - 2: a factorization c = rs with 1 < r, s < c, bounds justified, gives (r \cdot 1)(s \cdot 1) = 0, and the absence of zero divisors contradicts minimality. Fatal errors (0 for the step): “c \cdot 1 = 0, so c \mid n” for every n with n \cdot 1 = 0, without the division step; treating n \cdot 1 as the integer n (for instance “n \cdot 1 = 0, so n = 0” in 
F_p). [C2: Find the error] Here is an argument. Claim. A finite field F has prime characteristic. Proof. (1) The elements 1 \cdot 1, 2 \cdot 1, 3 \cdot 1, \dots of F cannot all be different, since F is finite. (2) So m \cdot 1 = k \cdot 1 for some positive integers k < m. (3) Hence (m - k) \cdot 1 = m \cdot 1 - k \cdot 1 = 0. (4) So m - k is the characteristic of F, and it is prime by @thm-characteristic-prime. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? Name the failing step, say what is wrong with it, and give a counterexample to the step. The conclusion is true: it is @cor-finite-field-prime-characteristic (a). Steps (1) and (2) are correct (they are the pigeonhole argument of that proof, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets), and so is step (3), by @lem-integer-multiples (d). Step (4) fails. Step (4). The argument only produces some positive integer with a vanishing multiple. The characteristic is the least one (@def-characteristic), and m - k need not be least: in 
F_3, 7 \cdot 1 = 1 = 1 \cdot 1 gives m - k = 6, while \operatorname{char} 
F_3 = 3. The step cites a property, “is the characteristic”, that no line supplies, which is (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. Repair. By (2) and @lem-integer-multiples (d), (m - k) \cdot 1 = 0 with m - k > 0, so the set of positive integers with a vanishing multiple is non-empty and \operatorname{char} F > 0 (@def-characteristic); then @thm-characteristic-prime makes it prime. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: the conclusion is true, with the reference. - 2: steps (1)–(3) are correct (including (m - k) \cdot 1 = 0 via @lem-integer-multiples (d)). - 6: step (4) named: only some positive multiple vanishes, the characteristic is the least one (@def-characteristic), with a counterexample to the step. [C3: The four-element field] Let F = \{0, 1, \alpha,  eta\} be the four-element field of @exr-finite-fields-from-modular-arithmetic-c1, with  eta = 1 + \alpha, \alpha^2 =  eta and \alpha eta = 1. 1. Show that \operatorname{char} F = 2. 2. Show that the prime subfield of F is \{0, 1\}, and that it is isomorphic to 
F_2. 3. Show that the map F 	o F, x \mapsto x^2, is an automorphism of F that exchanges \alpha and  eta. (a) 1 \cdot 1 = 1 
e 0, and 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = (1 + 1) + (0 + 0)\alpha = 0 by the addition rule of @exr-finite-fields-from-modular-arithmetic-c1, coefficient by coefficient in 
F_2. So \operatorname{char} F = 2. (b) By @thm-prime-subfield (a), the prime subfield is the image of \iota_F \colon 
F_2 	o F, which is \{0 \cdot 1, 1 \cdot 1\} = \{0, 1\}, and \iota_F is an isomorphism from 
F_2 onto it. (c) Let s(x) \coloneqq x^2. For x, y \in F, (x + y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (d), where 2xy = (1 + 1)(xy) = 0\,(xy) = 0, since 1 + 1 = 2 \cdot 1 = 0 by part (a) and 0\,(xy) = 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (d); so s(x + y) = s(x) + s(y). Next (xy)^2 = (xy)(xy) = (xx)(yy) = x^2 y^2 by (F5) and (F6), and 1^2 = 1. So s is a homomorphism (@def-field-homomorphism). Its values are s(0) = 0 , \quad s(1) = 1 , \quad s(\alpha) = \alpha^2 =  eta , \quad s( eta) = (1 + \alpha)^2 = 1 + \alpha^2 = 1 +  eta = \alpha , using the additivity just proved and 1 +  eta = 1 + 1 + \alpha = \alpha. So s permutes the four elements, is bijective, and is an automorphism exchanging \alpha and  eta. (The next section shows that x \mapsto x^p is a homomorphism in every field of characteristic p, and an automorphism when the field is finite.)

title: 2.6 The Binomial Theorem, the Frobenius Map, and Fermat's Little Theorem
content:
The Binomial Theorem, the Frobenius Map, and Fermat’s Little Theorem In 
F_5, compute (1 + 2)^5 and 1^5 + 2^5. The first is 3^5 = 243, and 243 = 48 \cdot 5 + 3, so it is 3. The second is 1 + 32 = 33 = 6 \cdot 5 + 3, so it is 3 as well. The rule “(x + y)^n = x^n + y^n”, the classic error of school algebra, is a theorem when n is the characteristic p of the field. This section proves it, and deduces Fermat’s little theorem from it with the rigidity of Section 2.5: a homomorphism of 
F_p to itself is the identity. The tool is the binomial theorem. School proves it for numbers; we need it in an arbitrary commutative ring, with the binomial coefficients acting as integer multiples, and so we first set up finite sums in a ring. Sums and powers in a commutative ring Sets and Functions, Chapter 3 defines finite sums, products and powers of real numbers by recursion (@fd2:def-sum-product, @fd2:def-power, both from @fd2:thm-recursion). The definitions use nothing about 
R except an addition with a 0 and a multiplication with a 1. So, read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b), with X = R, they define in every commutative ring R: - sums \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k of elements a_k \in R, with the empty sum 0, and the three remarks after @fd2:def-sum-product: a sum depends only on the terms it adds (finite lists), shifting the index, and splitting off the last term, \sum_{k=m}^{n+1} a_k = \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1} for m \le n + 1; - powers x^0 \coloneqq 1, x^{n+1} \coloneqq x^n x for x \in R and n \in 
N, with the laws of @fd2:prp-power-laws (a)–(c): x^{m+n} = x^m x^n , \qquad (x^m)^n = x^{mn} , \qquad (xy)^n = x^n y^n . The proofs of those laws in Sets and Functions use only (F1)–(F7), (F9) and induction, so they run unchanged in R. We use this paragraph as a template and do not repeat it. (Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 proves the same power laws for every commutative ring as @fd4:prp-power-laws-commutative-ring; we compare, and cite the template.) In particular 1^n = 1 for every n, by induction: 1^0 = 1 and 1^{n+1} = 1^n \cdot 1 = 1. The binomial theorem rearranges sums term by term, and the rules it needs are collected in the next lemma. The sums start at k = 0; by the definition, \sum_{k=0}^{0} a_k = 0 + a_0 = a_0. [Finite Sums in a Commutative Ring] Let R be a commutative ring, n \in 
N, c \in R, and let (a_k)_{k \in 
N} and (b_k)_{k \in 
N} be sequences in R. 1. \sum_{k=0}^{n} (a_k + b_k) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k + \sum_{k=0}^{n} b_k. 2. c \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} c\, a_k. 3. \sum_{k=0}^{n} m \cdot a_k = m \cdot \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k for every m \in 
Z. 4. Let j \in 
N, and suppose a_k = 0 for every k 
e j. Then \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = a_j if j \le n, and \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = 0 if j > n. 5. -\sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k = \sum_{k=0}^{n} (-a_k). 6. (Splitting off the first term.) \sum_{k=0}^{n+1} a_k = a_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{k+1}. In words: a finite sum may be split termwise, multiplied termwise, and negated termwise; a sum with one non-zero term is that term; and the first term may be split off, the rest being re-indexed from 0. By the finite-lists remark, the lemma applies to finitely many terms a_0, \dots, a_n as well. A sum up to n + 1 is the sum up to n plus one term, so every rule that holds for one term and survives adding one more term holds for all sums: an induction on n whose step is a single axiom, (F1)–(F2) for (a), (F9) for (b), and associativity for (f). Parts (c) and (e) need no induction, because a multiple is a product, m \cdot a = (m \cdot 1)a, so they are (b) in disguise. Each part is an induction on n (@fd1:ax-induction), splitting off the last term at the step, except (c) and (e), which follow from (b). (a) For n = 0 both sides are a_0 + b_0. If (a) holds for n, then splitting off the last term, \sum_{k=0}^{n+1} (a_k + b_k) = \Bigl( \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k + \sum_{k=0}^{n} b_k \Bigr) + (a_{n+1} + b_{n+1}) , which is  igl( \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1}  igr) +  igl( \sum_{k=0}^{n} b_k + b_{n+1}  igr) by (F1) and (F2), and that is the right side for n + 1. (b) For n = 0 both sides are c a_0. At the step, c  igl( \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1}  igr) = c \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k + c a_{n+1} by (F9), and the induction hypothesis rewrites the first term. (c) By @lem-integer-multiples (c), which holds for m \in 
Z by part (d) there, m \cdot a_k = (m \cdot 1) a_k and m \cdot \sum a_k = (m \cdot 1) \sum a_k. So (c) is (b) with c = m \cdot 1. (d) For n = 0: if j = 0 the sum is a_0 = a_j; if j > 0, then 0 
e j, so the sum is a_0 = 0. Suppose (d) holds for n, and split off a_{n+1}. If j \le n, the sum up to n is a_j and a_{n+1} = 0 (as n + 1 
e j), so the total is a_j. If j = n + 1, the sum up to n is 0 (as j > n) and the total is 0 + a_{n+1} = a_j. If j > n + 1, both parts are 0. (e) By (c) with m = -1, since (-1) \cdot x = -(1 \cdot x) = -x (@lem-integer-multiples (d)). (f) For n = 0 both sides are a_0 + a_1. If (f) holds for n, then \sum_{k=0}^{n+2} a_k = \Bigl( a_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_{k+1} \Bigr) + a_{n+2} = a_0 + \sum_{k=0}^{n+1} a_{k+1} , by splitting off the last term, the induction hypothesis, (F2), and splitting off the last term of the sequence (a_{k+1})_k, whose term at k = n + 1 is a_{n+2}. This proves the lemma. Binomial coefficients In (x + y)^n, each product x^k y^{n-k} appears a certain number of times, and that number is the binomial coefficient. We define it by Pascal’s rule, which is how the coefficients arise when (x + y)^n is multiplied by x + y, and we never divide. Binomial Coefficients The binomial coefficients  inom{n}{k} \in 
N, for n, k \in 
N, are defined by recursion on n (@fd2:thm-recursion, with X the set of functions 
N 	o 
N):  egin{aligned}  inom{0}{0} &\coloneqq 1 , &  inom{0}{k} &\coloneqq 0 \quad (k \ge 1) , \  inom{n + 1}{0} &\coloneqq 1 , &  inom{n + 1}{k + 1} &\coloneqq  inom{n}{k} +  inom{n}{k + 1} \quad (k \in 
N) . \end{aligned} In words: row n + 1 starts with 1, and each later entry is the sum of the two entries of row n above it (Pascal’s rule). Each row is a whole function 
N 	o 
N, so the recursion has values for every k, and a coefficient is a natural number, never a quotient. Three facts follow by one induction on n each. -  inom{n}{k} = 0 for k > n. title: Groups, Subgroups, and Homomorphisms
content:
Groups, Subgroups, and Homomorphisms The same four rules keep turning up. Add integers, multiply non-zero rationals, multiply the units of 
Z/12
Z, compose the bijections of a set: in each case two elements combine to give an element of the same set, the combining is associative, one element changes nothing, and every element can be undone. This chapter names that pattern a group and proves its basic laws once, from three axioms, so that they hold in all four cases and in every later one. It then makes two habits honest that school algebra uses without comment: dropping the brackets from a product of many factors, and writing powers g^n for every integer n, negative ones included. One warning runs through the whole chapter: a group need not be abelian, so no factor may be moved past another unless a hypothesis allows it. After the structure come its substructures, the subgroups, and its maps, the homomorphisms. The subgroups of (
Z, +) turn out to be exactly the sets n
Z, by the move that gave greatest common divisors in Chapter 1. A homomorphism sends products to products, and its kernel, the set of elements it sends to the identity, measures how much it forgets. The chapter ends with one group studied in detail, the permutations of \{1, \dots, n\}, on which every determinant in linear algebra is built. Every permutation breaks into disjoint cycles, and every one, for n \ge 2, is a product of swaps of two points. Different words for the same permutation can use different numbers of swaps; that the parity of the number never changes is the theorem on the sign of a permutation, which later volumes prove. A language more than a subject. Linear algebra and algebra both speak of groups, and this chapter supplies the vocabulary and the few facts they use constantly. Much of group theory is deliberately left out, and each omission is named once, where it would come up, as a pointer and never as a claim. Cyclic groups and the least m \ge 1 with g^m = e are studied in Groups, the chapter “Cyclic Groups” (Section 3.2 points there). Cosets and Lagrange’s theorem are in its chapter “Cosets and Lagrange’s Theorem” (Section 3.3, Exercise C2, and review exercise R4 of Section 3.5). The uniqueness of the disjoint cycle decomposition, conjugacy in S_n and the sign of a permutation are in its chapter “Symmetric Groups and the Sign of a Permutation” (Sections 3.4 and 3.5), and the sign is also proved in Determinants and the Structure of Operators, the chapter “Determinants”. Quotient groups and the isomorphism theorems are in the chapter “Normal Subgroups, Quotient Groups, and the Isomorphism Theorems” of Groups (the closing remark of Section 3.3). Nothing in this chapter depends on any of them. What you need. Sets and Functions, Chapter 2 (functions, composition, bijections and inverses), Chapters 3 and 4 (induction from any base, the recursion theorem and, in Section 4.1, finite sets) and Section 5.2 (equivalence relations, for one exercise); Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 2 (commutative rings and 
Z) and Section 2.5 (division with remainder), with Chapter 1 of this volume (
Z/n
Z and units); induction from Logic and Proof, Chapter 4. Throughout, 
N is \omega and 
Z, 
Q are the integers and rationals of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3, and results of the first two volumes about 
N are read on \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification, from its Chapter 1, as that volume does. - From Sets and Functions, Chapters 1 and 2: functions, Cartesian products, composition and its associativity, equality of functions, the empty function, and the theorem that a composite of bijections is a bijection (@fd2:def-function, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:def-composition, @fd2:prp-composition-associative, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:prp-empty-function, @fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective), which make the bijections of a set a group and S_0 the trivial group; inverse functions, the uniqueness of inverses, and bijections as the invertible functions (@fd2:def-inverse-function, @fd2:prp-inverse-unique, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse), whose argument Section 3.1 repeats with functions erased; images (@fd2:def-image), for the image of a homomorphism; intersections of families (@fd2:def-family-union-intersection), for intersections of subgroups. - From Sets and Functions, Chapter 3: induction from a base other than 0 (@fd2:thm-induction), in Section 3.5; the recursion theorem, with its finite sums and products as the pattern for products of lists in a group and for n! (@fd2:thm-recursion, @fd2:def-sum-product), in Sections 3.1 and 3.4; equivalence relations and their classes (@fd2:def-equivalence-relation, @fd2:thm-classes-partition), from its Section 5.2, in review exercise R4 of Section 3.5. From its Section 5.1: finite sets, subsets and disjoint unions of finite sets, the pigeonhole principle, and the uniqueness of size (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count, @fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique), for counting S_n, for the decomposition into cycles, and in exercises; a finite set has no proper subset of the same size (@fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy), in review exercise R3. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3: commutative rings and fields and their algebra (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra), whose additive clauses are the group axioms for (R, +); 
Z as an ordered commutative ring with a least element in every non-empty set bounded below (@fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring, @fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules, @fd3:prp-integer-least-element); every integer as n or -n with n \in 
N (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers), which defines negative powers; the multiples n \cdot a of the “Multiples” paragraph of its Section 3.3, which Section 3.1 shows to be the multiples of the group (R, +); and 
Q as an ordered field (@fd3:thm-rationals-field, @fd3:thm-rationals-ordered-field), with the rule that the reciprocal of a positive element of an ordered field is positive (@fd3:prp-reciprocal-order), used for 
Q_{>0} in Sections 3.1 and 3.2 and for 
R_{>0} in Section 3.3. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.5, and from Chapter 1 of this volume: division with remainder, the rules for divisibility, and parity (@fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @fd3:cor-integers-even-odd); integer linear combinations and Bézout’s identity (@def-integer-linear-combinations, @thm-integers-bezout, @cor-coprime-iff-combination), whose proof is the model for the subgroups of 
Z and which Section 3.2’s Exercise B3 recovers; ideals, quotient rings and the rings 
Z/n
Z (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal, @def-integers-mod-n-ring, @thm-integers-mod-n-ring, @exm-integers-mod-six), the first finite groups of the chapter; the principal ideals of 
Z (@thm-integer-ideals-principal), compared with in Section 3.2; and units, the units of 
Z/n
Z, the field 
Z/p
Z and the Chinese remainder map (@def-ring-unit, @thm-units-mod-n, @thm-integers-mod-prime-field, @thm-chinese-remainder-two). Section 3.1 also uses the prime factorization (@def-prime-factorization) as a second instance of the recursion pattern, and Section 3.2’s Exercise C3 recovers @exr-unique-factorization-b2. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5, in examples only: 
R as an ordered field (@fd3:thm-reals-ordered-field), for the groups (
R, +) and (
R_{>0}, \cdot). - From Logic and Proof: induction and strong induction (@fd1:ax-induction, @fd1:thm-strong-induction), from Section 4.2; and, for the two find-the-error exercises (Exercise C2 of Sections 3.1 and 3.5), the catalogue of moves that are not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), from Section 8.6. - From Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1, in examples only: the complex numbers as a field, i^2 = -1 with 
R identified inside 
C, the modulus and its product rule, the unit circle 
T and the roots of unity \mu_n (@fd4:def-complex-numbers, @fd4:prp-reals-embed-complex, @fd4:thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd4:def-conjugate-modulus, @fd4:thm-conjugate-properties, @fd4:prp-unit-circle, @fd4:exm-roots-of-unity), for the subgroups 
T and \mu_n of 
C \setminus \{0\} in Section 3.2 and the modulus as a homomorphism in Section 3.3. - From Chapter 2, in examples, remarks and review exercise R1 only: fields (@def-field) and the rule that a product of non-zero elements is non-zero (@thm-field-basic-properties); integer multiples in a commutative ring (@lem-integer-multiples), compared with the group multiples in a second-reading fold of Section 3.1; field homomorphisms (@def-field-homomorphism, @prp-field-homomorphism-properties), in the closing remark of Section 3.3; and the characteristic (@def-characteristic, @thm-characteristic-prime), which review exercise R1 of Section 3.5 reaches again through the subgroups of 
Z. No proof of a result of this chapter uses 
R, 
C or Chapter 2. The chapter also pays two debts of Chapter 1: its Exercise C2 of Section 1.3 becomes a theorem here (@thm-subgroups-of-integers), and its remark that the units of a commutative ring form a group is proved in Section 3.1 (@prp-units-form-group). Chapter 4 returns to groups and homomorphisms in its review exercise R1. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - Groups. Four familiar situations with the same three rules; groups, abelian groups and additive notation; (R, +) for a commutative ring, F \setminus \{0\} for a field, the bijections of a set, the trivial group and the rotations of a square, with non-examples and the warning to check closure first; the basic laws, the uniqueness of the identity and of inverses, (ab)^{-1} = b^{-1}a^{-1}, cancellation and the unique solution of ax = b, proved once; products of lists by recursion and the laws that let us drop brackets; integer powers and the power laws, with (gh)^n = g^n h^n only when gh = hg; and the units R^{	imes} of a commutative ring as an abelian group, with 
Z^{	imes}, (
Z/n
Z)^{	imes} and F^{	imes}. - Subgroups and the Subgroups of the Integers. Subgroups and the one-condition subgroup test; examples from 
Z, 
Q \setminus \{0\}, 
Z/6
Z, (
Z/8
Z)^{	imes}, the bijections fixing a point, and 
T and \mu_n inside 
C \setminus \{0\}, with minimal-change non-examples; intersections of subgroups, and a union that is not one; the subgroup \langle g angle generated by one element, the smallest subgroup containing g, listed explicitly when some g^m = e; and the theorem that the subgroups of (
Z, +) are exactly the sets n
Z, each for exactly one n \in 
N, with exercises recovering Bézout’s identity and the least common multiple. - Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms. Two tables that differ only in names; homomorphisms, isomorphisms and kernels, with no clause for the identity, which follows; the product of two groups; examples 
Z 	o 
Z/n
Z, k \mapsto g^k, conjugation, squaring in an abelian group, the Chinese remainder map and the modulus, and the non-example x \mapsto x + 1; identities, inverses and powers preserved, kernels and images subgroups; composites and inverses of homomorphisms, so that \cong behaves like equality; injective exactly when the kernel is trivial; isomorphic and non-isomorphic small groups, with the warning that the same number of elements decides nothing; and a remark on where homomorphisms go next. - Permutations and Cycle Notation. The symmetric groups S_X and S_n, the support, two-line notation and products read right to left; cycles and transpositions, computing with them, S_n not abelian for n \ge 3, and two warnings, on the order of reading and on (\sigma	au)^2 
e \sigma^2	au^2; the permutations of n + 1 points fixing the last one as a copy of S_n, and \card{S_n} = n!; disjoint permutations commute; and every permutation a product of disjoint cycles, by following the orbit of a moved point and peeling off the cycle found, with a worked run and exercises on the table of S_3, the number of k-cycles, the rotations of a square and powers of disjoint cycles. - Transpositions Generate the Symmetric Group. A k-cycle as a product of k - 1 transpositions; every permutation of n \ge 2 points a product of transpositions, proved by fixing the last point and inducting, with the route through the cycle decomposition as a remark; the word is not unique, and the parity of its length, the sign, is left to later volumes; 3-cycles do not generate S_3; adjacent transpositions suffice; and review exercises on the kernel of k \mapsto k \cdot 1_F and the characteristic of a field, on 
Z/6
Z, (
Z/7
Z)^{	imes} and 
Z/2
Z 	imes 
Z/3
Z, on the permutations of a set with finite support, and on an element g 
e e with g^2 = e in a group with an even number of elements. Named moves - Multiply by the inverse. To remove a factor from one side of an equation in a group, multiply both sides on the same side by its inverse, then regroup with (G1); there is no “dividing”, and the side matters because a group need not be abelian. Named in Section 3.1, where it proves the uniqueness of inverses and cancellation (@thm-group-basic-properties (2), (4)). Section 3.3 uses it to show that a homomorphism sends the identity to the identity and that a trivial kernel forces injectivity. Exercise B2 of Section 3.1 leaves its last step to you, and Exercise C1 of Section 3.2 its last half. - Check closure first. Before checking (G1)–(G3), check that combining two elements of the set gives an element of the set: closure is not a fourth axiom but is built into “binary operation”. The warning of Section 3.1 names it, with 
Z_{>0} under subtraction, and @exm-group-nonexamples and Exercise B1 of Section 3.1 show sets that fail at closure before any axiom is in question. In Section 3.2 the subgroup test packs closure under products and inverses into the one condition ab^{-1} \in H, and Exercise C1 there shows that for a finite subset closure under products is enough. - Least positive element, then divide. In a subgroup of 
Z other than \{0\}, take the least positive element n and divide any element by it: the remainder lies in the subgroup and is smaller than n, so it is 0. It is the move of Section 1.1, now with only subtraction available. It proves @thm-subgroups-of-integers in Section 3.2, which turns Exercises B3 and C3 there into one-line consequences and reaches the characteristic of a field in review exercise R1 of Section 3.5. - Follow the orbit, then peel it off. Start at a point the permutation moves and apply it until the point returns; record the cycle found, remove it, and induct on what is left, which moves fewer points. Named in Section 3.4, it proves @thm-disjoint-cycle-decomposition there, and Exercise A1 of Section 3.4 runs it by hand. Its one-transposition version, fix one point, then induct, proves @thm-transpositions-generate in Section 3.5: one swap makes the permutation fix the last point, and a permutation fixing the last point is a permutation of one point fewer (@lem-permutations-fixing-last-point). Exercise A1 of Section 3.5 runs it, and its Exercise C1 asks for the proof as an exit check.

title: 3.1 Groups
content:
Groups Several structures met so far behave alike: the integers under addition, the non-zero rationals under multiplication, the units of 
Z/n
Z (Section 1.4), and the bijections of a set under composition (Sets and Functions, Chapter 2). This section names their common structure, a group, and proves its basic laws once, from three axioms, so that they hold in all of these at once. It then makes two habits honest: dropping brackets from a product of many factors, and writing powers g^n with n \in 
Z. Throughout the chapter 
N is \omega, and 
Z, 
Q are the integers and rationals built in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3. Induction and recursion on 
N are @fd1:ax-induction and @fd2:thm-recursion, read on \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b). Strong induction, @fd1:thm-strong-induction, holds on \omega too, since its proof uses only @fd1:ax-induction and the order facts @fd3:thm-omega-order (a), (b), (d). Four situations side by side Look at four situations in which two things are combined into a third. - In (
Z, +) we add integers. The integer 0 does nothing, a + 0 = a, and -a undoes a, a + (-a) = 0. - In 
Q \setminus \{0\} we multiply. The rational 1 does nothing, and a^{-1} undoes a. - Among the units of 
Z/12
Z, which are [1], [5], [7], [11] by @thm-units-mod-n (the classes of the integers coprime to 12), we multiply classes. The class [1] does nothing, and each unit undoes itself: [5][5] = [25] = [1], [7][7] = [49] = [1] and [11][11] = [121] = [1], since 25 = 2 \cdot 12 + 1, 49 = 4 \cdot 12 + 1 and 121 = 10 \cdot 12 + 1. - Among the bijections X 	o X of a set we compose. The identity map \id_X does nothing, and each bijection f is undone by its inverse f^{-1} (@fd2:def-inverse-function). The objects differ, and so do the ways of combining them, but the rules used are the same three: the combining is associative, one element changes nothing, and every element can be undone. So we give the pattern a name. A group is a set with one way of combining two elements into a third, in which combining is associative, some element does nothing, and every element can be undone. [Group] A group is a set G together with a binary operation on G, that is, a function G 	imes G 	o G, (a, b) \mapsto ab (@fd2:def-function, with G 	imes G the Cartesian product of @fd2:def-cartesian-product), such that: 1. (Associativity) (ab)c = a(bc) for all a, b, c \in G; 2. (Identity) there is an element e \in G with ea = ae = a for every a \in G; 3. (Inverses) for every a \in G there is b \in G with ab = ba = e, where e is the element of (G2). The group is abelian if moreover ab = ba for all a, b \in G. In words: the operation is a function on pairs, so the combination of two elements of G lies in G again. This “closure” is not a fourth axiom; it is built into the phrase “binary operation G 	imes G 	o G”. (G1) says that the two ways of combining three elements in a fixed order agree. (G2) asks for an element that changes nothing, from both sides. (G3) asks that each element can be undone, again from both sides, back to that same e. We write a group as (G, \cdot), or simply G when the operation is clear, and call ab the product of a and b, whatever the operation is. When the operation is an addition we write a + b, 0 and -a in place of ab, e and the inverse of a. This additive notation is used only for abelian groups. Groups Check that each of (a)–(d) is a group, and decide which are abelian. 1. (R, +) for a commutative ring R (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field); in particular (
Z, +), (
Q, +), (
R, +) and (
Z/n
Z, +) for n \in 
Z_{>0}. 2. (
Q \setminus \{0\}, \cdot), and (F \setminus \{0\}, \cdot) for any field F; in particular (
Z/p
Z \setminus \{[0]\}, \cdot) for a prime p. 3. The set of bijections X 	o X of a set X, under composition \circ. 4. A one-element set \{e\} with ee \coloneqq e. 5. (A fifth situation, described here and checked in Section 3.4.) The four rotations of a square about its center, by no turn, a quarter turn, a half turn and three quarter turns. Label the corners 1, 2, 3, 4 in order around the square; the quarter turn moves each label to the next corner, which is the bijection i \mapsto i + 1 for i < 4, 4 \mapsto 1 of \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. e g \circ f. There is no counterexample to the conclusion, which is true. By @prp-group-list-product-laws (a) and (b), the product of the list is the bracketing (g_1 \cdots g_{i-1})(g_i g_{i+1})(g_{i+2} \cdots g_r) , where an empty product is e. The list with g_i and g_{i+1} swapped has, in the same way, the product (g_1 \cdots g_{i-1})(g_{i+1} g_i)(g_{i+2} \cdots g_r). Since G is abelian, g_i g_{i+1} = g_{i+1} g_i, so the two products are equal. 2. By @fd1:ax-induction on the number k of swaps: for k = 0 the list is unchanged, and a rearrangement by k + 1 swaps is one swap applied to a rearrangement by k swaps, whose product equals the original product by the hypothesis; the last swap does not change the product, by (a). Fatal errors (0 for the step): (a) swaps the two entries inside a product written without brackets, with no appeal to the list-product laws; (b) “and so on” in place of an induction.

Homomorphisms and Isomorphisms Section 3.1 named the pattern shared by (
Z, +), the units of a ring and the bijections of a set, and Section 3.2 looked inside one group at a time, at its subgroups. This section compares two groups. A map between groups that respects the two operations is a homomorphism; a bijective one is an isomorphism, and it says that two groups differ only in the names of their elements. The elements a homomorphism sends to the identity form its kernel, a subgroup that measures how much the map forgets. Maps that respect the operation Write out the addition table of 
Z/2

The two groups are the same table with different names. The renaming is a function \varphi with \varphi([0]) = 1 and \varphi([1]) = -1, and “entry for entry” says that the entry for a, b is sent to the entry for \varphi(a), \varphi(b): \varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b). Maps with this property are worth having even when they are not bijections. The map 
Z 	o

A homomorphism is a map between groups that sends products to products; an isomorphism is a bijective one, a renaming of the elements. [Group Homomorphism] Let G and H be groups. A function \varphi \colon G 	o H is a homomorphism if \varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) for all a, b \in G. A bijective homomorphism is an isomorphism. The groups G and H are isomorphic, written G \cong H, if there exists an isomorphism G 	o H. The kernel of \varphi is \ker \varphi \coloneqq \{ g \in G : \varphi(g) = e_H \} , where e_H is the identity of H. In words: the product ab on the left is taken in G, and the product \varphi(a)\varphi(b) on the right is taken in H. So “\varphi respects the operation” compares two different operations, and either group may be written additively. For \varphi \colon (

We write e_G and e_H whenever both groups are in play. The definition asks for one equation and nothing else. It does not ask that \varphi(e_G) = e_H or that \varphi respect inverses: both follow, by @thm-homomorphism-basic-properties below. This differs from the field homomorphisms of Chapter 2, which must send 1 to 1 by a clause of their own: the map sending every element of a field to 0 respects + and \cdot, yet 1 \mapsto 0. In a group, every element can be canceled, and that is what makes the clause redundant. It is bijective (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse, with inverse \id_G), so it is an isomorphism, and its kernel is \{e_G\}. It forgets nothing. These two extremes are why we say that the kernel measures what \varphi forgets: the larger \ker \varphi, the more elements \varphi sends to the same place. @prp-homomorphism-injective-iff-kernel-trivial below makes the slogan exact at the end where nothing is forgotten. title: 3.4 Permutations and Cycle Notation
content:
Permutations and Cycle Notation Shuffle three cards, then shuffle them again. Two shuffles in a row are a shuffle, every shuffle can be undone, and the order of the two shuffles matters. This is the group of bijections of a finite set (@exm-groups (c)), and it is the one group of this chapter studied in detail, because every determinant in linear algebra is built from it. This section gives it a compact notation, cycle notation, learns to multiply in it, counts its elements, and proves that every permutation breaks into independent loops: follow the orbit, then peel it off. Permutations and two-line notation Section 3.1 showed that the bijections of a set form a group under composition. On the set \{1, \dots, n\} they are the rearrangements of n objects, and they get a name of their own. A permutation is a rearrangement: a bijection of a set to itself. [Permutations and the Symmetric Group] Let X be a set. A permutation of X is a bijection X 	o X. The permutations of X, with the operation \sigma	au \coloneqq \sigma \circ 	au, form the group S_X of @exm-groups (c). For n \in 
N, the symmetric group is S_n \coloneqq S_{\{1, \dots, n\}} , where \{1, \dots, n\} is empty for n = 0. The support of \sigma \in S_X is the set of points it moves, \supp \sigma \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \sigma(x) 
e x \} . In words: S_X is not a new group. It is the group of bijections of X, with the product written as juxtaposition. Its identity is \id_X, written \id when X is clear, and the inverse of \sigma is the inverse function \sigma^{-1} (@fd2:def-inverse-function). The support of \id is empty, and the support is empty only for \id: if \sigma(x) = x for every x, then \sigma = \id_X (@fd2:prp-function-equality). The product is read right to left. In S_X the product \sigma	au is the composite \sigma \circ 	au: first apply 	au, then \sigma, exactly as g \circ f applies f first (@fd2:def-composition). So (\sigma	au)(x) = \sigma(	au(x)), and a longer product \sigma_1\sigma_2 \cdots \sigma_r applies \sigma_r first and \sigma_1 last. Two-line notation. A permutation \sigma \in S_n is given by its values, and we write them under the points: \sigma =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \cdots & n \ \sigma(1) & \sigma(2) & \cdots & \sigma(n) \end{pmatrix} . This array is a table of values, not a matrix. For example,  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \ 3 & 1 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} \in S_4 sends 1 \mapsto 3, 2 \mapsto 1, 3 \mapsto 2 and fixes 4; its support is \{1, 2, 3\}. The bottom row of a permutation lists each of 1, \dots, n exactly once: once at least, because \sigma is surjective, and at most once, because it is injective. The smallest symmetric groups. S_0 has one element, the empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset (@fd2:prp-empty-function (a)), which is a bijection because there is nothing to check; it is the trivial group. S_1 has one element, \id, since the only function \{1\} 	o \{1\} sends 1 \mapsto 1. S_2 has two elements, \id and the permutation swapping 1 and 2: a bijection of \{1, 2\} either fixes 1, and then also 2, or sends 1 \mapsto 2, and then 2 \mapsto 1. These degenerate cases are where inductions on n start, here and in Section 3.5. Cycles Two-line notation lists every value, even the values of points that do not move. Most permutations met in practice move a few points around a loop and leave the rest alone, and a notation that records only the loop is shorter and shows more. A cycle moves a list of distinct points one step along the list, the last back to the first, and fixes everything else. [Cycle, Transposition] Let n \in 
N and k \ge 2, and let i_1, \dots, i_k \in \{1, \dots, n\} be distinct. The k-cycle (i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_k) \in S_n is the permutation \gamma with \gamma(i_j) \coloneqq i_{j+1} \ 	ext{ for } 1 \le j < k , \qquad \gamma(i_k) \coloneqq i_1 , and \gamma(x) \coloneqq x for every x \in \{1, \dots, n\} not among i_1, \dots, i_k. A 2-cycle (i\ j) is a transposition. Two cycles are disjoint if their supports are disjoint. In words: i_1 \mapsto i_2 \mapsto \cdots \mapsto i_k \mapsto i_1, and the points off the list stay put. A transposition (i\ j) swaps i and j. Well-definedness. Because the entries are distinct, each point of \{1, \dots, n\} receives exactly one value from the rule, so \gamma is a function. It is a bijection: the cycle (i_k\ \cdots\ i_2\ i_1), the list read backwards, undoes it point by point (i_{j+1} \mapsto i_j and i_1 \mapsto i_k, and the other points are fixed by both), so it is a two-sided inverse and @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse applies. Hence (i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_k)^{-1} = (i_k\ \cdots\ i_2\ i_1) . Every entry is moved, since i_{j+1} 
e i_j and i_1 
e i_k by distinctness and k \ge 2; so \supp (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k) = \{ i_1, \dots, i_k \}. A transposition is its own inverse: (i\ j)(i\ j) = \id. Examples. In S_4, (1\ 2\ 3) sends 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 1 and fixes 4; in two-line notation it is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \ 2 & 3 & 1 & 4 \end{pmatrix}. The same cycle may be written starting at any of its entries: (1\ 2\ 3) = (2\ 3\ 1) = (3\ 1\ 2), since all three describe the loop 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1. But (1\ 3\ 2) is a different permutation: it sends 1 \mapsto 3. The cycles (1\ 2) and (3\ 4) are disjoint; (1\ 2) and (2\ 3) are not. The identity is not a cycle. The definition asks for k \ge 2: a “1-cycle” (i) would be the identity, and so would every one of them, so the notation would not be telling us anything. The identity is instead the empty product of cycles (@def-group-list-product), and that is how it will appear in the decomposition theorem below. Which of these are equal in S_4: (2\ 4\ 1), (1\ 2\ 4), (1\ 4\ 2)? Write the one that differs in two-line notation. (2\ 4\ 1) is the loop 2 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, and (1\ 2\ 4) is the same loop started at 1: both send 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 4, 4 \mapsto 1 and fix 3. So they are equal. (1\ 4\ 2) runs the loop backwards: it sends 1 \mapsto 4, 4 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 1, so it differs from the other two at 1. In two-line notation it is  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \ 4 & 1 & 3 & 2 \end{pmatrix}; it is the inverse of the other two. Products of cycles are computed by following each point through the factors, from right to left. [Computing with Cycles] In S_3, compute (1\ 3)(1\ 2) and (1\ 2)(1\ 3). In S_5, write \sigma =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \ 3 & 5 & 1 & 2 & 4 \end{pmatrix} as a product of cycles. For (1\ 3)(1\ 2), follow each point through (1\ 2) first, then (1\ 3): 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1. So (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3). For (1\ 2)(1\ 3): 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1. So (1\ 2)(1\ 3) = (1\ 3\ 2). The two products differ, so S_3 is not abelian. For every n \ge 3, the same two transpositions lie in S_n, the same computation applies at 1, 2, 3, and both products fix every point \ge 4; so S_n is not abelian for every n \ge 3. For \sigma, start at 1 and follow: 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1, a loop (1\ 3). The smallest point not yet used is 2: 2 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 2, a loop (2\ 5\ 4). Every point is now used, so \sigma = (1\ 3)(2\ 5\ 4). To check, follow each point through (2\ 5\ 4) first, then (1\ 3): 1 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 3, 2 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 5, 3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1, 4 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 2, 5 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 4, which is the bottom row 3, 5, 1, 2, 4. The two cycles move disjoint sets of points, and the product in the other order, (2\ 5\ 4)(1\ 3), is also \sigma, as the same check shows. For S_n with n \le 2 the situation is different: S_0, S_1 and S_2 have at most two elements, and any two of their elements commute, since one of them is \id or both are equal. So S_n is abelian exactly when n \le 2. Mind the order. \sigma	au applies 	au first, as g \circ f applies f first. Reading a product of cycles from left to right gives a wrong answer: read that way, (1\ 3)(1\ 2) would send 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1, that is, “(1\ 3\ 2)”; but the example computed (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3). The left-to-right reading computes the product in the other order. Section 3.1 noted that the power law (gh)^n = g^n h^n of @prp-group-power-laws (d) needs gh = hg. In S_3 it fails without that hypothesis. (\sigma	au)^2 = \sigma^2	au^2 is false in general. Take \sigma = (1\ 2) and 	au = (1\ 3). By the example, \sigma	au = (1\ 3\ 2), and (1\ 3\ 2)(1\ 3\ 2) sends 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1, so (\sigma	au)^2 = (1\ 2\ 3). But transpositions are their own inverses, so \sigma^2	au^2 = \id \cdot \id = \id. Here \sigma	au 
e 	au\sigma, and the law fails. Compute (1\ 2\ 3)(1\ 2) in S_3. Apply (1\ 2) first: 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3, 2 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1. So 1 and 3 are swapped and 2 is fixed: (1\ 2\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 3). Counting permutations How many permutations does S_n have? There are n choices for \sigma(1), then n - 1 for \sigma(2), and so on, which suggests n!. We make this precise by induction on n, and the induction needs one structural fact: the permutations of \{1, \dots, n + 1\} that fix the last point are, in effect, the permutations of \{1, \dots, n\}. Section 3.5 uses the same fact for a different induction. [Permutations Fixing the Last Point] Let n \in 
N, and let S' \coloneqq \{ \sigma \in S_{n+1} : \sigma(n + 1) = n + 1 \}, a subgroup of S_{n+1}. 1. For \sigma \in S', the restriction \sigma' of \sigma to \{1, \dots, n\}, with codomain \{1, \dots, n\}, is a permutation of \{1, \dots, n\}. 2. The map S' 	o S_n, \sigma \mapsto \sigma', is an isomorphism. Its inverse sends ho \in S_n to its extension  arho \in S', defined by  arho(i) \coloneqq ho(i) for i \le n and  arho(n + 1) \coloneqq n + 1. That S' is a subgroup is @exm-subgroups (e), with X = \{1, \dots, n + 1\} and the chosen point n + 1. A permutation fixing n + 1 cannot send any other point to n + 1, since that value is taken; so it maps \{1, \dots, n\} into itself. It also reaches every point there, because whatever reaches j \le n cannot be n + 1. Restricting and extending undo each other, and restriction respects composition. (a) Let \sigma \in S' and i \in \{1, \dots, n\}. If \sigma(i) = n + 1 = \sigma(n + 1), then i = n + 1 by injectivity, which is false; so \sigma(i) \in \{1, \dots, n\}, and \sigma' \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, \sigma'(i) \coloneqq \sigma(i), is a function. It is injective because \sigma is. It is surjective: for j \in \{1, \dots, n\} there is i \in \{1, \dots, n + 1\} with \sigma(i) = j, since \sigma is surjective, and i 
e n + 1, since \sigma(n + 1) = n + 1 
e j. So \sigma' \in S_n. (b) Write R(\sigma) \coloneqq \sigma' and E(ho) \coloneqq  arho. E maps into S'. The extension  arho is a function on \{1, \dots, n + 1\} with values in that set, and \overline{ho^{-1}} undoes it point by point: for i \le n, \overline{ho^{-1}}( arho(i)) = ho^{-1}(ho(i)) = i, and both fix n + 1; the other composite is the same with ho and ho^{-1} exchanged. So  arho is a bijection (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse) fixing n + 1. R and E are mutually inverse. For \sigma \in S', \overline{\sigma'} agrees with \sigma at every i \le n and at n + 1, so E(R(\sigma)) = \sigma (@fd2:prp-function-equality). For ho \in S_n, ( arho)' agrees with ho at every i \le n, so R(E(ho)) = ho. Hence R is a bijection with inverse E (@fd2:def-inverse-function, @fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse). R is a homomorphism. Let \sigma, 	au \in S' and i \le n. By (a), 	au(i) \le n, so (\sigma	au)'(i) = \sigma(	au(i)) = \sigma'(	au'(i)) = (\sigma'	au')(i) . So (\sigma	au)' = \sigma'	au', and R is an isomorphism. Its inverse E is an isomorphism by @prp-homomorphism-composition-inverse (b). This proves the lemma. So inside S_{n+1} sits a copy of S_n, the permutations that leave the last point alone. The factorial n! is that of @fd2:def-sum-product, read in 
N: 0! = 1 and (n + 1)! = n! \, (n + 1). [The Symmetric Group Has n! Elements] For every n \in 
N, S_n is finite and has n! elements: \card{S_n} = n!. Sort the permutations of \{1, \dots, n + 1\} by where they send the last point. Those sending it to n + 1 are a copy of S_n, by the lemma. Those sending it to k \le n are matched with the first kind by composing with the swap (k\ \ n{+}1). So there are n + 1 classes of n! permutations each. We use induction on n (@fd1:ax-induction). For n = 0, S_0 has exactly one element, the empty function (@fd2:prp-empty-function (a)), and 0! = 1. Suppose S_n has n! elements. For k \in \{1, \dots, n + 1\} let A_k \coloneqq \{ \sigma \in S_{n+1} : \sigma(n + 1) = k \} . Every \sigma \in S_{n+1} lies in exactly one A_k, namely for k = \sigma(n + 1). So the sets A_1, \dots, A_{n+1} are pairwise disjoint and their union is S_{n+1}. The class A_{n+1}. A_{n+1} is the subgroup S' of @lem-permutations-fixing-last-point. By the induction hypothesis there is a bijection \{1, \dots, n!\} 	o S_n (@fd2:def-finite); composing it with the bijection S_n 	o S' of the lemma gives a bijection \{1, \dots, n!\} 	o A_{n+1} (@fd2:thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)). So A_{n+1} has n! elements. The classes A_k, k \le n. Let 	au \coloneqq (k\ \ n{+}1), a transposition with 	au	au = \id. If \sigma \in A_k, then (	au\sigma)(n + 1) = 	au(k) = n + 1, so 	au\sigma \in A_{n+1}; if ho \in A_{n+1}, then (	auho)(n + 1) = 	au(n + 1) = k, so 	auho \in A_k. The maps A_k 	o A_{n+1}, \sigma \mapsto 	au\sigma, and A_{n+1} 	o A_k, ho \mapsto 	auho, are mutually inverse, since 	au(	au\sigma) = (	au	au)\sigma = \sigma by (G1), 	au	au = \id and (G2), and likewise for ho. So \sigma \mapsto 	au\sigma is a bijection A_k 	o A_{n+1} (@fd2:thm-bijection-iff-inverse), and composing as before, A_k has n! elements. Adding up. We prove, by @fd2:thm-induction with base 1 (read on \omega by @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)), the statement P(j): “if j \le n + 1, the union A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_j has j \, n! elements”. For j = 1 this is the count of A_1, and the step adds the n! elements of A_{j+1}, disjoint from A_1 \cup \dots \cup A_j, by @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count, with j \, n! + n! = (j + 1) \, n!. For j = n + 1, S_{n+1} has (n + 1) \, n! = (n + 1)! elements. This completes the induction and proves the proposition. So S_3 has 6 elements, S_4 has 24, and S_{10} already has 3628800. For S_3 all six can be listed: \id, the three transpositions (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3), and the two 3-cycles (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2). These are six different permutations, so by the proposition they are all of S_3: a proper subset of a 6-element set has fewer elements (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique). Disjoint cycles and the decomposition theorem In @exm-cycle-notation, \sigma came apart into the loops (1\ 3) and (2\ 5\ 4), which move disjoint sets of points, and the order of the two factors did not matter. Both observations hold in general. We start with the second: permutations moving disjoint sets of points do not interfere with each other. [Disjoint Permutations Commute] Let n \in 
N and \sigma, 	au \in S_n with \supp \sigma \cap \supp 	au = \emptyset. Then \sigma	au = 	au\sigma. Moreover, every permutation \sigma maps \supp \sigma onto itself: \sigma(\supp \sigma) = \supp \sigma. In particular, disjoint cycles commute. A point moved by \sigma is fixed by 	au, and so is its image under \sigma, because \sigma keeps its moved points among its moved points. So on \supp \sigma only \sigma acts, on \supp 	au only 	au, and elsewhere neither: the order of application cannot matter. \sigma maps its support onto itself. Let i \in \supp \sigma. If \sigma(i) 
otin \supp \sigma, then \sigma(\sigma(i)) = \sigma(i), and injectivity gives \sigma(i) = i, against i \in \supp \sigma. So \sigma(\supp \sigma) \subseteq \supp \sigma. Conversely, let j \in \supp \sigma and i \coloneqq \sigma^{-1}(j). If i 
otin \supp \sigma, then j = \sigma(i) = i 
otin \supp \sigma, a contradiction; so i \in \supp \sigma and j = \sigma(i) \in \sigma(\supp \sigma). Hence \sigma(\supp \sigma) = \supp \sigma. Commuting. Let i \in \{1, \dots, n\}. There are three cases, since i lies in at most one of the disjoint supports. Case 1: i \in \supp \sigma. Then i 
otin \supp 	au, so 	au(i) = i. Also \sigma(i) \in \supp \sigma by the first part, so \sigma(i) 
otin \supp 	au and 	au(\sigma(i)) = \sigma(i). Hence (\sigma	au)(i) = \sigma(i) = (	au\sigma)(i). Case 2: i \in \supp 	au. The same argument with \sigma and 	au exchanged gives (	au\sigma)(i) = 	au(i) = (\sigma	au)(i). Case 3: i lies in neither support. Then \sigma(i) = i = 	au(i), and both products send i to i. So \sigma	au and 	au\sigma agree at every point, and \sigma	au = 	au\sigma (@fd2:prp-function-equality). This proves the proposition. The hypothesis “disjoint” cannot be dropped: (1\ 2) and (1\ 3) share the point 1, and @exm-cycle-notation shows that they do not commute. Exercise C1 looks at the dropped hypothesis more closely. Now the main theorem. To break a permutation into loops, start at a point it moves and follow it until it comes back. The loop found is a cycle; remove it, and fewer points are moved, so induction finishes the job. [Disjoint Cycle Decomposition] Let n \in 
N. Every \sigma \in S_n is a product \sigma = \gamma_1 \gamma_2 \cdots \gamma_s, s \in 
N, of pairwise disjoint cycles, each with support contained in \supp \sigma. For \sigma = \id the product is empty (s = 0). The clause about supports is part of the statement because the induction needs it: it is what makes the new cycle disjoint from the old ones. The theorem says nothing about uniqueness; that the decomposition is unique up to the order of the factors is proved in Groups, the chapter “Symmetric Groups and the Sign of a Permutation”. Induction on the number m of points that \sigma moves. ① Pick a moved point i and follow its orbit i, \sigma(i), \sigma^2(i), \dots. There are only n points, so the orbit repeats, and it repeats first at i itself. ② The points before the return form a cycle \gamma on which \sigma acts exactly as \gamma does. ③ Peel it off: ho \coloneqq \gamma^{-1}\sigma fixes the orbit and everything \sigma fixes, so it moves fewer points, and the induction hypothesis decomposes it. Then \sigma = \gammaho. Before reading on: why must the orbit of i return to i itself, and not to some later point? We use strong induction (@fd1:thm-strong-induction) on m \in 
N, for the statement: every \sigma \in S_n whose support has m elements is a product of pairwise disjoint cycles with supports in \supp \sigma. Every support is a subset of \{1, \dots, n\}, which has n elements, so it is finite (@fd2:prp-subset-finite), and every \sigma is covered by the statement for some m. Let \sigma \in S_n, let \supp \sigma have m elements, and suppose the statement holds for every smaller number. If m = 0, then \supp \sigma = \emptyset, so \sigma = \id, the empty product (@def-group-list-product). Let m \ge 1 and choose i \in \supp \sigma. Follow the orbit. Powers are taken in the group S_n (@def-group-integer-power). The map \{0, 1, \dots, n\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, c \mapsto \sigma^c(i), goes from a set of n + 1 elements to a set of n elements, so it is not injective (@fd2:cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a)): \sigma^a(i) = \sigma^b(i) for some 0 \le a < b \le n. Apply \sigma^{-a} to both sides. By @prp-group-power-laws (a), \sigma^{-a}\sigma^a = \sigma^0 = \id and \sigma^{-a}\sigma^b = \sigma^{b-a}, so i = \sigma^{b-a}(i) , \qquad b - a \ge 1 . So the set of c \in 
Z_{>0} with \sigma^c(i) = i is non-empty and bounded below by 0, and it has a least element r (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element). Since \sigma(i) 
e i, r \ge 2. The points i, \sigma(i), \dots, \sigma^{r-1}(i) are distinct. Indeed, if \sigma^c(i) = \sigma^d(i) with 0 \le c < d \le r - 1, the argument just given yields \sigma^{d-c}(i) = i with 0 < d - c < r, against the minimality of r. Let O \coloneqq \{ \sigma^c(i) : 0 \le c \le r - 1 \} , \qquad \gamma \coloneqq  igl(i\ \ \sigma(i)\ \cdots\ \sigma^{r-1}(i) igr) , an r-cycle (@def-cycle) with \supp \gamma = O. \sigma acts on O as \gamma does. For 0 \le c < r - 1, \gamma(\sigma^c(i)) = \sigma^{c+1}(i) = \sigma(\sigma^c(i)), where \sigma^{c+1} = \sigma\sigma^c by @prp-group-power-laws (a). For c = r - 1, \gamma(\sigma^{r-1}(i)) = i = \sigma^r(i) = \sigma(\sigma^{r-1}(i)). So \sigma(x) = \gamma(x) for every x \in O. In particular \sigma moves every point of O, since \gamma does, and O \subseteq \supp \sigma. Peel it off. Let ho \coloneqq \gamma^{-1}\sigma. For x \in O, ho(x) = \gamma^{-1}(\sigma(x)) = \gamma^{-1}(\gamma(x)) = x. For x 
otin \supp \sigma, we have x 
otin O, so \gamma(x) = x and hence \gamma^{-1}(x) = x; then ho(x) = \gamma^{-1}(x) = x. So ho fixes every point of O and every point outside \supp \sigma: \supp ho \subseteq \supp \sigma \setminus O . Since i \in O, the set \supp \sigma \setminus O is a proper subset of \supp \sigma, so it has fewer than m elements, and so does its subset \supp ho (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, twice). By the induction hypothesis, ho = \gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_s with pairwise disjoint cycles \gamma_j and \supp \gamma_j \subseteq \supp ho \subseteq \supp \sigma \setminus O. Each \gamma_j is therefore disjoint from \gamma, whose support is O. Finally, \gammaho = \gamma\gamma^{-1}\sigma = \sigma, so by @prp-group-list-product-laws (a) \sigma = \gamma\gamma_1 \cdots \gamma_s , a product of pairwise disjoint cycles, with \supp \gamma = O \subseteq \supp \sigma and \supp \gamma_j \subseteq \supp \sigma. This completes the induction and proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. The orbit returns to i itself because \sigma is injective; in the proof, that is the step “apply \sigma^{-a}”. If the first repetition were \sigma^b(i) = \sigma^a(i) with a \ge 1, applying \sigma^{-1} would give the earlier repetition \sigma^{b-1}(i) = \sigma^{a-1}(i). For a function that is not injective this fails: f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2\} with f(1) = f(2) = 2 has the orbit 1, 2, 2, 2, \dots, which never comes back to 1. The proof is an algorithm. Here it is run on one permutation. A worked run. Let \sigma \in S_6 send 1 \mapsto 4, 2 \mapsto 6, 3 \mapsto 3, 4 \mapsto 1, 5 \mapsto 2, 6 \mapsto 5. Its support is \{1, 2, 4, 5, 6\}. Start at 1: 1 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 1, so r = 2 and \gamma = (1\ 4). Peel it off: ho = (1\ 4)^{-1}\sigma = (1\ 4)\sigma fixes 1 and 4 and agrees with \sigma elsewhere, with support \{2, 5, 6\}. Start again at 2: 2 \mapsto 6 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 2, so r = 3 and the next cycle is (2\ 6\ 5). Peeling it off leaves the identity, and the point 3, fixed by \sigma, never enters. So \sigma = (1\ 4)(2\ 6\ 5) . Decompose  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \ 3 & 6 & 5 & 4 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix} \in S_6 into disjoint cycles. Start at 1: 1 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 1, the cycle (1\ 3\ 5). The next moved point is 2: 2 \mapsto 6 \mapsto 2, the cycle (2\ 6). The point 4 is fixed. So the permutation is (1\ 3\ 5)(2\ 6), and by @prp-disjoint-cycles-commute also (2\ 6)(1\ 3\ 5). By @prp-disjoint-cycles-commute, two neighboring factors of a disjoint cycle decomposition may be exchanged; for instance (1\ 3\ 5)(2\ 6) = (2\ 6)(1\ 3\ 5). The next section breaks each cycle further, into transpositions. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Compute (1\ 2\ 3\ 4)(2\ 4) and (2\ 4)(1\ 2\ 3\ 4) in S_4, as products of disjoint cycles. 2. Find the inverse of (1\ 5\ 2\ 7) in S_7, written as a cycle starting at 1. 3. Run the proof of @thm-disjoint-cycle-decomposition on \sigma =  egin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \ 2 & 5 & 4 & 3 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \in S_5 , starting at i = 1: give the orbit of 1, the number r, the cycle \gamma, and ho = \gamma^{-1}\sigma; then finish the run. Which step of the proof uses that \sigma is injective? 4. Compute  igl((1\ 2)(2\ 3) igr)^2 and (1\ 2)^2(2\ 3)^2 in S_3. (a) For (1\ 2\ 3\ 4)(2\ 4), apply (2\ 4) first: 1 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 1, 3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 4, 4 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3. So the product is (1\ 2)(3\ 4). For (2\ 4)(1\ 2\ 3\ 4), apply (1\ 2\ 3\ 4) first: 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 4, 4 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 1, 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 2. So the product is (1\ 4)(2\ 3). The two orders give different permutations. (b) By the inverse formula after @def-cycle, (1\ 5\ 2\ 7)^{-1} = (7\ 2\ 5\ 1), which, started at 1, is (1\ 7\ 2\ 5). (c) The orbit of 1 is 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 1, so r = 3 and \gamma = (1\ 2\ 5), with \gamma^{-1} = (5\ 2\ 1) = (1\ 5\ 2). Then ho = \gamma^{-1}\sigma sends 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1, 2 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 2, 5 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 5, 3 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 4, 4 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3: ho = (3\ 4). Running the proof on ho, starting at 3: 3 \mapsto 4 \mapsto 3, so the cycle is (3\ 4), and peeling it off leaves \id. Hence \sigma = (1\ 2\ 5)(3\ 4). Injectivity is used where the orbit is shown to return to i itself: the step that applies \sigma^{-a} to \sigma^a(i) = \sigma^b(i). (d) (1\ 2)(2\ 3): 1 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1, so it is (1\ 2\ 3), and its square sends 1 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 1:  igl((1\ 2)(2\ 3) igr)^2 = (1\ 3\ 2). On the other hand (1\ 2)^2(2\ 3)^2 = \id, since transpositions are their own inverses. A second instance of the warning on (\sigma	au)^2. B. Practice [B1: The table of S_3] List the six elements of S_3 in cycle notation and write out the table whose entry in row x and column y is xy. Hence find all x \in S_3 with x^2 = \id, and all x that commute with every element of S_3. By the list after @prp-symmetric-group-order, the elements are \id, (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3), (1\ 2\ 3), (1\ 3\ 2). Computing each product right to left, as in @exm-cycle-notation, the entry in row x, column y is xy: ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- xy \id (1\ 2) (1\ 3) (2\ 3) (1\ 2\ 3) (1\ 3\ 2) ----------- ----------- ----------- ----------- ----------- ----------- ----------- \id \id (1\ 2) (1\ 3) (2\ 3) (1\ 2\ 3) (1\ 3\ 2) (1\ 2) (1\ 2) \id (1\ 3\ 2) (1\ 2\ 3) (2\ 3) (1\ 3) (1\ 3) (1\ 3) (1\ 2\ 3) \id (1\ 3\ 2) (1\ 2) (2\ 3) (2\ 3) (2\ 3) (1\ 3\ 2) (1\ 2\ 3) \id (1\ 3) (1\ 2) (1\ 2\ 3) (1\ 2\ 3) (1\ 3) (2\ 3) (1\ 2) (1\ 3\ 2) \id (1\ 3\ 2) (1\ 3\ 2) (2\ 3) (1\ 2) (1\ 3) \id (1\ 2\ 3) ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- For example, the entry in row (1\ 2), column (2\ 3) is (1\ 2)(2\ 3): 1 \mapsto 1 \mapsto 2, 2 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 1, which is (1\ 2\ 3). Reading the diagonal, x^2 = \id exactly for x = \id, (1\ 2), (1\ 3), (2\ 3). An element x commutes with every element exactly when row x equals column x. This holds for \id. We use one counting fact: if a finite set is the union of N pairwise disjoint subsets with q elements each, it has Nq elements. This is @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count applied N - 1 times, by induction on N, as in the proof of @prp-symmetric-group-order. Lists. Let T_k be the set of lists (i_1, \dots, i_k) of distinct elements of \{1, \dots, n\}. Then T_k has n(n - 1) \cdots (n - k + 1) elements, by induction on k: T_0 has one element, the empty list, and T_{j+1} is the disjoint union, over the lists t \in T_j, of the sets of lists extending t by a point x of the complement C of its entry set E. Here E has j elements, since the entries are distinct, so j + \card{C} = n (@fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count, @fd2:cor-finite-size-unique) and C has n - j elements. By the counting fact, T_{j+1} has (n - j) times as many elements as T_j. Since n(n - 1) \cdots (n - k + 1) \cdot (n - k)! = n!, this number is n!/(n - k)!. Lists to cycles. Each list in T_k defines the k-cycle (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k), and every k-cycle arises this way. Two lists give the same cycle exactly when one is a rotation of the other. Indeed, rotations give the same cycle (the remark after @def-cycle). Conversely, if (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k) = (j_1\ \cdots\ j_k) = \gamma, then j_1 lies in the support \{i_1, \dots, i_k\}, say j_1 = i_c, and then j_2 = \gamma(j_1) = i_{c+1}, and so on around the loop: the second list is the first rotated to start at i_c. The k rotations of a list are k different lists, since their first entries differ. So the lists fall into pairwise disjoint classes of k elements, one class per k-cycle, and by the counting fact, with N_k the number of k-cycles, k \, N_k =  rac{n!}{(n - k)!} . Dividing by k gives the formula. Check, n = 4. title: 3.5 Transpositions Generate the Symmetric Group
content:
Transpositions Generate the Symmetric Group Section 3.4 wrote permutations in cycle notation and showed that every permutation breaks into disjoint cycles (@thm-disjoint-cycle-decomposition). One small computation there, (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3) in @exm-cycle-notation, says more than it seems to: a 3-cycle is two swaps. This section shows that every permutation of \{1, \dots, n\}, for n \ge 2, is a product of swaps of two points. The determinant of linear algebra is built on exactly this fact, and so is the sign of a permutation, which later volumes define. Throughout, n \in 
N, products of permutations are read right to left (@def-symmetric-group: \sigma	au = \sigma \circ 	au applies 	au first), and a product 	au_1 	au_2 \cdots 	au_r is the product of a list in the group S_n (@def-group-list-product), so brackets may be dropped (@prp-group-list-product-laws (b)). Cycles as products of transpositions Recall from @def-cycle that a transposition is a 2-cycle (a\ b), with a 
e b: it swaps a and b and fixes every other point. Two facts about it are used constantly below. - (a\ b) = (b\ a), since both swap a and b and fix the rest (@fd2:prp-function-equality). - A transposition is its own inverse: (a\ b)(a\ b) = \id. Indeed a \mapsto b \mapsto a, b \mapsto a \mapsto b, and every other point is fixed twice. Equivalently, the inverse of (a\ b) is (b\ a) = (a\ b) (@def-cycle). The computation (1\ 3)(1\ 2) = (1\ 2\ 3) has a pattern: both transpositions contain the first entry 1 of the cycle, and the one applied first is (1\ 2), which sends 1 to the next entry. Longer cycles follow the same pattern. [A Cycle Is a Product of Transpositions] Let k \ge 2, and let i_1, i_2, \dots, i_k \in \{1, \dots, n\} be distinct. Then (i_1\ i_2\ \cdots\ i_k) = (i_1\ i_k)(i_1\ i_{k-1}) \cdots (i_1\ i_2) , a product of k - 1 transpositions. Read right to left, the factors are (i_1\ i_2), then (i_1\ i_3), and so on up to (i_1\ i_k). For k = 4: (1\ 2\ 3\ 4) = (1\ 4)(1\ 3)(1\ 2). Follow 2: the first factor (1\ 2) sends it to 1, the second sends 1 to 3, and the third fixes 3; so 2 \mapsto 3, as the cycle requires. Induct on the length. To pass from (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k) to (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k\ i_{k+1}), the only change is that i_k must now go to i_{k+1} instead of back to i_1, and i_{k+1} must go to i_1. One more swap of i_1 and i_{k+1}, applied after the shorter cycle, makes exactly this change. We prove, by @fd2:thm-induction with base 2 (read on \omega by @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)), the statement P(k): “for every list (i_1, \dots, i_k) of distinct points of \{1, \dots, n\}, the displayed equation holds”. Base, k = 2. The right-hand side is the list of one factor (i_1\ i_2), whose product is (i_1\ i_2) (@def-group-list-product), and this is the left-hand side. Step. Let k \ge 2, suppose P(k), and let i_1, \dots, i_{k+1} be distinct. Put \gamma \coloneqq (i_1\ \cdots\ i_k) and 	au \coloneqq (i_1\ i_{k+1}). We claim 	au\gamma = (i_1\ \cdots\ i_{k+1}), and check it point by point (@fd2:prp-function-equality). - For 1 \le j < k: \gamma(i_j) = i_{j+1}, which is neither i_1 (as j + 1 \ge 2) nor i_{k+1} (as j + 1 \le k), the entries being distinct; so 	au fixes it: 	au\gamma(i_j) = i_{j+1}. - \gamma(i_k) = i_1 and 	au(i_1) = i_{k+1}: so 	au\gamma(i_k) = i_{k+1}. - i_{k+1} is not among i_1, \dots, i_k, so \gamma fixes it, and 	au(i_{k+1}) = i_1: so 	au\gamma(i_{k+1}) = i_1. - Every other point x is fixed by \gamma and by 	au. These are the values of the (k+1)-cycle (@def-cycle), which proves the claim. By P(k) and the concatenation law @prp-group-list-product-laws (a), applied to the list (	au) and the list ((i_1\ i_k), \dots, (i_1\ i_2)), (i_1\ \cdots\ i_{k+1}) = 	au\gamma = (i_1\ i_{k+1})(i_1\ i_k) \cdots (i_1\ i_2) , which is P(k + 1). This proves the proposition. The proof never used that the cycle starts at its smallest entry, so the formula may be applied to any way of writing the cycle. Writing (1\ 2\ 3) as (2\ 3\ 1) gives (2\ 1)(2\ 3) = (1\ 2)(2\ 3), a second word for the same permutation; we return to this below. Write (2\ 5\ 3) as a product of transpositions, and check your answer point by point. By @prp-cycle-product-of-transpositions with i_1 = 2, i_2 = 5, i_3 = 3: (2\ 5\ 3) = (2\ 3)(2\ 5). Check, applying (2\ 5) first: 2 \mapsto 5 \mapsto 5, 5 \mapsto 2 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 3 \mapsto 2, and every other point is fixed. So 2 \mapsto 5, 5 \mapsto 3, 3 \mapsto 2, which is (2\ 5\ 3). Every permutation is a product of transpositions We say that \sigma \in S_n is a product of transpositions if \sigma = 	au_1 	au_2 \cdots 	au_r for some r \ge 1 and transpositions 	au_1, \dots, 	au_r \in S_n. The words “r \ge 1” matter for one permutation only: the identity is always the empty product (@def-group-list-product), but it is a product of at least one transposition only when a transposition exists, that is, when n \ge 2. Then \id = (1\ 2)(1\ 2). More generally, for a set T \subseteq S_n, \sigma is a product of elements of T if \sigma = t_1 t_2 \cdots t_r for some r \ge 1 and t_1, \dots, t_r \in T, and T generates S_n if every \sigma \in S_n is a product of elements of T.
