title: Formal Polynomials
content:
Formal Polynomials At school a polynomial is “an expression in x”, and x is a number not yet chosen. Over the field 
F_2 of Chapter 2 this picture breaks at once: x^2 + x takes the value 0 at both elements, so as a function it is the zero function, yet we want it to have degree 2. This chapter therefore decides that a polynomial is its list of coefficients, a sequence with only finitely many non-zero entries, and that x is the name of a position, never a number. From that one decision it builds the polynomial ring R[x] over any commutative ring R of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 3, and proves its laws with one device, check on monomials, extend by additivity, so that no double sum is ever reordered. It then attaches the degree and the leading coefficient, recovers “plugging in” as a ring homomorphism, and defines the derivative by its coefficients, with no limit in sight. Which school rules survive depends on R, and the chapter keeps count. Over 
Z/6
Z the degree of a product can drop, because [2][3] = [0]. Over 
Z/4
Z the polynomial 1 + [2]x is its own inverse. Over every finite ring with 1 
e 0 some non-zero polynomial vanishes at every element, so a polynomial is not its function. Over 
F_p the derivative of x^p is 0. Each result says what it needs from R: nothing at all, no zero divisors, a unit leading coefficient, finiteness with 1 
e 0, or, for the derivative, the characteristic of a field. The chapter ends where Chapter 5 begins, with R = F a field and division with remainder still to come. One construction, many rings. The linear-algebra companion defines polynomials over a field F, and its later chapters cite this chapter’s results with F a field. Every such statement is the case R = F of the statement proved here for a commutative ring, since a field is a commutative ring. Where a result really needs more than a commutative ring, the hypothesis is named at the point of use: no zero divisors (@thm-degree-of-product (b), @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors, @prp-polynomial-units), a unit leading coefficient (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), R finite with 1 
e 0 (@prp-polynomial-function-map (d)), or the characteristic of a field (@prp-formal-derivative-zero). What you need. Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 3 and 4 above all, with index arithmetic in 
N from its Chapter 2; Chapter 2 of this volume; Sets and Functions, Chapters 1, 2 and 4 and Section 3.3 (and Section 5.2 for R3); and induction from Logic and Proof, Chapter 4. - From Number Systems: From

Q(t) of @fd3:exm-rational-function-field took on school credit. - From Chapter 2: fields and the rule that a product of non-zero elements is non-zero (@def-field, @thm-field-basic-properties); 
F_p and the tables of 
F_2 (@def-field-fp, @exm-finite-fields); finite sums and integer multiples in a commutative ring (@lem-ring-finite-sums, @lem-integer-multiples); the characteristic, 0 or a prime (@def-characteristic, @thm-characteristic-prime); and, for Section 4.4’s Exercise C4, Fermat’s little theorem (@thm-fermat-little). - From Sets and Functions: functions and their equality, products and bijections (@fd2:def-function, @fd2:prp-function-equality, @fd2:def-cartesian-product, @fd2:def-bijective), from Chapter 1; the recursion theorem, with its sums, products and powers used as patterns (@fd2:thm-recursion, @fd2:def-sum-product, @fd2:def-power), from Section 3.3; finite sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:prp-subset-finite), from Section 4.1. - From Logic and Proof: induction (@fd1:ax-induction), from Section 4.2, and, for the two find-the-error exercises, the catalogue of moves that are not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), from Section 8.6. Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 and Chapter 2 enter only through the review exercises of Section 4.5: the complex numbers and their conjugate in R2, groups and their homomorphisms in R1. The countability results of Sets and Functions, Chapter 4, and its quotient sets (@fd2:def-quotient-set, Section 5.2) enter only through R3. Sections 4.1 and 4.4 also compare two results with Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 (@fd4:prp-power-laws-commutative-ring, @fd4:lem-difference-of-powers) without using them. Outside R2, no proof in the chapter uses 
R or 
C. Time. About 25 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 35 hours for everything. Roadmap - Polynomials as Coefficient Sequences. Why “an expression in x” fails over 
F_2; a polynomial over a commutative ring as a sequence 
N 	o R with only finitely many non-zero entries, with monomials, x = (0, 1, 0, \dots), equality by comparing coefficients, the display \sum_k p_k x^k as notation only, the zero ring, and the non-example (1, 1, 1, \dots); and a lemma collecting finite sums (which need only an addition), products of lists, powers and multiples, with the proofs of its new parts in a second-reading fold. - The Polynomial Ring. The sum taken position by position and the product as a convolution, closed in R[x] and computed over 
Q, 
F_3 and 
Z/6
Z; every polynomial an honest sum of its monomials; multiplication by a monomial as a shift and a scaling; the lemma that two maps additive in each argument and equal on monomials are equal; and the theorem that R[x] is a commutative ring containing R as its constants, with associativity proved on monomials instead of by reordering double sums. - Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains. Degree with \deg 0 = -\infty, the leading coefficient and monic polynomials; the degree of a sum; the degree of a product, whose top coefficient is \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q) in every commutative ring, so that degrees add exactly when that product is non-zero, as over a ring with no zero divisors or for a unit leading coefficient; integral domains, with R[x] an integral domain exactly when R is; the units of R[x] over an integral domain, and the non-constant unit 1 + [2]x over 
Z/4
Z; and the sets R[x]_{\le n} and R[x]_{= n}. - Evaluation, Substitution, and Polynomial Functions. The value p(c), roots, and evaluation respecting sums and products; ring homomorphisms and two impostors; the substitution principle, that one ring homomorphism R[x] 	o S extends a given \varphi \colon R 	o S and sends x to a given s, and only one; changing coefficients along \varphi, with reduction modulo n and the exact condition for the degree to drop, and the composition p \circ q; and the ring R^R of functions, with polynomial composition matching composition of functions and, over every finite ring with 1 
e 0, a non-zero polynomial whose function is 0. - The Formal Derivative. The derivative defined by (f')_k = (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1}, the role of the element n \cdot 1, and examples in five rings; the sum, product and power rules in every commutative ring, the product rule by checking on monomials; over a field, f' = 0 exactly for the constants in characteristic 0 and exactly for the polynomials in x^p in characteristic p; and review exercises that return to groups (Chapter 3), complex conjugation (Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1) and countability (Sets and Functions, Chapter 4). Named moves - Compare coefficients. Two polynomials are equal if and only if their coefficients agree in every position, so an identity in R[x] is proved by computing the k-th coefficient of both sides for an arbitrary k. It is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 3’s “reduce to the level below”, now with sequences. Named in Section 4.1, it proves the additive laws and both distributive laws of R[x] in Section 4.2 and the linearity of the derivative in Section 4.5. - Check on monomials, extend by additivity. Two maps of up to three polynomial arguments that are additive in each argument, and agree when every argument is a monomial, agree everywhere (@lem-check-on-monomials). It proves commutativity and associativity of the product in Section 4.2, evaluation and substitution respecting products in Section 4.4, and the product rule in Section 4.5. Exercise B2 of Section 4.2 leaves its last step to you, and Exercise C2 of Section 4.4 its second half. - Look at the top coefficient. The coefficient of x^{\deg p + \deg q} in pq is \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q), and nothing sits above it; every question about the degree of a product becomes the question whether that one element of R is 0. It proves the degree formula in Section 4.3 and, through it, the absence of zero divisors and the units of R[x]; in Section 4.4 it shows that the product of the factors x - c over a finite ring is monic, and Exercise B1 there uses it for the degree of a composition. - A homomorphism out of R[x] is fixed by the constants and x. To show that two ring homomorphisms out of R[x] agree, check that they agree on the constants and on x (@thm-polynomial-substitution (b)). Named in Section 4.4, it proves there that composing polynomials matches composing their functions, and Exercise B3 of Section 4.4 uses it to invert the shift p \mapsto p \circ (x + c).

title: 4.1 Polynomials as Coefficient Sequences
content:
Polynomials as Coefficient Sequences At school a polynomial is an expression such as 3x^2 - x + 2, and x is a number that has not been chosen yet. This chapter replaces that picture by a definition that works over every commutative ring of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 3 (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field): over 
Q, over the fields 
F_p of Chapter 2, and over rings such as 
Z/6
Z, where a product of two non-zero elements can be zero. This section makes the one decision the whole chapter rests on: a polynomial is its list of coefficients. It then collects the finite sums, powers and multiples that the next sections compute with. Throughout, R is a commutative ring, with a - b \coloneqq a + (-b). What goes wrong with “an expression in x” Take the field 
F_2 = \{0, 1\} of @def-field-fp, in which 1 + 1 = 0. Read x^2 + x the school way, as a rule: replace x by an element c and compute cc + c. The tables of @exm-finite-fields give 0 \cdot 0 + 0 = 0 , \qquad 1 \cdot 1 + 1 = 1 + 1 = 0 . So the rule c \mapsto cc + c and the rule c \mapsto 0 give the same output at both elements of 
F_2. As functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 they are equal, by @fd2:prp-function-equality: same domain, same codomain, same values. If a polynomial were the function it defines, then x^2 + x would be the zero polynomial over 
F_2. So would x^3 + x and x^4 + x^2, which also give 0 at 0 and 1 + 1 = 0 at 1. None of them would have a highest power of x, and the rule “the degree of a product is the sum of the degrees”, which we want over every field, would fail for x \cdot (x + 1) = x^2 + x: degrees 1 and 1, product “zero”. Over 
Q the problem never shows (Section 5.4 proves that over an infinite field a non-zero polynomial never gives the zero function), which is why school algebra can afford the picture. Over a finite ring with 1 
e 0 it cannot. So we decide the other way. Two polynomials are the same when their coefficients are the same, and the letter x is not a number at all. A polynomial is its list of coefficients; the letter x only marks the positions. Polynomials over a commutative ring A list of coefficients that goes on forever is a sequence, that is, a function on 
N. We keep only the sequences that stop being non-zero. [Polynomial] Let R be a commutative ring. A polynomial over R (in the indeterminate x) is a function p \colon 
N 	o R, written p = (p_0, p_1, p_2, \dots), such that only finitely many p_k are non-zero: there exists N \in 
N with p_k = 0 for every k > N. Such an N is called admissible for p. The element p_k is the coefficient of x^k in p. For a \in R and n \in 
N, the monomial a \, x^n is the polynomial with a in position n and 0 in every other position. We set x \coloneqq 1 \, x^1, and for a \in R the constant a is the monomial a \, x^0. The zero polynomial is 0 \coloneqq (0, 0, 0, \dots). The set of all polynomials over R is written R[x]. In words: the first clause says that a polynomial is an infinite list of elements of R, indexed from 0; the second says that from some position on, every entry is 0. The quantifiers are in the order “there is one N that works for every later k”: a sequence with infinitely many non-zero entries, however sparse, is excluded. A monomial has at most one non-zero entry, so n is admissible for it, and it is a polynomial. The symbol x is the particular sequence (0, 1, 0, 0, \dots): an element of R[x], never an element of R, and never a variable that takes values. Equality. Two polynomials p, q \in R[x] are functions with the same domain 
N and the same codomain R. By @fd2:prp-function-equality, p = q \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad p_k = q_k \ 	ext{ for every } k \in 
N . To prove an identity between polynomials we therefore compute the k-th coefficient of both sides, for an arbitrary k. We call this move compare coefficients. It is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 3’s “reduce to the level below” once more: a statement about polynomials becomes a statement about elements of R, one position at a time. The display. If N is admissible for p, we write p = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k = p_0 + p_1 x + p_2 x^2 + \dots + p_N x^N . For now this is notation only. No addition of polynomials has been defined yet, so the plus signs are not an operation: the display names the sequence by listing its entries, each with a marker x^k for its position. We drop terms whose coefficient is 0, write a x for a x^1, a for a x^0, x^k for 1 x^k, and - a x^k for (-a) x^k. So 3x^2 - x + 2 over 
Q names the sequence with p_0 = 2, p_1 = -1, p_2 = 3 and p_k = 0 for k \ge 3. Section 4.2 defines the sum of two polynomials and proves that the display is then an honest sum of monomials. There is one thing to check about the display. The admissible N is not unique: if N is admissible, so is every M \ge N, since k > M implies k > N. Passing from N to M only adds the terms 0 x^k for N < k \le M, which the convention drops. So every admissible N names the same sequence, and the display is well defined. Why “only finitely many”. Two later uses need it. In Section 4.4 we put an element c \in R in place of x and form \sum_k p_k c^k; in a ring only finite sums are defined, and finiteness is what makes the sum finite. In Section 4.3 every non-zero polynomial gets a degree, the highest position holding a non-zero coefficient; without finiteness there may be no highest position. The degenerate cases. The zero polynomial has every N admissible, including N = 0, and it is the monomial 0 \, x^n for every n. It is the one polynomial with no non-zero coefficient at all, and Section 4.3 will need a convention for its degree. At the other extreme, let R be the zero ring \{0\} of the examples after @fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, where 1 = 0. There is exactly one function 
N 	o \{0\}, so R[x] has exactly one element, the zero polynomial, and x = 1 \, x^1 = 0 \, x^1 = 0. This is why some results below assume 1 
e 0 in R. [Reading off coefficient sequences] Write the coefficient sequence of each polynomial, and check it against @def-polynomial. In a ring

Z, a natural number m written as an element stands for m \cdot [1] = [m] (@thm-integers-mod-n-ring (d)), just as @def-field-fp does for

F_2 (7 - 1 = 6 = 3 \cdot 2). The same symbol 7 names three different polynomials, one in each ring, and in each ring N = 0 is admissible. (e) (0, 0, 0, \dots), with every N admissible: the degenerate case. Now a non-example, by a minimal change. Start from 1 + x + x^2 \in 
Q[x], the sequence (1, 1, 1, 0, 0, \dots), and change every later 0 to 1. The result (1, 1, 1, 1, \dots), informally “1 + x + x^2 + \cdots”, is still a function

The price is that school rules about polynomials cannot be assumed: each one that survives is proved, here or (division with remainder, counting roots) in Chapter 5, and each result says what it needs from R (nothing at all, no zero divisors, a unit leading coefficient, finiteness with 1 
e 0, or, for the derivative, the characteristic of a field). p_2 is a coefficient; p(2) will be a value. Section 4.4 writes p(c) for the result of putting c \in R in place of x. For p = x^2 + 1 \in

This book never writes p(k) for a coefficient: the coefficient of x^k is p_k, always with a subscript. Is 6x^2 equal to the zero polynomial in (

e 0, while the zero polynomial has 0 there. Same display, two rings, two answers. Sums, powers and multiples The next section defines the product of two polynomials by a formula whose k-th coefficient is a finite sum \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i q_{k-i} of products in R. Later sections raise elements of R, and polynomials, to powers, and use multiples k \cdot a. This subsection collects what we use about all three. Most of it is already proved: finite sums and multiples in a commutative ring are Chapter 2’s (@lem-ring-finite-sums, @lem-integer-multiples), and the recursions follow the patterns that Sets and Functions, Section 3.3 set up for real numbers (@fd2:def-sum-product, @fd2:def-power). The patterns are reused; no fact about 
R is. One point deserves care before we start. The sums of polynomials in Section 4.2 must be formed before we know that R[x] is a commutative ring, because they are used to prove it. Let T be a set with a function + \colon T 	imes T 	o T and an element 0 \in T with 0 + u = u for every u \in T. For a sequence (u_i)_{i \in 
N} in T there is exactly one way to define \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i \in T, for k \in 
N, such that \sum_{i=0}^{0} u_i = u_0 , \qquad \sum_{i=0}^{k+1} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + u_{k+1} , starting from the empty sum 0. The sum \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i depends only on u_0, \dots, u_k; so a finite list u_0, \dots, u_k has a sum, computed from any extension of the list to a sequence. Likewise, a finite list s_1, \dots, s_r in R has a product \prod_{j=1}^{r} s_j, with \prod_{j=1}^{0} s_j = 1 and \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} s_j =  igl( \prod_{j=1}^{r} s_j  igr) s_{r+1}. 2. (Rules for sums in R.) For k \in 
N, c \in R and elements u_i, v_i \in R: (Σ1) \sum_{i=0}^{k} (u_i + v_i) = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + \sum_{i=0}^{k} v_i; (Σ2) c \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} c \, u_i; (Σ3) for j \in 
N: if u_i = 0 for every i \le k with i 
e j, then \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = u_j when j \le k, and \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = 0 when j > k; (Σ4) -\sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} (-u_i). 3. (Powers.) For s \in R and n \in 
N, s^0 \coloneqq 1 and s^{n+1} \coloneqq s^n s define s^n for every n, and for all s, t \in R and m, n \in 
N, s^{m+n} = s^m s^n , \qquad (s^m)^n = s^{mn} , \qquad (st)^n = s^n t^n . 4. (Multiples.) For all a, b \in R and m, n \in 
Z,  egin{aligned} (m + n) \cdot a &= m \cdot a + n \cdot a , & m \cdot (a + b) &= m \cdot a + m \cdot b , \ (m \cdot a) b &= m \cdot (ab) , & (m \cdot 1) a &= m \cdot a , \ (mn) \cdot a &= m \cdot (n \cdot a) . \end{aligned} In words: (a) says that a finite list in a set with an addition has a sum, built one term at a time, and that terms beyond the list do not matter; it needs no law of addition beyond 0 + u = u. (b) says that a finite sum of ring elements can be split into two sums, multiplied through by a constant, collapsed to its one non-zero term, or negated term by term. (c) is the three laws of exponents in a commutative ring. (d) is the arithmetic of the multiples m \cdot a of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 3.3 (“Multiples”), extended to m \in 
Z in Chapter 2: a dot with an integer on its left is always a multiple, and the product of two ring elements is written by juxtaposition. Parts (b) and (d) are cited from Chapter 2: (Σ1)–(Σ4) are @lem-ring-finite-sums (a), (b), (d), (e) (for (Σ3), apply @lem-ring-finite-sums (d) to the sequence that agrees with u_0, \dots, u_k and is 0 beyond k; by the finite-lists clause of part (a) above it has the same sum), and the five rules of part (d) above are @lem-integer-multiples (c), (d). Parts (a) and (c) are the recursions of Sets and Functions, Section 3.3, read in T and in R; each is built by @fd2:thm-recursion, and each of its laws is one short induction. Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1 proves the same three power laws for every commutative ring (@fd4:prp-power-laws-commutative-ring); we only compare with it, and prove (c) again from the template, so that this chapter’s main line rests on Chapter 2 and not on Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1. Each statement comes from @fd2:thm-recursion, and each law is one induction on one index, following the clauses of the recursion: the base case uses the starting value, and the step peels off the last term or factor. Only the laws of R named at each step are used. (a) Apply @fd2:thm-recursion (read on 
N = \omega through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) with X = T, starting value 0 and step (j, y) \mapsto y + u_j, a function 
N 	imes T 	o T because + maps T 	imes T into T. It gives exactly one sequence (S_j)_{j \in 
N} in T with S_0 = 0 and S_{j+1} = S_j + u_j. Set \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i \coloneqq S_{k+1}. Then \sum_{i=0}^{0} u_i = 0 + u_0 = u_0 by the hypothesis on 0, and \sum_{i=0}^{k+1} u_i = S_{k+1} + u_{k+1} = \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i + u_{k+1}. At j = k + 1 this gives \sum_{i=0}^{k} u_i = \sum_{i=0}^{k} v_i. The argument used only that + is a function on T. If s^{m+n} = s^m s^n, then s^{m+(n+1)} = s^{(m+n)+1} = s^{m+n} s = (s^m s^n) s = s^m (s^n s) = s^m s^{n+1} , using m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 (@fd3:thm-omega-arithmetic-laws (c)), the recursion, the hypothesis and (F5). We will use (a) twice over: for sums of ring elements, as in the product formula of Section 4.2, and for sums in R[x] of finitely many monomials, which Section 4.2 forms with its coefficientwise addition before any ring law of R[x] is known. title: 4.2 The Polynomial Ring

The Polynomial Ring Section 4.1 made a polynomial a coefficient sequence, and the display \sum_k p_k x^k only a way of writing it down. This section gives the sequences their sum and product, read off from what school algebra does with expressions, and proves that the result obeys every law of a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field). The obvious proof of associativity needs a theorem about reordering double sums that we have not proved. We avoid it with one device, check on monomials, extend by additivity, which returns in Sections 4.4 and 4.5. Throughout, R is a commutative ring and R[x] is the set of polynomials over R (@def-polynomial). Adding and multiplying coefficient sequences At school, (3x^2 - x + 2)(x + 1) is computed by multiplying every term of the first factor by every term of the second, using a_i x^i \cdot b_j x^j = a_i b_j x^{i+j}, and then collecting the terms with the same power. The coefficient of x^k in the result collects the products a_i b_j over all pairs with i + j = k, that is, over i = 0, \dots, k with j = k - i. Addition collects like powers too, so it adds coefficients position by position. We turn these two recipes into definitions. Add position by position; multiply by collecting, in position k, every product of a coefficient from position i with one from position k - i. The Polynomial Ring Let R be a commutative ring. For p, q \in R[x] and k \in 
N define (p + q)_k \coloneqq p_k + q_k , \qquad (-p)_k \coloneqq -p_k , \qquad (pq)_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i \, q_{k-i} . The set R[x] with this addition and this multiplication is the polynomial ring over R. In words: the sum and the negative act on each position separately. The product is the convolution of the two sequences: its entry in position k is a sum of k + 1 products in R, and the two positions in each product add up to k. For i \le k, the index k - i lies in

Z[x], (p_0, p_1, p_2, p_3) = (4, -1, 0, 2) and (q_0, q_1, q_2, q_3) = (3, 0, 1, -2), with 3 admissible for both; so (pq)_k = 0 for k > 6, and  egin{aligned} (pq)_0 &= 4 \cdot 3 = 12 , \ (pq)_1 &= 4 \cdot 0 + (-1) \cdot 3 = -3 , \ (pq)_2 &= 4 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 0 + 0 \cdot 3 = 4 , \ (pq)_3 &= 4 \cdot (-2) + (-1) \cdot 1 + 0 \cdot 0 + 2 \cdot 3 = -3 , \ (pq)_4 &= (-1)(-2) + 0 \cdot 1 + 2 \cdot 0 = 2 , \ (pq)_5 &= 0 \cdot (-2) + 2 \cdot 1 = 2 , \ (pq)_6 &= 2 \cdot (-2) = -4 , \end{aligned} where in positions 4, 5, 6 the terms with an index above 3 are 0 and have been left out. Hence pq = -4x^6 + 2x^5 + 2x^4 - 3x^3 + 4x^2 - 3x + 12 . In 
F_2[x] the displays name other sequences: 2 = 0, 4 = 0, -1 = 1, -2 = 0 and 3 = 1 in 
F_2, so the first factor is x and the second is x^2 + 1. By @lem-monomial-product (a) with a = 1, m = 1, the product shifts (1, 0, 1, 0, \dots) one place up: x(x^2 + 1) = x^3 + x. This agrees with reducing the integer coefficients 12, -3, 4, -3, 2, 2, -4 modulo 2, which gives 0, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 0. [B2: Changing the sign of x] Define \sigma \colon R[x] 	o R[x] by \sigma(p)_k \coloneqq (-1)^k p_k, where (-1)^k is the power in R (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)). Then \sigma(p) is a polynomial, since (-1)^k \cdot 0 = 0. We want to prove that \sigma(pq) = \sigma(p) \sigma(q) for all p, q \in R[x]. You may use the following, without proof. The map \sigma is additive: \sigma(p + q) = \sigma(p) + \sigma(q), position by position by (F9). Hence, with (\ast) and (\ast\ast), the maps \Phi(p, q) \coloneqq \sigma(pq) and \Psi(p, q) \coloneqq \sigma(p) \sigma(q) are additive in each argument. The last step is blank. Name the move, then complete it. The move is check on monomials, extend by additivity. Let a, b \in R and m, n \in 
N. The monomial a x^m has only position m possibly non-zero, so \sigma(a x^m) =  igl( (-1)^m a  igr) x^m. By @lem-monomial-product (b), \Phi(a x^m, b x^n) = \sigma igl( (ab) x^{m+n}  igr) =  igl( (-1)^{m+n} ab  igr) x^{m+n} , \Psi(a x^m, b x^n) =  igl( (-1)^m a  igr) x^m \cdot  igl( (-1)^n b  igr) x^n =  igl( (-1)^m a \, (-1)^n b  igr) x^{m+n} . The two coefficients agree: (-1)^m a \, (-1)^n b =  igl( (-1)^m (-1)^n  igr) (ab) = (-1)^{m+n} ab, by (F5) and (F6) in R and the first power law of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c). So \Phi and \Psi agree on monomials, and by @lem-check-on-monomials with two arguments and T = R[x], \sigma(pq) = \sigma(p) \sigma(q) for all p, q. Also \sigma(1) = 1, since (-1)^0 = 1. Section 4.4 writes \sigma(p) as p(-x). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the ring laws] Let R be a commutative ring. Prove, from @def-polynomial-ring, that the multiplication of R[x] is commutative and associative. You may use the laws of R, @lem-finite-sums-and-powers, @fd1:ax-induction and @fd2:prp-function-equality, but no result of this section after @def-polynomial-ring. Distributivity. For p, p', q, q' \in R[x], the k-th coefficient of (p + p')q is \sum_{i=0}^{k} (p_i + p'_i) q_{k-i}. Inside each term, (F6), (F9), (F6) give p_i q_{k-i} + p'_i q_{k-i}, and (Σ1) splits the sum into (pq)_k + (p'q)_k. So (p + p')q = pq + p'q, and in the same way, with (F9) directly, p(q + q') = pq + pq'. Hence (p, q) \mapsto pq and (p, q) \mapsto qp are additive in each argument, and so are (p, q, r) \mapsto (pq)r and (p, q, r) \mapsto p(qr), by applying the two laws twice. Monomials. For a, b \in R and m, n \in 
N, the k-th coefficient of (a x^m)(b x^n) is \sum_{i=0}^{k} (a x^m)_i (b x^n)_{k-i}. Every term with i 
e m is 0, and the term with i = m (present when m \le k) is a \, (b x^n)_{k-m}, which is ab if k = m + n and 0 otherwise. By (Σ3), (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n}. Reduction. (i) For p \in R[x], the sum s_N \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k in (R[x], +) (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a)) has p_j in position j \le N and 0 beyond, by @fd1:ax-induction on N: s_0 = p_0 x^0, and s_{N+1} = s_N + p_{N+1} x^{N+1} has coefficients p_j + 0, 0 + p_{N+1} and 0 + 0 for j \le N, j = N + 1 and j > N + 1, by (F1) and (F3). So p = s_N for admissible N (@fd2:prp-function-equality). (ii) Let \Phi, \Psi \colon R[x] 	o R[x] be additive and agree on monomials. By @fd1:ax-induction on N, \Phi(p) = \Psi(p) for every p for which N is admissible: for N = 0, p = p_0 x^0 by (i); if N + 1 is admissible for p, then p = s_N + p_{N+1} x^{N+1} with N admissible for s_N, by (i), and \Phi(p) = \Phi(s_N) + \Phi(p_{N+1} x^{N+1}) = \Psi(s_N) + \Psi(p_{N+1} x^{N+1}) = \Psi(p) by additivity, the induction hypothesis with the monomial case, and additivity. Every polynomial has an admissible N, so \Phi = \Psi. (iii) With two arguments, fix a monomial u and apply (ii) to v \mapsto \Phi(u, v) and v \mapsto \Psi(u, v); then fix any q and apply (ii) to the first argument. With three, treat the third, the second and the first argument in turn. Commutativity. (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n} = (ba) x^{n+m} = (b x^n)(a x^m), by (F6) in R and m + n = n + m in 
N; the reduction gives pq = qp. Associativity.  igl( (a x^m)(b x^n)  igr)(c x^l) =  igl( (ab)c  igr) x^{(m+n)+l} and (a x^m) igl( (b x^n)(c x^l)  igr) =  igl( a(bc)  igr) x^{m+(n+l)}, equal by (F5) in R and associativity of + in 
N; the reduction with three arguments gives (pq)r = p(qr). Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: both distributive laws from the coefficient formula, naming the rule for a single-index sum ((Σ1)) and the law of R used inside each term. - 2: the product of two monomials, (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n}, with the vanishing of the other terms shown. - 3: the reduction to monomials, with additivity in each argument stated and used one argument at a time (both inductions proved in the answer; citing @lem-check-on-monomials earns none of these points). - 1: commutativity on monomials, naming (F6) in R. - 2: associativity on monomials, naming (F5) in R and the law of 
N used for the exponents. Fatal errors (0 for the step): treating polynomials as functions on R and citing the laws of R “pointwise”; checking only on x^m and x^n, with no account of the coefficients (the coefficients are where (F5) and (F6) of R are needed). A direct route works with coefficients throughout: commutativity by (F6) and the reversal i \mapsto k - i of a finite sum, associativity by rewriting both triple products as one sum over all (i, j, l) with i + j + l = k. Each needs a lemma that (Σ1)–(Σ4) do not contain, proved by induction. Commutativity with the reversal proved earns 3 points (the monomial product and commutativity on monomials); associativity with the reindexing proved earns the other 7. An unproved reversal or reindexing earns 0 for that step. [C2: Formal power series] Let R^{
N} be the set of all sequences 
N 	o R, with sum and product given by the formulas of @def-polynomial-ring. 1. Show that the formulas define functions R^{
N} 	imes R^{
N} 	o R^{
N}. 2. Show that R[x] \subseteq R^{
N} is closed under the sum and the product. 3. Let s \coloneqq (1, 1, 1, \dots). Show that (1 - x) s = 1. 4. Which step of the proof of @lem-check-on-monomials (with one argument) does not reach the elements of R^{
N}? (a) For p, q \in R^{
N} and k \in 
N, p_k + q_k \in R, and \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i q_{k-i} is a sum of k + 1 elements of R, defined by @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a). No finiteness of p or q is needed: each coefficient of the product only looks at positions 0, \dots, k. So both formulas give sequences 
N 	o R. (b) This is the closure paragraph after @def-polynomial-ring: if m and n are admissible for p and q, then \max(m, n) is admissible for p + q and m + n for pq. (c) 1 - x = (1, -1, 0, 0, \dots). In position 0,  igl( (1 - x)s  igr)_0 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1. In position k \ge 1, write the i-th term as v_i + w_i (by (F1) and (F3)), with v_0 = 1 \cdot 1, w_1 = (-1) \cdot 1 and every other v_i, w_i equal to 0, since for i \ge 2 the term is 0 \cdot 1 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) with (F6)). By (Σ1) and (Σ3), the sum is 1 \cdot 1 + (-1) \cdot 1 = 1 + (-1) = 0, by (F7) and (F4). So (1 - x)s = (1, 0, 0, \dots) = 1. (d) The induction proves \Phi(p) = \Psi(p) only for sequences p that have an admissible N; the step from it to \Phi = \Psi uses that every polynomial has one. The sequence s has none, and it is not a finite sum of monomials either, since by (b) such a sum is a polynomial. So @lem-check-on-monomials says nothing about s, and the proof of @thm-polynomial-ring-laws does not apply to R^{
N}. The ring laws do hold in R^{
N}, the ring of formal power series, though we do not prove this here; nothing in this book depends on it. So (1 - x)s = 1 among all sequences, while Section 4.3 shows that over 
Z, 1 - x is not a unit of 
Z[x].

title: 4.3 Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains
content:
Degree, Leading Coefficients, and Integral Domains Section 4.2 made R[x] a commutative ring for every commutative ring R (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws). This section attaches to each non-zero polynomial its degree, the position of its last non-zero coefficient, and asks the school question: is the degree of a product the sum of the degrees? Over 
Z it is. Over 
Z/6
Z it is not, and the reason is a single product of two elements of R. Sorting out which rings behave like 
Z leads to the integral domains, and to the two facts later chapters use most: a polynomial ring over an integral domain has no zero divisors, and its units are the units of R. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), and polynomials are coefficient sequences (@def-polynomial), with the sum and product of @def-polynomial-ring. Degree and leading coefficient Here is the computation that drives the section. Multiply p = 2x + 1 by q = 3x^2 + x by the product formula of @def-polynomial-ring, once in 
Z[x] and once in (
Z/6
Z)[x]. The coefficients of p are 1, 2, 0, 0, \dots and those of q are 0, 1, 3, 0, \dots, so  egin{aligned} (pq)_0 &= p_0 q_0 = 0, \ (pq)_1 &= p_0 q_1 + p_1 q_0 = 1, \ (pq)_2 &= p_0 q_2 + p_1 q_1 + p_2 q_0 = 3 + 2 = 5, \ (pq)_3 &= p_0 q_3 + p_1 q_2 + p_2 q_1 + p_3 q_0 = 2 \cdot 3 = 6, \end{aligned} and (pq)_k = 0 for k \ge 4. Over 
Z the product is 6x^3 + 5x^2 + x, with its last non-zero coefficient in position 3 = 1 + 2. Over 
Z/6
Z the same sums are read modulo 6: (pq)_3 = [6] = [0], and the product is [5]x^2 + x, whose last non-zero coefficient sits in position 2. The top coefficient of the product was 2 \cdot 3, the product of the top coefficients of the factors, and in 
Z/6
Z that product is [0] (@exm-integers-mod-six). To state any of this we need a name for “the position of the last non-zero coefficient”. A non-zero polynomial has one, because only finitely many of its coefficients are non-zero. The degree of a polynomial is the position of its last non-zero coefficient; the leading coefficient is the coefficient sitting there. [Degree, Leading Coefficient, Monic] Let R be a commutative ring and p \in R[x]. 1. If p 
e 0, the degree \deg p is the largest n \in 
N with p_n 
e 0. The leading coefficient of p is \operatorname{lc}(p) \coloneqq p_{\deg p}, and p is monic if \operatorname{lc}(p) = 1. 2. The zero polynomial has degree \deg 0 \coloneqq -\infty, and no leading coefficient. Here -\infty is a symbol not in 
N, with the conventions -\infty < n and -\infty + n = n + (-\infty) = -\infty for every n \in 
N, and -\infty + (-\infty) = -\infty. In words: (a) looks along the coefficient sequence and stops at the last place where it is non-zero; that place is the degree, and the entry there is the leading coefficient. A polynomial is monic when that entry is 1. Clause (b) gives the zero polynomial, which has no non-zero coefficient at all, a degree below every natural number. Well-definedness. Let p 
e 0, and let N be admissible for p: p_k = 0 for every k > N (@def-polynomial). The set S \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : p_n 
e 0 \} is non-empty, since p is not the zero sequence, and every element of S is at most N. Read in 
Z \supseteq 
N (@fd3:prp-naturals-embed-integers), S is a non-empty set of integers bounded above, so it has a greatest element (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element). That element is \deg p. Two facts come with it, and every proof below uses them: p_{\deg p} 
e 0 , \qquad p_k = 0 \ 	ext{ for every } k > \deg p . The second says that \deg p is itself admissible for p, and the least admissible N: any smaller N would leave the non-zero coefficient p_{\deg p} beyond it. Examples. - In 
Q[x], \deg(3x^2 - x + 2) = 2 with leading coefficient 3; x^2 + 1 is monic of degree 2. The monomial a x^n with a 
e 0 has degree n and leading coefficient a. - A non-zero constant a = a x^0 has degree 0. The constant 0 has degree -\infty, not 0: degree 0 means “a constant, and not the zero one”. - Degree depends on the ring. The integer polynomial 6x^3 + 5x^2 + x has degree 3 in 
Z[x]; its coefficients read in 
Z/6
Z give [5]x^2 + x, of degree 2. Read in 
Z/5
Z they give x^3 + x ([6] = [1], [5] = [0]), monic of degree 3. - The degenerate ring. If 1 = 0 in R, then every a \in R is a = a \cdot 1 = a \cdot 0 = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b)), so R = \{0\}, and the only polynomial over R is the zero sequence. Every polynomial over the zero ring has degree -\infty, and no polynomial over it is monic. This is why “monic” will never need the hypothesis 1 
e 0: a monic polynomial is non-zero, so its ring has 1 = \operatorname{lc}(p) 
e 0. Non-example by minimal change. The sequence (1, 1, 1, \dots) has no degree: the set S of its non-zero positions is all of 
N, which has no greatest element. It fails exactly the clause “only finitely many” of @def-polynomial, which is what made S bounded above. Any value given to \deg 0 is a convention, and the choice is made so that the rule “degrees add under products” survives the zero polynomial. For every q, 0 \cdot q = 0, so the rule asks for \deg 0 = \deg 0 + \deg q. If \deg 0 were an integer d, then in any ring with 1 
e 0 the case q = x, of degree 1, would give d = d + 1. No integer works; a symbol -\infty with -\infty + n = -\infty does. The order -\infty < n then lets “\deg p \le n” include the zero polynomial, which is what the sets R[x]_{\le n} at the end of this section need. The leading coefficient is the coefficient of the highest power, not the first one written. In 2 + x - 5x^3 \in 
Q[x], the leading coefficient is -5, and the polynomial is not monic although its x has coefficient 1. And the zero polynomial has no leading coefficient at all: “\operatorname{lc}(p)” silently assumes p 
e 0. The degree of a sum A sum cannot raise the degree, because adding coefficients position by position creates no non-zero coefficient beyond the last non-zero ones of the summands. [Degree of a Sum] Let R be a commutative ring and p, q \in R[x]. Then \deg(p + q) \le \max(\deg p, \deg q) , with equality when \deg p 
e \deg q. Beyond the larger of the two degrees both summands have only zero coefficients, so the sum does too. When one degree is strictly larger, the other summand contributes 0 at that top position, and the top coefficient survives. Let M \coloneqq \max(\deg p, \deg q). If M = -\infty, then p = q = 0, so p + q = 0 and both sides are -\infty. Otherwise M \in 
N, and for k > M we have k > \deg p and k > \deg q, so p_k = 0 and q_k = 0 (by the two facts after @def-degree when the polynomial is non-zero, and trivially when it is 0). Hence (p + q)_k = p_k + q_k = 0 + 0 = 0 for every k > M, by @def-polynomial-ring and (F3). So either p + q = 0, with degree -\infty < M, or p + q 
e 0 and its last non-zero coefficient is at a position \le M. In both cases \deg(p + q) \le M. Now let \deg p 
e \deg q; by symmetry \deg q < \deg p, so p 
e 0 and M = \deg p. Then q_M = 0, and (p + q)_M = p_M + q_M = p_M + 0 = p_M 
e 0 , so p + q 
e 0 and \deg(p + q) \ge M. With the first part, \deg(p + q) = M. The inequality is strict exactly when \deg p = \deg q = M \in 
N and the leading coefficients cancel, p_M + q_M = 0: for example (x^2 + x) + (-x^2 + 1) = x + 1, of degree 1 < 2, and x + (-x) = 0, of degree -\infty < 1. The degree of a product The opening computation suggests how a product behaves at the top. In (pq)_k = \sum_{i=0}^{k} p_i q_{k-i}, a term can be non-zero only if i \le \deg p and k - i \le \deg q; for k = \deg p + \deg q that leaves exactly one term. We call this move look at the top coefficient. [Degree of a Product] Let R be a commutative ring, let p, q \in R[x] be non-zero, and let m \coloneqq \deg p, n \coloneqq \deg q. 1. (pq)_k = 0 for every k > m + n, and (pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). Hence \deg(pq) \le \deg p + \deg q for all p, q \in R[x], zero or not; and if p = 0 or q = 0, then pq = 0 and \deg(pq) = -\infty = \deg p + \deg q. 2. \deg(pq) = m + n if and only if \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q) 
e 0, and then \operatorname{lc}(pq) = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). This holds in particular - when R has no zero divisors (ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0), for example when R is a field (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)); together with the last clause of (a), \deg(pq) = \deg p + \deg q then holds for all p, q \in R[x], zero or not; - when \operatorname{lc}(p) is a unit of R (@def-ring-unit), in particular when p is monic. In words: (a) says that the product has nothing above position m + n, and that what sits at m + n is the product of the two leading coefficients, in every commutative ring; (b) says that the degree formula holds precisely when that one product is non-zero, and names two common situations where it is. The top of a product comes from the tops of the factors alone. Above m + n every term p_i q_{k-i} has a factor beyond the top of p or beyond the top of q; at m + n exactly one term escapes, p_m q_n. So the only question is whether p_m q_n can be 0, and that is a question about R, not about polynomials. Before reading on: which line needs R to have no zero divisors, and which works in every ring? (a) Let k \ge m + n and 0 \le i \le k, and consider the term p_i q_{k-i} of (pq)_k (@def-polynomial-ring). If i > m, then p_i = 0. If i \le m, then k - i \ge k - m \ge n, and k - i > n (so q_{k-i} = 0) unless k = m + n and i = m. So every term with i 
e m, or with k > m + n, has a factor 0, and is 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) with (F6). For k > m + n, all terms of (pq)_k are 0, so (pq)_k = 0 by (Σ3) of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b) (with j = 0). For k = m + n, every term with i 
e m is 0, and m \le m + n, so (Σ3) with j = m leaves (pq)_{m+n} = p_m q_n = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q) . For the inequality, let p, q \in R[x] be arbitrary. If p = 0, every coefficient of pq is a sum of terms 0 \cdot q_{k-i} = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), (F6)), so pq = 0, and both sides of the inequality are -\infty by the conventions of @def-degree, which is also the last clause of (a); likewise if q = 0. If p, q 
e 0 and pq = 0, the left side is -\infty < m + n. Otherwise pq 
e 0, and since (pq)_k = 0 for every k > m + n, its last non-zero coefficient is at a position \le m + n: \deg(pq) \le m + n. (b) By (a), m + n is admissible for pq, and (pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). If this element is non-zero, then pq 
e 0, its last non-zero coefficient is at m + n, and so \deg(pq) = m + n and \operatorname{lc}(pq) = (pq)_{m+n} = \operatorname{lc}(p) \operatorname{lc}(q). If it is 0, then (pq)_k = 0 for every k \ge m + n, so \deg(pq) < m + n. For the two situations: p_m 
e 0 and q_n 
e 0 by @def-degree, so if R has no zero divisors, p_m q_n 
e 0. If u \coloneqq p_m is a unit and u q_n = 0, then q_n = (u^{-1} u) q_n = u^{-1}(u q_n) = u^{-1} \cdot 0 = 0, by (F6), (F7), (F5) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), against q_n 
e 0; so p_m q_n 
e 0. A monic p has p_m = 1, a unit since 1 \cdot 1 = 1. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. Part (a), including the inequality, uses only (F1)–(F7), (F9), @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b), (Σ3) of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b), and the two facts after @def-degree and its conventions, all valid in every commutative ring: it holds over 
Z/6
Z as over 
Q. Part (b) as an equivalence also holds in every ring. “No zero divisors” enters in one line, the first sentence of the last paragraph, and only to decide that p_m q_n 
e 0; the unit hypothesis is a second, different way to decide the same thing. The degree formula is not automatic. In (
Z/6
Z)[x], the opening computation gives ([2]x + [1])([3]x^2 + x) = [5]x^2 + x , a product of polynomials of degrees 1 and 2 that has degree 2, not 3. The coefficient (pq)_3 is \operatorname{lc}(p)\operatorname{lc}(q) = [2][3] = [6] = [0] (@exm-integers-mod-six). Part (a) of @thm-degree-of-product holds here; the hypothesis of (b) fails. Let p, q \in 
Q[x] with \deg p = 3 and \deg q = 2. What are \deg(pq), \deg(p + q) and \deg(p^2), where p^2 \coloneqq pp? Can you say what \deg(p - x^3) is? \deg(pq) = 5 and \deg(p^2) = 6, by @thm-degree-of-product (b): 
Q is a field (@fd3:thm-rationals-field), so it has no zero divisors. \deg(p + q) = 3, by the equality case of @thm-degree-of-sum, since 3 
e 2. The degree of p - x^3 is not determined: it is 3 if \operatorname{lc}(p) 
e 1, at most 2 if p is monic, and -\infty if p = x^3. The difference has coefficient \operatorname{lc}(p) - 1 at position 3, and that coefficient decides. Integral domains @thm-degree-of-product (b) asks for one property of R: a product of two non-zero elements is non-zero. The integers have it, every field has it, 
Z/6
Z lacks it. A ring that has it, and is not the zero ring, gets a name. An integral domain is a commutative ring in which a product is zero only when a factor is zero. [Integral Domain] An integral domain is a commutative ring R with 1 
e 0 and no zero divisors: for all a, b \in R, if ab = 0, then a = 0 or b = 0. In words: the zero ring is excluded, and the rule “a product vanishes only if a factor vanishes”, the rule used to solve (x - 1)(x - 2) = 0 at school, holds in R. Equivalently, by contraposition: the product of two non-zero elements is non-zero. [Which Rings Are Integral Domains] Decide which of the following are integral domains: 
Z; a field, and in particular 
Q and 
Z/p
Z for a prime p; 
Z/n
Z for n \ge 2 not prime (@fd2:def-prime); 
Z/1
Z; and 
Z 	imes 
Z with componentwise operations, (a, b) + (c, d) \coloneqq (a + c, b + d) and (a, b)(c, d) \coloneqq (ac, bd). 
Z: yes. It is a commutative ring with 1 
e 0 (@fd3:thm-integers-commutative-ring), and an ordered commutative ring (@fd3:thm-integers-ordered-ring), so ab = 0 implies a = 0 or b = 0 by @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (f). A field: yes. A field has 1 
e 0 (@def-field) and no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)). So 
Q (@fd3:thm-rationals-field) and 
Z/p

title: 4.4 Evaluation, Substitution, and Polynomial Functions
content:
Evaluation, Substitution, and Polynomial Functions A polynomial, in this chapter, is a sequence of coefficients (@def-polynomial), not a function. But every polynomial defines a function: put an element c of the ring in place of x and add up. More generally we can put in place of x a class modulo n, or another polynomial, after first moving the coefficients into the ring where the substitution happens. This section proves one theorem, the substitution principle, that covers all of these at once, because each is a ring homomorphism out of R[x] determined by where it sends the constants and x. Then it compares a polynomial with its function, and shows that over every finite ring other than the zero ring the passage from polynomials to functions loses information. Throughout, R and S are commutative rings (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field), and powers s^n and finite sums are those of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers. Evaluating a polynomial To evaluate a polynomial at c, replace each monomial a x^k by the element a c^k and add. [Evaluation, Root, Polynomial Function] Let R be a commutative ring, p \in R[x] and c \in R. The value of p at c is p(c) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k \in R , for any N \in 
N with p_k = 0 for every k > N. The element c is a root of p if p(c) = 0. The polynomial function of p is the function R 	o R, c \mapsto p(c). In words: the value is the finite sum of the coefficients times the powers of c, with c^0 = 1, so the constant coefficient enters as itself. The sum runs far enough to include every non-zero coefficient, and how far beyond that is our choice. Only finitely many coefficients are non-zero, and this is what makes the sum finite; a sequence such as (1, 1, 1, \dots) would ask for an infinite sum, which a ring does not provide. Well-definedness. The definition allows many N, and they all give the same element: enlarging N only adds terms 0 \cdot c^k = 0. The fold below writes this out. Let N be admissible for p. We show by @fd1:ax-induction on j (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) that \sum_{k=0}^{N+j} p_k c^k = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k. The case j = 0 is trivial, and the sum recursion of @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a) gives  egin{aligned} \sum_{k=0}^{N+j+1} p_k c^k &= \sum_{k=0}^{N+j} p_k c^k + p_{N+j+1} c^{N+j+1} \ &= \sum_{k=0}^{N+j} p_k c^k + 0 , \end{aligned} since p_{N+j+1} = 0 and 0 \cdot c^{N+j+1} = 0 (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b) with (F6)); then (F3) and the hypothesis finish. Q the implication does hold: Chapter 5 proves it for every infinite field, by bounding the number of roots of a non-zero polynomial. Over 
Z it follows, though we do not prove it here: read p \in 
Z[x] as a polynomial with the same coefficients in 
Q[x], where it vanishes at infinitely many points. In this chapter, two polynomials are equal only when their coefficients are equal. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about @thm-polynomial-substitution and its proof, except the last. 1. Where in the proof is \varphi(1) = 1 used? 2. Where is the commutativity of S used? 3. Run the theorem with R = 
Z, S = 
Z/5
Z, \varphi the quotient map, s = [2] and p = x^2 + 3x + 1: compute \Phi(p). For the uniqueness half, explain why any ring homomorphism \Psi with \Psi(a) = [a] on constants and \Psi(x) = [2] must send 3x^2 to [2]. 4. Give the idea of the proof in two sentences. 5. In 
F_3[x], compute the values of (x + 2)(x^2 + x + 1) at 0, 1, 2, and find all its roots in 
F_3. (a) Twice: for \Phi(1) = \varphi(1) s^0 = 1, and for \Phi(x) = \varphi(1) s^1 = s. (b) Essentially once: in the monomial computation, to rewrite \varphi(a)\varphi(b) s^m s^n as  igl(\varphi(a) s^m igr) igl(\varphi(b) s^n igr), which moves \varphi(b) past s^m by (F6) in S. The proof also uses (F6) in S for 0 \cdot s^k = 0, for the right distributive law in the additivity steps, and for 1 \cdot s = s; these uses only give the mirror forms of a \cdot 0 = 0, (F9) and (F7). An answer that lists them too, with this distinction, is correct. (c) The coefficients of p are 1, 3, 1, so \Phi(p) = [1] + [3][2] + [1][2]^2 = [1 + 6 + 4] = [11] = [1]. For the uniqueness half: 3x^2 is the product of the constant 3 and x^2 (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (c)), so \Psi(3x^2) = \Psi(3)\Psi(x)^2 = [3][2]^2 = [12] = [2]. No other value is possible, because \Psi respects products. (d) A ring homomorphism out of R[x] has no freedom: it must send a x^n to \varphi(a) s^n, so the formula is forced and uniqueness follows by additivity. The only work is to show that the forced formula respects products, and that is a check on monomials, where it becomes the power law and one reordering of factors in the commutative ring S. (e) Evaluation respects products (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so the value is the product of the values of the factors. At 0: 2 \cdot 1 = 2. At 1: (1 + 2)(1 + 1 + 1) = 0 \cdot 0 = 0. At 2: (2 + 2)(4 + 2 + 1) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1 (in 
F_3, 4 = 7 = 1). So the only root is 1. Multiplied out by the product formula, the polynomial is x^3 + 3x^2 + 3x + 2 = x^3 + 2 in 
F_3[x], the second example after @def-polynomial-evaluation, whose values 2, 0, 1 agree. B. Practice [B1: The degree of a composition] Let R be an integral domain, p, q \in R[x], p 
e 0, and \deg q \ge 1. Prove that \deg(p \circ q) = \deg p \cdot \deg q. Show by an example that the hypothesis \deg q \ge 1 cannot be dropped. Let d \coloneqq \deg p and e \coloneqq \deg q \ge 1. Powers of q. By @fd1:ax-induction on k, q^k 
e 0, \deg q^k = ke and \operatorname{lc}(q^k) = \operatorname{lc}(q)^k. For k = 0, q^0 = 1 has degree 0 and leading coefficient 1 (as 1 
e 0). For the step, q^{k+1} = q^k q, and since R has no zero divisors, @thm-degree-of-product (b) gives degree ke + e = (k + 1)e and leading coefficient \operatorname{lc}(q)^k \operatorname{lc}(q). The top term. By @def-polynomial-composition with N = d, p \circ q = \sum_{k=0}^{d} p_k q^k. The term p_d q^d is the product of the non-zero constant p_d (degree 0) and q^d, so by @thm-degree-of-product (b) it has degree de. Every other term p_k q^k with k < d is 0 or has degree ke < de, since e \ge 1 (@thm-degree-of-product (a)). By @thm-degree-of-sum and induction along the sum recursion, r \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} p_k q^k has \deg r < de (for d = 0, r is the empty sum 0). Then p \circ q = r + p_d q^d, and the equality case of @thm-degree-of-sum gives \deg(p \circ q) = de. The hypothesis on q. Take R = 
Z, p = x - 1 and q = 1, of degree 0. Then p \circ q = 1 - 1 = 0, of degree -\infty, while \deg p \cdot \deg q = 1 \cdot 0 = 0. A constant q can make the top terms cancel. [B2: All polynomials of degree at most two over the field with two elements] List the elements of 
F_2[x]_{\le 2} with their degrees and their functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 (given by the values at 0 and 1). How many functions 
F_2 	o 
F_2 are there, and how many of the eight polynomials give each one? By @def-polynomials-bounded-degree, the elements are a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 with a_i \in \{0, 1\}; there are eight (@exr-degree-b3 for 
F_2, n = 2). The value at 0 is a_0, and the value at 1 is a_0 + a_1 + a_2 in 
F_2.  egin{array}{l|c|c|c} p & \deg p & p(0) & p(1) \ \hline 0 & -\infty & 0 & 0 \ 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \ x & 1 & 0 & 1 \ x + 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \ x^2 & 2 & 0 & 1 \ x^2 + 1 & 2 & 1 & 0 \ x^2 + x & 2 & 0 & 0 \ x^2 + x + 1 & 2 & 1 & 1 \end{array} A function 
F_2 	o 
F_2 is determined by its two values, so there are 2 \cdot 2 = 4 of them, and each occurs for exactly two polynomials in the table: (0, 0) for 0 and x^2 + x; (1, 1) for 1 and x^2 + x + 1; (0, 1) for x and x^2; (1, 0) for x + 1 and x^2 + 1. In each pair the two polynomials differ by x^2 + x, the polynomial of @exm-polynomial-vs-function-f2. [B3: Shifting the variable] Let R be a commutative ring and c \in R. Define T_c \colon R[x] 	o R[x] by T_c(p) \coloneqq p \circ (x + c). Prove that T_c is a bijective ring homomorphism with inverse T_{-c}. By @def-polynomial-composition, T_c is a ring homomorphism that fixes every constant and sends x to x + c; likewise T_{-c} fixes constants and sends x to x - c. The composite T_{-c} \circ T_c is a ring homomorphism (after @def-ring-homomorphism) that fixes constants, and T_{-c}(T_c(x)) = T_{-c}(x + c) = T_{-c}(x) + T_{-c}(c) = (x - c) + c = x . The identity map of R[x] is also a ring homomorphism that fixes constants and sends x to x. By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-substitution (b), with S = R[x], \varphi the constants and s = x, T_{-c} \circ T_c = \id_{R[x]}. Exchanging c and -c (and -(-c) = c), T_c \circ T_{-c} = \id_{R[x]}. So T_c has the inverse T_{-c}, and is a bijection (@fd2:def-bijective). C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: the substitution principle] State and prove @thm-polynomial-substitution. Statement. Let R and S be commutative rings, \varphi \colon R 	o S a ring homomorphism and s \in S, and let \Phi(p) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} \varphi(p_k) s^k for N admissible for p. Then \Phi \colon R[x] 	o S is a well-defined ring homomorphism with \Phi(a) = \varphi(a) for constants and \Phi(x) = s, and it is the only ring homomorphism R[x] 	o S with these two properties. Well defined. Enlarging N by one adds the term \varphi(0) s^{k} = 0 \cdot s^k = 0, since \varphi(0) + \varphi(0) = \varphi(0) gives \varphi(0) = 0; by induction any two admissible N give the same sum. In particular \Phi(a x^m) = \varphi(a) s^m, the other terms being 0. Additive. With N admissible for p and q, \Phi(p + q) = \sum_k \varphi(p_k + q_k) s^k = \sum_k  igl(\varphi(p_k) s^k + \varphi(q_k) s^k igr) = \Phi(p) + \Phi(q), by additivity of \varphi, (F9) and (F6) in S, and (Σ1). Multiplicative. The maps (p, q) \mapsto \Phi(pq) and (p, q) \mapsto \Phi(p)\Phi(q) are additive in p for fixed q, and in q for fixed p: the first because multiplication in R[x] distributes over addition and \Phi is additive, the second because \Phi is additive and multiplication in S distributes. On monomials, \Phi igl((ab) x^{m+n} igr) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b) s^m s^n =  igl(\varphi(a) s^m igr) igl(\varphi(b) s^n igr) , by multiplicativity of \varphi, s^{m+n} = s^m s^n, and (F5), (F6) in S to move \varphi(b) past s^m. Since (a x^m)(b x^n) = (ab) x^{m+n}, the two maps agree on pairs of monomials, so they agree everywhere by @lem-check-on-monomials. The one, constants and x. \Phi(1) = \varphi(1) s^0 = 1, \Phi(a x^0) = \varphi(a), and \Phi(x) = \varphi(1) s = s. Uniqueness. If \Psi is a ring homomorphism with \Psi(a x^0) = \varphi(a) and \Psi(x) = s, then, as a x^n is the constant a times the n-th power of x, \Psi(a x^n) = \varphi(a) s^n = \Phi(a x^n). Both maps are additive and agree on monomials, so \Psi = \Phi by @lem-check-on-monomials with one argument. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: gives the formula for \Phi and proves it does not depend on N, from \varphi(0) = 0. - 1: proves \Phi additive. - 3: reduces multiplicativity to monomials (in one argument or in both), justifying the additivity it uses. - 2: computes the monomial case correctly, justifying the reordering of factors in S (commutativity). - 1: shows \Phi(1) = 1 and \Phi(x) = s (and \Phi(a) = \varphi(a)). - 2: proves uniqueness: the values on monomials are forced, then additivity. Fatal errors (0 for the step): proving multiplicativity only for p, q of degree at most 1; assuming that a homomorphism is determined by its value at x alone, without using \Psi(a) = \varphi(a) on constants. A proof of multiplicativity by expanding \Phi(p)\Phi(q) as a double sum and regrouping by i + j = k earns the 3 points of the reduction step only if the regrouping is proved. [C2: Composition is associative] Let R be a commutative ring and p, q, r \in R[x]. Prove that (p \circ q) \circ r = p \circ (q \circ r). The first half of a proof is given. Fix q and r. Both sides are additive in p: the left side is p \mapsto p \circ q followed by u \mapsto u \circ r, two ring homomorphisms (@def-polynomial-composition), and the right side is p \mapsto p \circ (q \circ r), a ring homomorphism. The second half is blank. Name the move, then complete it. One move is check on monomials, extend by additivity. Let p = a x^n. Since u \mapsto u \circ q is a ring homomorphism fixing the constant a and sending x to q, and a x^n is the product of a and x^n (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (c)), (a x^n) \circ q = (a \circ q)(x \circ q)^n = a q^n , by the power property of ring homomorphisms (after @def-ring-homomorphism). Applying the ring homomorphism u \mapsto u \circ r in the same way, (a q^n) \circ r = (a \circ r)(q \circ r)^n = a \, (q \circ r)^n . On the other side, the same computation with q \circ r in place of q gives (a x^n) \circ (q \circ r) = a \, (q \circ r)^n. So the two sides agree on every monomial. Both are additive in p, so by @lem-check-on-monomials (with one argument and T = R[x]) they agree for every p. Also correct: the move a homomorphism out of R[x] is fixed by the constants and x. Both sides are ring homomorphisms R[x] 	o R[x] (composites of ring homomorphisms, after @def-ring-homomorphism), both fix every constant ((a \circ q) \circ r = a \circ r = a and a \circ (q \circ r) = a), and both send x to q \circ r: (x \circ q) \circ r = q \circ r and x \circ (q \circ r) = q \circ r. So they are equal by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-substitution (b), with S = R[x], \varphi \colon a \mapsto a x^0 and s = q \circ r. [C3: The factor theorem over any commutative ring] Let R be a commutative ring and c \in R. 1. Prove that for every n \ge 1, x^n - c^n = (x - c) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{\,n-1-j} x^j . 2. Prove that for p \in R[x], p(c) = 0 if and only if p = (x - c) q for some q \in R[x]. 3. In 
Z/8
Z, find all roots of x^2 - 1. The usual argument that a quadratic polynomial cannot have more than two roots goes: “if c_1 is a root, then p = (x - c_1) q with \deg q = 1; a second root c_2 
e c_1 has (c_2 - c_1) q(c_2) = 0, so q(c_2) = 0”. Which step fails in 
Z/8
Z? [Hint 1] For (a), compare coefficients: multiplying a polynomial by x shifts its coefficients up by one place (@lem-monomial-product (a)). For (b) (\Rightarrow), reduce to (a). [Hint 2] For (b), let N be admissible for p and start from p - p(c) = \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k - \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k, with p(c) read as a constant. (a) Let u \coloneqq \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^{\,n-1-j} x^j, so u_j = c^{\,n-1-j} for 0 \le j \le n - 1 and u_j = 0 for j \ge n. By @lem-monomial-product (a) and @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (d), (x - c)u = xu - cu has coefficient -c u_0 at 0 and u_{k-1} - c u_k at k \ge 1. So: - at k = 0: -c \cdot c^{n-1} = -c^n; - at 1 \le k \le n - 1: c^{\,n-k} - c \cdot c^{\,n-1-k} = 0, by the power law; - at k = n: u_{n-1} - c u_n = c^0 - 0 = 1; - at k > n: 0 - 0 = 0. These are the coefficients of x^n - c^n. This is Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1’s difference-of-powers identity (@fd4:lem-difference-of-powers), read in the commutative ring R[x] with z = x and w = c; the proof above does not use it. (b) (\Leftarrow) By @thm-evaluation-respects-operations, p(c) = (c - c)\, q(c) = 0 \cdot q(c) = 0. (\Rightarrow) Let N be admissible for p. By @prp-polynomial-sum-of-monomials and @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (b), (c), and since the constants respect sums,  egin{aligned} p - p(c) &= \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k x^k - \sum_{k=0}^{N} p_k c^k \ &= \sum_{k=1}^{N} p_k  igl(x^k - c^k igr) , \end{aligned} where the term k = 0 is p_0 (1 - 1) = 0. By (a), each x^k - c^k with k \ge 1 is (x - c) u^{(k)} for a polynomial u^{(k)}, so by the distributive law p - p(c) = (x - c) q with q \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{N} p_k u^{(k)}. If p(c) = 0, then p = (x - c) q. (c) The squares in 
Z/8
Z of [0], \dots, [7] are [0], [1], [4], [1], [0], [1], [4], [1] (for instance [5]^2 = [25] = [1], [7]^2 = [49] = [1]). So x^2 - 1 has the four roots [1], [3], [5], [7]. The failing step is “(c_2 - c_1) q(c_2) = 0, so q(c_2) = 0”: it needs 
Z/8
Z to have no zero divisors. With c_1 = [1], q = x + 1 and c_2 = [3], (c_2 - c_1) q(c_2) = [2][4] = [8] = [0], with both factors non-zero. Chapter 5 proves the factor theorem over a field again, by division with remainder. [C4: A second proof of Fermat’s little theorem] Let p be a prime. Give another proof that a^{p-1} = 1 for every non-zero a \in 
F_p, along the following steps, and then compare x^p - x with its function. 1. Let a \in 
F_p be non-zero. Show that b \mapsto ab is a bijection from 
F_p \setminus \{0\} to itself. 2. Deduce that a^{p-1} = 1, by computing the product of all non-zero elements of 
F_p in two ways. 3. Show that x^p - x 
e 0 in 
F_p[x], but \varepsilon(x^p - x) = 0. Write F \coloneqq 
F_p, a field (@def-field-fp); then F \setminus \{0\} has the p - 1 elements 1, \dots, p - 1 (@thm-integers-mod-n-ring (b)). (a) For b \in F \setminus \{0\}, ab 
e 0, since F has no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)); so b \mapsto ab maps F \setminus \{0\} to F \setminus \{0\}. It is injective: ab = ab' gives a(b - b') = 0, so b = b'. Its image is a subset of the finite set F \setminus \{0\} in bijection with F \setminus \{0\}; if the image were a proper subset, this would contradict @fd2:thm-finite-no-proper-copy. So the map is surjective, hence a bijection. (b) A rearranged product is the same product. For a list t_1, \dots, t_r in a commutative ring and a bijection \sigma of \{1, \dots, r\}, we show \prod_{j=1}^{r} t_{\sigma(j)} = \prod_{j=1}^{r} t_j, by @fd1:ax-induction on r. For r = 0 both sides are the empty product 1. For the step, first a deletion rule: for a list u_1, \dots, u_{r+1} and a position k, the product equals u_k times the product of the list with position k deleted. For k = r + 1 this is the product recursion; for k \le r, it follows from the rule for the first r entries (induction on the length) and (F5), (F6):  egin{aligned} \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} u_j = \Bigl(\prod_{j=1}^{r} u_j\Bigr) u_{r+1} &= \Bigl( igl(	extstyle\prod_{j \le r,\, j 
e k} u_j igr) u_k\Bigr) u_{r+1} \ &= \Bigl( igl(	extstyle\prod_{j \le r,\, j 
e k} u_j igr) u_{r+1}\Bigr) u_k , \end{aligned} and the bracket in the last line is the product of the list with position k deleted, by the product recursion, since that list ends with u_{r+1}. Now let u_j \coloneqq t_{\sigma(j)} and k \coloneqq \sigma^{-1}(r + 1). Deleting position k leaves the list t_{\sigma'(1)}, \dots, t_{\sigma'(r)}, where \sigma'(i) \coloneqq \sigma(i) for i < k and \sigma'(i) \coloneqq \sigma(i + 1) for i \ge k, a bijection of \{1, \dots, r\}: its values lie in \{1, \dots, r\}, since \sigma(m) = r + 1 only for m = k and the index used (i for i < k, i + 1 for i \ge k) is never k; it is injective because \sigma and this index map are; and every j \le r is \sigma(m) for some m 
e k, so j = \sigma'(m) if m < k and j = \sigma'(m - 1) if m > k. By the deletion rule and the hypothesis for r, \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} t_{\sigma(j)} =  igl(\prod_{i=1}^{r} t_i igr) t_{r+1} = \prod_{j=1}^{r+1} t_j. The two computations. List F \setminus \{0\} as b_1, \dots, b_{p-1}, and let Q \coloneqq \prod_{j=1}^{p-1} b_j. By (a), a b_j = b_{\sigma(j)} for a bijection \sigma of \{1, \dots, p - 1\}, so the list a b_1, \dots, a b_{p-1} is a rearrangement of b_1, \dots, b_{p-1}, and its product is Q. By (F5), (F6) and induction on the length, the same product is a^{p-1} Q. So a^{p-1} Q = Q = 1 \cdot Q. Since Q is a product of non-zero elements of a field, Q 
e 0 (@thm-field-basic-properties (f), by induction), and canceling Q (@thm-field-basic-properties (b)) gives a^{p-1} = 1. (c) The polynomial x^p - x has coefficient 1 at position p (since p \ge 2, the positions p and 1 differ), and 1 
e 0 in F; so it is not the zero polynomial. For every c \in F, c^p - c = 0: if c 
e 0, c^p = c^{p-1} c = c by (b); and 0^p = 0 since p \ge 1. So \varepsilon(x^p - x) is the zero function. This gives a second proof, by Fermat rather than by the factors x - c, that \varepsilon is not injective over 
F_p. The two witnesses are in fact the same polynomial: Chapter 5 shows that x^p - x = \prod_{c \in 
F_p} (x - c), the P of @prp-polynomial-function-map (d) with R = 
F_p (@exm-polynomial-function-finite-field (b)). This is the second proof of @thm-fermat-little (b); the first, in Chapter 2, went through the Frobenius map. Part (c) also follows directly from @thm-fermat-little (a).

title: 4.5 The Formal Derivative
content:
The Formal Derivative The polynomials of this chapter are coefficient sequences, and @thm-polynomial-substitution showed how to evaluate them and how to substitute into them. One more operation from school survives the passage to an arbitrary commutative ring: the derivative. This section defines it by its coefficients, proves the sum, product and power rules with the move of @lem-check-on-monomials, and asks when a derivative can be 0. Over a field the answer depends on the characteristic of Chapter 2, and over 
F_p it is not the answer of calculus. At school a double root shows itself in the graph. The parabola y = (x - 1)^2 touches the axis at 1 instead of crossing it, and its slope there is 0: the derivative 2(x - 1) vanishes at 1 as well. Over 
F_p there is no graph and no slope; the field has p elements and no limits. What survives is the formula: the derivative of a x^n is n a x^{n-1}. We keep the formula and drop the limit. Chapter 5 uses the result to detect repeated roots; this section builds the tool. Throughout, R is a commutative ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field). Polynomials are written f, g, h, with coefficients f_k, g_k, h_k, because the letter p is kept for a prime. A dot with an integer on its left is a multiple, n \cdot a = a + \dots + a with n terms (the “Multiples” paragraph of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 2.4, collected in @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (d)); the product of two ring elements is written by juxtaposition. The derivative by coefficients At school, (3x^4 + 5x^2)' = 12x^3 + 10x. Each term moves down one place, and its coefficient is multiplied by the exponent it had. In R[x] “multiplied by the exponent” has a meaning without any division or limit: the exponent n is a natural number, and n \cdot a is the n-th multiple of a. That recurring computation deserves a name. The formal derivative moves every coefficient down one place and takes it as many times as its old exponent. [Formal Derivative] Let R be a commutative ring and f \in R[x]. The formal derivative of f is the sequence f' \colon 
N 	o R given by (f')_k \coloneqq (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1} \qquad 	ext{for every } k \in 
N , where (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1} is the (k + 1)-th multiple of f_{k+1}. The higher derivatives are defined by f^{(0)} \coloneqq f , \qquad f^{(k+1)} \coloneqq  igl( f^{(k)}  igr)' \quad (k \in 
N) , and we write f'' for f^{(2)}. In words: the coefficient of x^k in f' is read off from the coefficient of x^{k+1} in f, added to itself k + 1 times. The definition uses only the addition of R, so it makes sense, word for word, over 
Z, 
Q, 
Z/6
Z and 
F_p. Well-definedness. Two things need checking: that f' is again a polynomial, and that the higher derivatives exist. - f' \in R[x]. First, m \cdot 0 = 0 for every m \in 
N: by @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (d), m \cdot 0 = (m \cdot 1) 0, and this is 0 by @fd3:prp-ring-algebra (b). Now choose N \in 
N with f_k = 0 for every k > N (@def-polynomial). For k \ge N we have k + 1 > N, so f_{k+1} = 0 and (f')_k = (k + 1) \cdot 0 = 0. So f' has only finitely many non-zero terms, and f' \in R[x]. Moreover (f')_k = 0 for k > N - 1, so for N \ge 1, @prp-polynomial-sum-of-monomials writes f' as an honest sum: f' = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1}  igl( (k + 1) \cdot f_{k+1}  igr) x^k = 1 \cdot f_1 + (2 \cdot f_2) x + \dots + (N \cdot f_N) x^{N-1} . - Higher derivatives. Since u \mapsto u' is a function R[x] 	o R[x], @fd2:thm-recursion, with X = R[x], starting value f and step (k, u) \mapsto u', gives exactly one sequence k \mapsto f^{(k)} with the two displayed properties. Monomials. Let a \in R and n \in 
N. The monomial a x^n has a in position n and 0 elsewhere (@def-polynomial), so (a x^n)_{k+1} is a when k + 1 = n and 0 otherwise. Hence ((a x^n)')_k is n \cdot a when k = n - 1, and (k + 1) \cdot 0 = 0 otherwise: (a x^n)' = (n \cdot a) \, x^{n-1} \quad (n \ge 1) , \qquad (a x^0)' = 0 . 	ag{M} The case n = 0 is separate because x^{n-1} has no meaning there: -1 
otin 
N. Every constant has derivative 0. The element n \cdot 1. By @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (d), n \cdot a = (n \cdot 1) a. So the exponent enters the derivative only through one element of R, the multiple n \cdot 1, and that element can be 0. In 
F_2, 2 \cdot 1 = 1 + 1 = 0, so (x^2)' = (2 \cdot 1) x = 0. This is the whole difference between the derivative here and the derivative of calculus, and the rest of the section keeps track of it. Why this definition. The formula is the school formula with the limit removed. Exercise C1 asks you to show that it is the only additive map R[x] 	o R[x] that sends constants to 0, sends x to 1 and obeys the product rule. A definition by limits is not available, since

Polynomials over a Field Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 did arithmetic in 
Z: divide with a remainder, take the least positive element of a set closed under combinations, and the greatest common divisor, Bézout’s identity, Euclid’s lemma and unique factorization follow. Chapter 4 of this volume built the ring F[x] and its degree, but it did not divide one polynomial by another with a remainder. This chapter shows that over a field F the polynomials have the same arithmetic, with the degree in the part of the size and “monic” in the part of “positive”. It also proves what 
Z has no analogue for. A polynomial can be evaluated, so it has roots, and roots occupy the second half of the chapter. A root c is a factor x - c; a non-zero polynomial has no more distinct roots than its degree; a repeated root shows up in the formal derivative of Section 4.5; and values at enough points determine a polynomial, which is interpolation. Interpolation turns out to be the Chinese remainder theorem for the moduli x - c, and the ring F[x]/\langle m angle, built by Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4’s quotient construction, is a field exactly when m is irreducible. The chapter ends with the question that algebra courses usually leave to analysis: does every non-constant complex polynomial have a root? It does, and Section 5.6 proves it with no convergent sequences, no compactness, no continuity theorem and no polar form. The one analytic input is the supremum property of 
R. It is used directly twice, to find a point where \abs{p} is smallest, and indirectly through the real square roots behind the modulus and behind the complex square roots. The factorization of real polynomials into linear factors and quadratics without real roots follows. Two rings, one arithmetic. The first half of the chapter runs Number Systems: From
