Q(i) and complex conjugation (@exm-subfields-gaussian, @exm-complex-conjugation-automorphism). Section 5.5 meets the four-element field of @exr-finite-fields-from-modular-arithmetic-c1 again, and Exercise R2 of Section 5.6 returns to @exm-q-sqrt2-field. - From Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1, for Section 5.6 (and the difference of powers also for Exercises B2 and B3 of Section 5.1): the complex numbers as a field containing 
R (@fd4:def-complex-numbers, @fd4:thm-complex-numbers-field, @fd4:prp-reals-embed-complex); the conjugate and the modulus and their rules (@fd4:def-conjugate-modulus, @fd4:thm-conjugate-properties, @fd4:prp-modulus-of-real, @fd4:lem-real-part-at-most-modulus); the triangle inequality and its variants (@fd4:thm-complex-triangle-inequality, @fd4:cor-complex-triangle-variants); powers (@fd4:prp-power-laws-commutative-ring, @fd4:lem-difference-of-powers); complex square roots (@fd4:prp-complex-square-roots); and conjugate roots (@fd4:prp-real-coefficients-conjugate-roots). Sections 5.2 and 5.5 use 
Q \subseteq 
R \subseteq 
C in examples, and Exercise B3 of Section 5.5 compares 
R[x]/\langle x^2 + 1 angle with 
C. Analytic Preliminaries, Chapter 1’s polar form and k-th roots are not used, and Chapter 2 is not used. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4: ideals, quotient rings and units (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, @thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal, @def-ring-unit), cited for F[x]; the rules for divisibility, Euclid’s lemma and fractions in lowest terms (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers, @thm-euclid-lemma-integers, @prp-rationals-lowest-terms), for the rational root test; even and odd integers (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd); the integer gcd and its Euclidean step (@def-integer-gcd, @lem-gcd-remainder-step), in two exercises; and the integer twins compared with in Sections 5.1–5.5: those in the table above and @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, @thm-integer-ideals-principal, @thm-euclidean-algorithm-integers, @exr-gcd-and-bezout-c2, @lem-least-divisor-prime, @thm-integers-mod-n-ring and @thm-units-mod-n. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 3: 
N = \omega, its order and well-ordering, and even and odd exponents (@fd3:cor-omega-identification, @fd3:thm-omega-order, @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering, @fd3:prp-omega-powers-parity); commutative rings and the rules of an ordered ring (@fd3:def-commutative-ring-and-field, @fd3:prp-ring-algebra, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules); greatest elements of bounded sets of integers (@fd3:prp-integer-least-element), for multiplicities; the irrationality of \sqrt2 (@fd3:thm-no-rational-square-two), and the gap at \sqrt2 in 
Q (@fd3:thm-rationals-gap-sqrt2), in Exercise C1 of Section 5.6; and maps on classes (@fd3:thm-well-defined-on-classes), for the Chinese remainder theorem. - From Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 4–6, for Section 5.6: absolute values and powers in an ordered field (@fd3:prp-absolute-value-ordered-field, @fd3:def-naturals-in-ordered-field), from Chapter 4; 
R as a complete ordered field, its Archimedean property and the bound on powers of 2 (@fd3:def-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:thm-reals-complete-ordered-field, @fd3:thm-constructed-reals-archimedean, @fd3:lem-power-two-bound), with @fd3:exm-representatives-need-choice compared with, from Chapter 5; and non-negative square roots in 
R (@fd3:prp-cof-square-roots), from Chapter 6, which also supply \sqrt2 for examples in Sections 5.2–5.5. - From Sets and Functions: bijections (@fd2:def-bijective), from Chapter 1; the well-ordering of 
N and the recursion theorem with its finite sums and products (@fd2:thm-well-ordering, @fd2:thm-recursion, @fd2:def-sum-product), from Chapter 2; equivalence classes and quotient sets, and suprema and infima (@fd2:thm-classes-partition, @fd2:def-quotient-set, @fd2:def-order-supremum), from Chapter 4; and finite and infinite sets (@fd2:def-finite, @fd2:def-infinite, @fd2:prp-subset-finite, @fd2:prp-disjoint-union-count), from Section 4.1, for Section 5.4 and Exercise C3 of Section 5.3. - From Logic and Proof: induction and strong induction (@fd1:ax-induction, @fd1:thm-strong-induction), from Section 4.2, and, for the two find-the-error exercises, the catalogue of moves that are not allowed (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue), from Section 8.6. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - Division with Remainder. Divisibility over a field, associates and the one monic associate of a non-zero polynomial; division with remainder, with existence by an element of least degree and uniqueness by comparing degrees, and long division over 
Q and 
F_3; and the remainder and factor theorems, which make a root c the same thing as a factor x - c. - Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm. The ideal generated by finitely many polynomials; every ideal of F[x] generated by exactly one monic polynomial; the gcd defined as the monic common divisor that every common divisor divides, with Bézout’s theorem and coprimality; the Euclidean algorithm as a recursively defined sequence, with back-substitution; and division and the gcd unchanged when the field is enlarged. - Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization. Irreducibility over a field, decided by roots in degrees 2 and 3 and not beyond, as x^4 + 4 shows; Euclid’s lemma and its consequences for irreducibles; an irreducible factor of least degree; unique factorization into monic irreducibles, with uniqueness stated by a bijection of indices; the factorizations of x^4 - 1 over five fields; and the rational root test. - Roots, Multiplicity, and the Formal Derivative. At most n roots for a non-zero polynomial of degree n; a polynomial fixed by its values at n + 1 points, and over an infinite field by its function, but not over 
F_p; the expansion in powers of x - c; multiplicity, splitting off all roots, and splitting over a field; and repeated roots and repeated factors detected by the formal derivative and by \gcd(f, f'). - Interpolation, Quotient Rings, and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. Lagrange polynomials and the unique interpolating polynomial of degree at most n; congruence modulo a polynomial and the ring F[x]/\langle m angle, named by the remainders and a field exactly when m is irreducible, with a field of four elements and a copy of 
C; the Chinese remainder theorem for any number of pairwise coprime moduli; interpolation as its case of linear moduli; and values and derivatives prescribed at once. - The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra. Why the field axioms cannot suffice; a growth bound and a Lipschitz bound in place of continuity; the minimum of \abs{p}, found by nested squares and two uses of the supremum property; d’Alembert’s lemma, with its direction found by square roots instead of polar form; the theorem and the splitting of complex polynomials; and real polynomials, whose irreducible factors are linear or quadratic without real root, so that one of odd degree has a real root. Review exercises return to Chapters 2 and 4 and to Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4. Named moves - Least degree, then divide. In a set of polynomials closed under the right operations, take a non-zero element d of least degree and divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and has smaller degree, so it is 0. It is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4’s “least positive element, then divide”, with degree in place of size. Named in Section 5.2, it proves there that every ideal of F[x] has one monic generator (@thm-polynomial-ideals-principal), and Bézout’s theorem with it; its first, unnamed use is the existence half of division with remainder in Section 5.1. Exercise C1 of Section 5.2 asks for the whole proof, Exercise B2 of Section 5.3 leaves its last step to you, and Exercise C2 of Section 5.6 asks you to name it and carry it out. - Evaluate at a root. In f = qg + r, evaluate at a root of g: the term qg vanishes, and the value of r is read off. Named in Section 5.1, it proves the remainder theorem and finds remainders without dividing (@exm-polynomial-remainders-without-dividing, Exercise C2). In Section 5.5 it makes each Lagrange polynomial vanish at the other nodes, turns a congruence modulo x - c into a value at c (@prp-interpolation-as-chinese-remainder), and reads a value and a derivative off a congruence modulo (x - c)^2 (@exm-hermite-by-chinese-remainder). - Compare degrees. To show that two polynomials are equal, show that their difference has smaller degree than any non-zero polynomial of its kind can have: a non-zero multiple of g has degree at least \deg g, and a non-zero polynomial with n + 1 distinct roots has degree at least n + 1. Named in Section 5.1, it gives the uniqueness of the quotient and the remainder in Section 5.1, of the expansion in powers of x - c in Section 5.4, of the representative of degree less than \deg m in each class and of the solution of the Chinese remainder theorem in Section 5.5, and, with the root count, of the polynomial through given points in Sections 5.4 and 5.5. - Keep the quarter that keeps the infimum. To find a point where a quantity bounded below attains its infimum, halve a square, keep the first quarter in a fixed order whose infimum is the same, and take the point common to all the squares, which completeness supplies. It is Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 5’s bisection, now in the plane, and the fixed order makes each step a rule, so no choice is made. Named in Section 5.6, it proves there that \abs{p} attains its minimum (@thm-complex-polynomial-minimum); Exercise A1 there runs it for x^2 + 1, and Exercise C3 uses it to repair a flawed proof. - Multiply the Bézout identity, reused from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4. From af + bg = 1, multiply by h and read off what divides h. It proves Euclid’s lemma for polynomials (@thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma) and the rule for coprime divisors (@prp-polynomial-coprime-divisors-product) in Section 5.3. In Section 5.5 two such identities multiplied together show that coprimality survives products (@lem-polynomial-coprime-to-product), the identity read modulo m gives inverses in F[x]/\langle m angle, and one identity per modulus builds the solution of the Chinese remainder theorem. That chapter’s third move, computing on representatives, is not repeated: Section 5.5 cites its quotient-ring theorem.

title: 5.1 Division with Remainder
content:
Division with Remainder Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.1 divided -17 by 5 and kept the remainder 3: a quotient times the divisor, plus something smaller than the divisor. Chapter 4 built the ring F[x] of polynomials over a field and gave every non-zero polynomial a degree. For polynomials, “smaller” will mean “of smaller degree”. For instance, in 
Q[x], x^4 + 2x^3 - x + 3 = (x^2 + x)(x^2 + x - 1) + 3 , and the leftover 3 has degree 0, below the degree 2 of x^2 + x - 1. Three questions are open. Why can one always go on until the degree drops below that of the divisor? Why is the answer unique? And where does it matter that the coefficients lie in a field? This section answers all three, and then uses the answer to connect a root of a polynomial with a factor of degree 1. Throughout the chapter, F is a field (@def-field), and F[x] is the ring of polynomials over F (@def-polynomial-ring), a commutative ring by @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a). A field is an integral domain (@exm-integral-domains), so the results of Chapter 4 stated for integral domains apply to F[x]. We use the degree \deg p and the leading coefficient \operatorname{lc}(p) of @def-degree, with \deg 0 = -\infty, and the conventions -\infty < n and -\infty + n = -\infty for n \in 
N that come with it. A constant a \in F is identified with the polynomial a x^0 (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (b)), and (ap)_k = a p_k for a constant a (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (d)). Numerals in F are multiples of 1: 2 \coloneqq 1 + 1, 3 \coloneqq 2 + 1, and so on, so that 2 = 0 in 
F_2 and 3 = 0 in 
F_3 (@def-field-fp). Divisibility over a field In 
Z, “a divides b” asked whether b is some integer times a. The same question makes sense in any commutative ring, and in F[x] it is the question this chapter is built on. The one new feature is that the answer can depend on the field. A polynomial g divides f when f is g times some polynomial over the same field. [Divisibility of Polynomials] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x]. 1. g divides f over F, written g \mid f, if there exists h \in F[x] with f = gh. Then g is a divisor (or factor) of f, and f is a multiple of g. We write g 
mid f when g does not divide f. 2. f and g are associates if f = cg for some non-zero constant c \in F. In words: (a) asks for a cofactor h, and the cofactor must have its coefficients in F; (b) says that two polynomials are associates when they differ by a non-zero constant factor. When two fields are in play, “g \mid f in F[x]” names the field. Four instances, chosen so that the same symbols give different answers: - x - 1 \mid x^2 - 1 in 
Q[x], since x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1). - 2x - 2 \mid x^2 - 1 in 
Q[x], since x^2 - 1 = (2x - 2) igl(	frac12 x + 	frac12 igr). The polynomials x - 1 and 2x - 2 = 2(x - 1) are associates, and the cofactor 	frac12 x + 	frac12 needs the inverse of 2. - x + 1 \mid x^2 + 1 in 
F_2[x], since (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^2 + 1 there: 2 = 0 in 
F_2. - x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1 in 
Q[x]. Suppose x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)h with h \in 
Q[x]. Evaluating at -1 respects sums and products (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so (-1)^2 + 1 = (-1 + 1) \cdot h(-1), that is, 2 = 0 \cdot h(-1) = 0 in 
Q, which is false. Non-example by minimal change. The last two lines use the same symbols, x + 1 and x^2 + 1. Only the field changed, from 
F_2 to 
Q, and with it the value of 2: the evaluation argument gives 2 = 0, which is true in 
F_2 and false in 
Q. So “g \mid f” is a statement about g, f and F, which is why the definition says “over F”. Degenerate cases. Every g divides 0, since 0 = g \cdot 0. The zero polynomial divides only 0. And a non-zero constant c divides every f, since f = c(c^{-1}f); this is (F8), inverses of non-zero elements, at work in general (the cofactor of 2x - 2 above was one instance), and it means that non-zero constants are as invisible to divisibility as \pm 1 were in 
Z. In 
F_3[x], does x + 1 divide x^2 + 1? Evaluate at -1 = 2. No. If x^2 + 1 = (x + 1)h, evaluating at 2 (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) gives 2^2 + 1 = (2 + 1)h(2), that is, 5 = 0 \cdot h(2) = 0. In 
F_3, 5 = 2 
e 0. So x + 1 
mid x^2 + 1 in 
F_3[x]. The rules below are the ones the chapter uses. Parts (a)–(d) are identities in the commutative ring F[x], plus the inverse of a non-zero constant (F8) for the last clause of (a) and one degree count; parts (e) and (f) say exactly what “invisible” means. [Rules for Divisibility of Polynomials] Let F be a field and f, g, h \in F[x]. 1. g \mid 0. 0 \mid f if and only if f = 0. Every non-zero constant divides every polynomial. 2. If f \mid g and g \mid h, then f \mid h. 3. If h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid af + bg for all a, b \in F[x]. 4. If g \mid f and f 
e 0, then \deg g \le \deg f. 5. The units of F[x] (@def-ring-unit) are exactly the non-zero constants. 6. f \mid g and g \mid f if and only if f and g are associates (this includes f = g = 0). Every non-zero f has exactly one monic associate, namely \operatorname{lc}(f)^{-1} f. Two monic polynomials that divide each other are equal. Parts (a)–(c) are rearrangements of equations f = gh by the ring laws, except that the last clause of (a) also uses c^{-1}, from (F8). Part (d) is the degree of a product: a non-zero multiple of g has degree \deg g plus something in 
N. Part (e) is Chapter 4’s description of the units of R[x], read with R = F. For (f), mutual divisibility gives f = f \cdot uv, and canceling f makes u a unit, which (e) identifies as a non-zero constant. We use the ring laws of F[x] (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a)) and @fd3:prp-ring-algebra without further mention. (a) 0 = g \cdot 0, so g \mid 0. If 0 \mid f, then f = 0 \cdot k = 0 for some k; conversely 0 \mid 0 by the first claim. If c \in F is a non-zero constant, then c^{-1} exists by (F8) of @def-field, and f = (c c^{-1}) f = c (c^{-1} f), so c \mid f. (b) Let g = fu and h = gv. Then h = (fu)v = f(uv), so f \mid h. (c) Let f = hu and g = hv. Then af + bg = a(hu) + b(hv) = h(au + bv), so h \mid af + bg. (d) Let f = gu with u \in F[x]. Since f 
e 0, neither g nor u is 0. The field F has no zero divisors (@thm-field-basic-properties (f)), so @thm-degree-of-product (b) gives \deg f = \deg g + \deg u. Here \deg u \in 
N, so \deg g \le \deg f. (e) By @prp-polynomial-units, applied to the integral domain F (@exm-integral-domains), the units of F[x] are the constants that are units of F. In a field every non-zero a is a unit, by (F8), and 0 is not, since 0 \cdot v = 0 
e 1 for every v (@thm-field-basic-properties (d) and (F7) of @def-field). So the units of F[x] are the non-zero constants. (f) (\Leftarrow) Let f = cg with c 
e 0 a constant. Then g \mid f, and g = c^{-1} f, so f \mid g. (\Rightarrow) Let f \mid g and g \mid f. If f = 0, then 0 \mid g, so g = 0 by (a), and f = 1 \cdot g. Otherwise write g = fu and f = gv. Then f = fuv, so f(1 - uv) = 0. Since f 
e 0, @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (a) gives 1 - uv = 0, that is, uv = 1. So v is a unit of F[x], hence a non-zero constant by (e), and f = vg: f and g are associates. The monic associate. Let f 
e 0 and a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(f) 
e 0. The polynomial a^{-1} f has the coefficients a^{-1} f_k (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (d)). These vanish exactly where the f_k do, since a^{-1} 
e 0 (as a \cdot 0 = 0 
e 1 = a a^{-1}, by @thm-field-basic-properties (d), (F7), (F8)) and F has no zero divisors, so \deg(a^{-1} f) = \deg f and \operatorname{lc}(a^{-1} f) = a^{-1} a = 1. If also cf is monic for a constant c 
e 0, the same computation gives \operatorname{lc}(cf) = ca = 1, so c = a^{-1} (uniqueness of inverses, @thm-field-basic-properties (c)). So a^{-1} f is the only monic associate of f. Monic and mutually dividing. Let f, g be monic with f \mid g and g \mid f. By what we proved, f = cg with a non-zero constant c, and comparing leading coefficients, 1 = \operatorname{lc}(f) = c \operatorname{lc}(g) = c. So f = g. This proves the proposition. Parts (e) and (f) are the polynomial form of a fact about 
Z: in @fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (f) and (g), the units of 
Z were \pm 1, and two positive integers that divide each other are equal. In F[x] the units are the non-zero constants, and the role of “positive” is played by “monic”: among the associates of a non-zero polynomial, exactly one is monic. So whenever a polynomial is to be singled out from its associates, it is made monic. The hypothesis f 
e 0 in (d) cannot be dropped: x^5 \mid 0, and \deg x^5 = 5 > -\infty = \deg 0. In 
Q[x], list the associates of 3x + 6 that have integer coefficients and leading coefficient between -3 and 3. Which one is monic? The associates are c(3x + 6) with c \in 
Q, c 
e 0; the leading coefficient is 3c. Leading coefficients \pm 1, \pm 2, \pm 3 give \pm(x + 2), \pm(2x + 4), \pm(3x + 6), all with integer coefficients. The monic one is x + 2 = 	frac13 (3x + 6). Division with remainder Now the theorem. The tool is the one Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.1 used for integers, with degree in place of size: among all f - hg, take one of least degree, and show that its degree is below \deg g. [Division with Remainder in F[x]] Let F be a field, and let f, g \in F[x] with g 
e 0. 1. There are unique q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad \deg r < \deg g . 2. g \mid f if and only if r = 0. The polynomials q and r are the quotient and the remainder of f on division by g. Since \deg 0 = -\infty < \deg g, the remainder r = 0 is allowed. Look at all polynomials f - hg, h \in F[x]. If 0 is among them, f is a multiple of g and we are done. Otherwise their degrees are natural numbers, and well-ordering gives one, r, of least degree n. If n \ge \deg g, we can kill the leading term of r by subtracting a constant times a power of x times g: the constant is \operatorname{lc}(r) \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1}, and that inverse is where the field is needed. The result is again of the form f - hg and has smaller degree, against the choice of r. Uniqueness: two answers give (q - q')g = r' - r, and a non-zero multiple of g cannot have degree below \deg g. We call this move compare degrees. (a) Existence. Let m \coloneqq \deg g \in 
N and b \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(g) 
e 0, and let S \coloneqq \{ f - hg : h \in F[x] \} . If 0 \in S, say 0 = f - qg, then r \coloneqq 0 and this q satisfy f = qg + r and \deg r = -\infty < m. Suppose 0 
otin S. Then every element of S has a degree in 
N, and D \coloneqq \{ \deg s : s \in S \} \subseteq 
N is non-empty, since f = f - 0 \cdot g \in S. By the well-ordering of 
N (@fd2:thm-well-ordering; on 
N = \omega it is @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering), D has a least element n. Choose q \in F[x] with r \coloneqq f - qg of degree n, and let a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(r) 
e 0. Suppose n \ge m. Let t \coloneqq (ab^{-1}) x^{n-m}, a monomial with n - m \in 
N and non-zero coefficient ab^{-1}: b^{-1} 
e 0, since b \cdot 0 = 0 
e 1 = b b^{-1} (@thm-field-basic-properties (d), (F7), (F8)), so ab^{-1} 
e 0 by @thm-field-basic-properties (f). Then \deg t = n - m and \operatorname{lc}(t) = ab^{-1}, so by @thm-degree-of-product (b), tg has degree (n - m) + m = n and leading coefficient ab^{-1} b = a. Let r_1 \coloneqq r - tg = f - (q + t) g , an element of S. By @thm-degree-of-sum (with \deg(-p) = \deg p for every p, since (-p)_k = -p_k), \deg r_1 \le \max(\deg r, \deg tg) = n, and the coefficient of x^n in r_1 is a - a = 0. So \deg r_1 < n (or r_1 = 0). But r_1 
e 0, since 0 
otin S, and then \deg r_1 \in D is smaller than the least element n of D. This contradiction shows n < m. So f = qg + r with \deg r < \deg g. Uniqueness. Let f = qg + r = q'g + r' with \deg r < m and \deg r' < m. Then (q - q')g = r' - r , and \deg(r' - r) \le \max(\deg r', \deg r) < m by @thm-degree-of-sum (using \deg(-r) = \deg r as above). If q 
e q', then @thm-degree-of-product (b) gives \deg igl((q - q')g igr) = \deg(q - q') + m \ge m, a contradiction. So q = q', hence r' - r = 0 \cdot g = 0 and r = r'. (b) (\Leftarrow) If r = 0, then f = qg, so g \mid f. (\Rightarrow) If f = hg, then f = hg + 0 with \deg 0 < \deg g is a division with remainder; by the uniqueness in (a), r = 0. This proves the theorem. The field is used in two places. The first is the inverse b^{-1} of the leading coefficient of g, which builds the monomial t. The second is the degree of a product, in \deg(tg) = n and in the uniqueness: @thm-degree-of-product (b) needs the product of the leading coefficients to be non-zero, and a field has no zero divisors. The hypothesis g 
e 0 is needed as well: for g = 0 no r has \deg r < -\infty. The existence proof is also a procedure. Each pass replaces r by r - tg, which removes the leading term of r, and the degree drops by at least one. Starting from f, at most \deg f - \deg g + 1 passes are needed when \deg f \ge \deg g, and none when \deg f < \deg g: then q = 0 and r = f. This is the long division of school algebra, now with a proof that it stops and that its answer is the only one. Chapter 4 did not divide polynomials with remainder, so this is where the volume first does it. Its integer twin is @fd3:thm-integers-division-remainder, whose least-element proof the one above follows. [Long division in two fields] (i) In 
Q[x], divide f = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 4x - 1 by g = 2x^2 - x + 3. (ii) In 
F_3[x], divide f = x^4 + x + 2 by g = 2x^2 + 1. (i) Here \operatorname{lc}(g) = 2, with inverse 	frac12. Each pass subtracts t g, where t is the leading term of the current remainder divided by 2x^2:  egin{aligned} f - x^2 g &= -2x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 1, \ (-2x^3 - 2x^2 + 4x - 1) - (-x) g &= -3x^2 + 7x - 1, \ (-3x^2 + 7x - 1) -  igl(-	frac32 igr) g &= 	frac{11}{2} x + 	frac72 . \end{aligned} The last line has degree 1 < 2, so we stop. Adding up the t’s, 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 + 4x - 1 =  igl(x^2 - x - 	frac32 igr)(2x^2 - x + 3) + 	frac{11}{2} x + 	frac72 . Check:  igl(x^2 - x - 	frac32 igr)(2x^2 - x + 3) = 2x^4 - 3x^3 + x^2 - 	frac32 x - 	frac92, and adding 	frac{11}{2} x + 	frac72 gives f. (ii) In 
F_3, 2 \cdot 2 = 4 = 1, so \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1} = 2^{-1} = 2. The first t is 1 \cdot 2 \cdot x^2 = 2x^2, and 2x^2 \cdot g = 4x^4 + 2x^2 = x^4 + 2x^2. The second t is 2, and 2g = 4x^2 + 2 = x^2 + 2:  egin{aligned} f - 2x^2 g &= -2x^2 + x + 2 = x^2 + x + 2, \ (x^2 + x + 2) - 2g &= x . \end{aligned} So x^4 + x + 2 = (2x^2 + 2)(2x^2 + 1) + x in 
F_3[x]. Check: (2x^2 + 2)(2x^2 + 1) = 4x^4 + 6x^2 + 2 = x^4 + 2 in 
F_3, and adding x gives f. Find two different pairs (q, r) with x^2 = q(x^2 + 1) + r in 
Q[x] and \deg r \le 2. Which condition in part (a) of the theorem does the second one fail? (q, r) = (1, -1): 1 \cdot (x^2 + 1) - 1 = x^2, with \deg(-1) = 0 < 2. And (q, r) = (0, x^2): 0 \cdot (x^2 + 1) + x^2 = x^2, with \deg r = 2. The second fails \deg r < \deg g = 2. Uniqueness holds only among remainders of degree strictly below that of the divisor; (1, -1) is the quotient and remainder. Division with remainder needs the leading coefficient of the divisor to be invertible. Take the polynomials in 
Q[x] all of whose coefficients lie in 
Z, and try to divide x^2 by 2x among them: x^2 = q \cdot 2x + r with \deg r < 1. Comparing the coefficients of x^2 gives 1 = 2q_1 (@lem-monomial-product (a)), and no integer q_1 satisfies it, since 1 is odd (@fd3:cor-integers-even-odd (a)). In 
Q[x] there is no problem: x^2 = 	frac12 x \cdot 2x + 0. Exercise C1 shows that integer coefficients are kept when the divisor is monic. Roots and factors of degree one Division by a polynomial of degree 1 has a remainder of degree at most 0, that is, a constant. Which constant? Evaluate: the divisor x - c vanishes at c, so the quotient term disappears and the remainder is read off. We call this move evaluate at a root. [Remainder Theorem and Factor Theorem] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] and c \in F. 1. The remainder of f on division by x - c is the constant f(c). 2. c is a root of f if and only if x - c \mid f. 3. f has a factor of degree 1 in F[x] if and only if f has a root in F. Divide by x - c and evaluate at c: the term with the quotient vanishes, and what is left is the remainder. Part (b) is then the divisibility test of @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (b), and for (c) a factor ax + b of degree 1 is made monic, which turns it into some x - c. (a) The polynomial x - c is non-zero, of degree 1 and monic. By @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a), f = q \cdot (x - c) + r with \deg r < 1, so r is a constant (possibly 0). Evaluation at c respects sums and products, sends x to c and a constant to itself (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), so f(c) = q(c) \cdot (c - c) + r = q(c) \cdot 0 + r = r . (b) By (a), f = q \cdot (x - c) + f(c) is the division of f by x - c. By @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (b), x - c \mid f if and only if this remainder is 0, that is, f(c) = 0. (c) (\Leftarrow) If f(c) = 0, then x - c \mid f by (b), and x - c has degree 1. (\Rightarrow) Let ax + b \mid f with a, b \in F, a 
e 0. Then ax + b = a igl(x - (-a^{-1}b) igr), so x - (-a^{-1}b) \mid ax + b, and by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b), x - (-a^{-1}b) \mid f. By (b), -a^{-1}b is a root of f. Part (b) is the factor theorem, and it turns a question about values (is f(c) = 0?) into a question about divisibility. Part (c) turns the search for factors of degree 1 into a search for roots. [Remainders without dividing] (a) In 
Q[x], find the remainder of f = x^5 - 3x^3 + 2x + 7 on division by x - 2. (b) In 
Q[x], find the remainder of x^5 on division by x^2 - x. (a) By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a), the remainder is f(2) = 32 - 24 + 4 + 7 = 19 . (b) The divisor x^2 - x has degree 2, so the remainder has degree at most 1: x^5 = q \cdot (x^2 - x) + ax + b with a, b \in 
Q (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a)). The divisor vanishes at 0 and at 1. Evaluating at both (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations), 0 = q(0) \cdot 0 + b, \qquad 1 = q(1) \cdot 0 + a + b , so b = 0 and a = 1. The remainder is x. Check: x^5 - x = (x^2 - x)(x^3 + x^2 + x + 1). Without dividing, decide whether x + 1 divides x^7 + 1 in 
Q[x], and whether x - 1 does. x + 1 = x - (-1), and (-1)^7 + 1 = -1 + 1 = 0, so x + 1 \mid x^7 + 1 by @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b). For x - 1, the remainder is 1^7 + 1 = 2 
e 0 in 
Q, so x - 1 
mid x^7 + 1. (Over 
F_2, 2 = 0 and both divide.) [Looking ahead] Section 5.5 builds, for any finite list of distinct points of F, the polynomial of least degree that takes prescribed values there. Exercise C2 below is the case of two points: the remainder of f on division by (x - a)(x - b). Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State @thm-polynomial-division-remainder with every hypothesis. 2. Name the two places in its proof where “F is a field” is used. 3. Let f \in F[x], and let c \in F be a non-zero constant. What are the quotient and the remainder of f on division by c? 4. True or false, with a reason: for f, g \in 
Q[x], if f \mid g and g \mid f, then f = g. The same question in 
F_2[x]. (a) Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x] with g 
e 0. Then there are unique q, r \in F[x] with f = qg + r and \deg r < \deg g; and g \mid f if and only if r = 0. (b) The inverse \operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1}, which builds the monomial t = \operatorname{lc}(r)\operatorname{lc}(g)^{-1} x^{n-m}; and the absence of zero divisors in F, through @thm-degree-of-product (b), which gives \deg(tg) = n and, in the uniqueness, \deg igl((q - q')g igr) \ge \deg g. (c) q = c^{-1} f and r = 0: indeed f = (c^{-1} f) c + 0, and \deg 0 = -\infty < 0 = \deg c. By uniqueness this is the division. (d) In 
Q[x]: false. x \mid 2x and 2x \mid x (x = 	frac12 \cdot 2x), but x 
e 2x. By @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f), mutual divisibility only makes f and g associates. In 
F_2[x]: true. By (f), f = cg with c a non-zero constant, and the only non-zero element of 
F_2 is 1; so f = g. B. Practice [B1: Two long divisions] 1. In 
Q[x], divide x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5 by 3x^2 - 1. 2. In 
F_5[x], divide x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 by 2x^2 + 3, and decide whether 2x^2 + 3 divides x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 in 
F_5[x]. (a) \operatorname{lc}(3x^2 - 1)^{-1} = 	frac13. The passes subtract 	frac13 x^2, -x and 	frac19 times the divisor:  egin{aligned} (x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5) - 	frac13 x^2 (3x^2 - 1) &= -3x^3 + 	frac13 x^2 + 2x - 5, \ (-3x^3 + 	frac13 x^2 + 2x - 5) + x(3x^2 - 1) &= 	frac13 x^2 + x - 5, \ (	frac13 x^2 + x - 5) - 	frac19 (3x^2 - 1) &= x - 	frac{44}{9} . \end{aligned} So the quotient is 	frac13 x^2 - x + 	frac19 and the remainder is x - 	frac{44}{9}, of degree 1 < 2. Check: (3x^2 - 1) igl(	frac13 x^2 - x + 	frac19 igr) = x^4 - 3x^3 + x - 	frac19, and adding x - 	frac{44}{9} gives x^4 - 3x^3 + 2x - 5. (b) In 
F_5, 2 \cdot 3 = 6 = 1, so 2^{-1} = 3. The passes subtract 3x^2, x and 3 times the divisor, with 3x^2(2x^2 + 3) = x^4 + 4x^2, x(2x^2 + 3) = 2x^3 + 3x and 3(2x^2 + 3) = x^2 + 4:  egin{aligned} (x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1) - (x^4 + 4x^2) &= 2x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 1, \ (2x^3 + x^2 + 3x + 1) - (2x^3 + 3x) &= x^2 + 1, \ (x^2 + 1) - (x^2 + 4) &= 2 , \end{aligned} using -4 = 1 and -3 = 2 in 
F_5. So the quotient is 3x^2 + x + 3 and the remainder is the constant 2. Since 2 
e 0 in 
F_5, @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (b) gives 2x^2 + 3 
mid x^4 + 2x^3 + 3x + 1 in 
F_5[x]. [B2: A factor of a difference of powers] Let F be a field, c \in F and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Deduce from @fd4:lem-difference-of-powers that x^n - c^n = (x - c) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^j x^{n-1-j} , and hence that x - c \mid x^n - c^n. Then give a second proof of the divisibility with @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor. F[x] is a commutative ring (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a)), so @fd4:lem-difference-of-powers applies in it. Take z = c and w = x: c^n - x^n = (c - x) \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} c^j x^{n-1-j} . Negate both sides: -(c^n - x^n) = x^n - c^n and - igl((c - x) s igr) = (x - c) s for every s \in F[x] (@fd3:prp-ring-algebra (a), (c)). This is the displayed identity, and it shows x - c \mid x^n - c^n. Taking z = c, w = x rather than z = x, w = c gives the sum in the stated order, with no re-indexing. Second proof. By @thm-polynomial-ring-laws (c), x^n is the monomial 1 x^n, whose value at c is 1 \cdot c^n = c^n (@def-polynomial-evaluation, the monomial example after it). So the value of x^n - c^n at c is c^n - c^n = 0 (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations, for the sum and the constant -c^n), so c is a root and x - c \mid x^n - c^n by @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b). This proof gives the divisibility at once but not the quotient. [B3: One remainder over every field] Let F be any field. Show that the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 1 in F[x] is 1. Then explain why, over 
Q, evaluating at the roots 1 and -1 also finds it, and why that method alone does not settle the question over 
F_2. By @fd4:lem-difference-of-powers in F[x] with z = x^2, w = 1 and n = 50, since (x^2)^k = x^{2k} and 1^k = 1 (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)), (x^2 - 1) \sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j} = x^{100} - 1 . So x^{100} =  igl(\sum_{j=0}^{49} x^{2j} igr)(x^2 - 1) + 1, and \deg 1 = 0 < 2 = \deg(x^2 - 1). By the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a), the remainder is 1, over every field. Over 
Q by evaluation. Write x^{100} = q(x^2 - 1) + ax + b. Evaluating at 1 and -1 gives 1 = a + b and 1 = -a + b; subtracting, 2a = 0, so a = 0 since 2 
e 0 in 
Q; then b = 1. Over 
F_2. There -1 = 1, so the two roots coincide and evaluation gives the single equation 1 = a + b. It does not determine a and b (both (0, 1) and (1, 0) satisfy it), so the uniqueness argument above is needed. C. Going deeper [C1: Monic divisors keep integer coefficients] Call p \in 
Q[x] an integer polynomial if every coefficient of p lies in 
Z. 1. Let f, g be integer polynomials with g monic. Prove that the quotient and the remainder of f on division by g in 
Q[x] are integer polynomials. 2. Prove the same if \operatorname{lc}(g) = -1. 3. Explain why the least-degree argument of @thm-polynomial-division-remainder still works when S is replaced by \{ f - hg : h 	ext{ an integer polynomial} \}, for g monic. [Hint 1] Rerun the existence proof of @thm-polynomial-division-remainder, but only with integer polynomials h. [Hint 2] Let S_
Z \coloneqq \{ f - hg : h 	ext{ an integer polynomial} \}. If 0 
otin S_
Z, take r = f - qg \in S_
Z of least degree n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering) and suppose n \ge \deg g. Sums, negatives and products of integer polynomials are integer polynomials: their coefficients are sums of products of coefficients (@def-polynomial-ring), and 
Z is closed under +, -, \cdot. (c) and (a). Let m \coloneqq \deg g and S_
Z \coloneqq \{ f - hg : h 	ext{ an integer polynomial} \} \subseteq 
Q[x] , whose elements are integer polynomials. Run the existence proof with S_
Z in place of S. If 0 \in S_
Z, then f = qg with q an integer polynomial and r = 0. Otherwise take r = f - qg \in S_
Z of least degree n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering), and suppose n \ge m. With a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(r) \in 
Z and b = 1, the monomial t = a x^{n-m} is an integer polynomial, so r - tg = f - (q + t)g \in S_
Z, and it has degree < n or is 0, exactly as in the proof. Both contradict the choice of r. So \deg r < m, and f = qg + r with q, r integer polynomials. This is a division with remainder in 
Q[x], so by uniqueness (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a)) these q, r are the quotient and remainder. The argument works because the step r \mapsto r - tg never leaves S_
Z: it needs b^{-1} \in 
Z, and b = 1 gives b^{-1} = 1. That answers (c). (d) If \operatorname{lc}(g) = -1, then b^{-1} = -1 \in 
Z, and the same proof runs with t = -a x^{n-m}. (Alternatively, divide f by the monic -g: f = q(-g) + r = (-q)g + r.) [C2: The remainder modulo a quadratic with known roots] Let F be a field, f \in F[x] and a, b \in F. 1. If a 
e b, prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)(x - b) is f(a) (a - b)^{-1} (x - b) + f(b) (b - a)^{-1} (x - a) . 2. If a = b, write f = (x - a)h + f(a) (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a)) and prove that the remainder of f on division by (x - a)^2 is h(a)(x - a) + f(a). 3. Hence find the remainder of x^{100} on division by x^2 - 3x + 2 in 
Q[x]. [Hint 1] The remainder has degree at most 1. Which values does it take at a and at b? [Hint 2] Write f = q(x - a)(x - b) + r with \deg r \le 1, and let s be the displayed polynomial. (a) The divisor (x - a)(x - b) is monic of degree 2 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), so @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a) gives f = q (x - a)(x - b) + r with \deg r \le 1. Evaluating at a and at b (@thm-evaluation-respects-operations) kills the first term: r(a) = f(a) and r(b) = f(b). Let s be the displayed polynomial; it has degree at most 1, and s(a) = f(a) \cdot 1 + f(b) \cdot 0 = f(a), s(b) = f(b). So r - s has degree at most 1 and the two roots a 
e b. If r - s 
e 0, then x - a \mid r - s (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b)), say r - s = (x - a)k, and \deg k \le 0 by @thm-degree-of-product (b), so k is a constant; evaluating at b gives 0 = (b - a) k, so k = 0 because b - a 
e 0, and then r - s = 0 after all. Hence r = s. (b) Divide h by x - a: h = (x - a)h_2 + h(a) (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (a)). Then f = (x - a)^2 h_2 + h(a)(x - a) + f(a) , and h(a)(x - a) + f(a) has degree at most 1 < 2. By uniqueness, it is the remainder. (c) x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2). By (a) with a = 1, b = 2, f(1) = 1 and f(2) = 2^{100}, the remainder is 1 \cdot (-1)^{-1} (x - 2) + 2^{100} \cdot 1^{-1} (x - 1) = (2^{100} - 1)x + (2 - 2^{100}) .

title: 5.2 Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm
content:
Ideals, the Greatest Common Divisor, and the Euclidean Algorithm Section 5.1 gave F[x] a division with remainder (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder). This section asks what two polynomials have in common. Here is a concrete version of the question. Which polynomials over 
Q can be written as a \cdot (x^2 - 1) + b \cdot (x^2 + x - 2) \qquad 	ext{with } a, b \in 
Q[x] \, ? Taking a = -1 and b = 1 gives x - 1, and hence, multiplying a and b by any h, every multiple h \cdot (x - 1). Nothing else can occur: x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) and x^2 + x - 2 = (x - 1)(x + 2), so x - 1 divides every such combination (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)). So the answer is “all multiples of x - 1, and nothing else”. Why x - 1, and why should the answer be the set of multiples of a single polynomial? The integer version of this question, in Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.2, was answered by a least element; here the answer is a polynomial of least degree. As in Section 5.1, F is a field and F[x] is a commutative ring (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a)). So the general notions of Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 4 apply to it without change: ideals (@def-ideal-commutative-ring, clauses (I1)–(I3)), quotient rings (@thm-quotient-ring-by-ideal) and units (@def-ring-unit). We recall the clauses: a subset I \subseteq F[x] is an ideal if (I1) 0 \in I, (I2) a + b \in I for all a, b \in I, and (I3) ra \in I for all a \in I and all r \in F[x]. The ideal generated by finitely many polynomials The combinations in the opening question form a set that deserves a name and a symbol. [Ideal Generated by Polynomials] Let F be a field, k \in 
Z_{>0} and f_1, \dots, f_k \in F[x]. The set \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle \coloneqq \{ a_1 f_1 + \dots + a_k f_k : a_1, \dots, a_k \in F[x] \} is the ideal generated by f_1, \dots, f_k. For one polynomial, \langle f angle = \{ af : a \in F[x] \} is the set of multiples of f. In words: \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle collects every way of multiplying each f_i by a polynomial and adding up. The coefficients a_i range over all of F[x], not over F. The name is earned by two facts. It is an ideal, and it contains every f_i. (I1): 0 = 0 \cdot f_1 + \dots + 0 \cdot f_k. (I2): \sum_i a_i f_i + \sum_i b_i f_i = \sum_i (a_i + b_i) f_i. (I3): r \sum_i a_i f_i = \sum_i (r a_i) f_i. These are the ring laws of F[x] applied to finite sums (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (b)). Taking a_i = 1 and the other coefficients 0 shows f_i \in \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle. It lies inside every ideal that contains every f_i. If J is an ideal with f_1, \dots, f_k \in J, then each a_i f_i \in J by (I3), and their sum lies in J by (I2), applied k - 1 times. So \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle \subseteq J. So \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle is the smallest ideal containing f_1, \dots, f_k. This “smallest” clause is how we will compare two such ideals: to show \langle g_1, \dots, g_l angle \subseteq \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle, it is enough to show that each g_j lies in \langle f_1, \dots, f_k angle. Examples: - \langle 0 angle = \{ a \cdot 0 \} = \{0\}, the degenerate case. It is the only ideal generated by one polynomial that contains no non-zero element, and the main theorem below treats it separately. - \langle c angle = F[x] for a non-zero constant c: every f equals (c^{-1} f) \cdot c. - For c \in F, let I_c \coloneqq \{ f \in F[x] : f(c) = 0 \}, the polynomials with root c. It is an ideal: 0(c) = 0, (f + g)(c) = f(c) + g(c) = 0, and (rf)(c) = r(c) f(c) = 0, by @thm-evaluation-respects-operations. Moreover I_c = \langle x - c angle: by the factor theorem (@thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b)), f(c) = 0 if and only if x - c \mid f, that is, f \in \langle x - c angle. - In the opening question, \langle x^2 - 1, x^2 + x - 2 angle = \langle x - 1 angle. The set T \coloneqq \{ f \in F[x] : \deg f \ge 3 \} \cup \{0\} satisfies (I1) and (I3) (a non-zero multiple of a polynomial of degree at least 3 has degree at least 3, by @thm-degree-of-product (b)). But (I2) fails: x^3 and -x^3 + x lie in T, and their sum x has degree 1. So T is not an ideal. “Large degree” is not a property that sums keep, because leading terms can cancel. Is \{ f \in 
Q[x] : f(0) = 1 \} an ideal of 
Q[x]? Name the first clause that fails. No. (I1) fails already: the zero polynomial has 0(0) = 0 
e 1. (So do (I2), since (1 + 1)(0) = 2, and (I3), with r = 0.) Compare I_0 = \{ f : f(0) = 0 \} = \langle x angle, which is an ideal. Every ideal has one generator Every example above turned out to be the set of multiples of a single polynomial. That is no accident. [Ideals of F[x] Are Principal] Let F be a field and I an ideal of F[x]. 1. If I = \{0\}, then I = \langle 0 angle. 2. If I 
e \{0\}, there is exactly one monic d \in F[x] with I = \langle d angle. Moreover d is the only monic element of I of least degree among the non-zero elements of I. Take a non-zero element of I of least degree, and scale it to be monic; call it d. Its multiples lie in I by absorption. Conversely, divide any f \in I by d: the remainder f - qd lies in I and has smaller degree than d, so it cannot be a non-zero element of I. It is 0, and f is a multiple of d. Uniqueness comes from @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f): two monic generators divide each other. Before reading on: where is “least degree” used, and why is d made monic? (a) If I = \{0\}, then I = \{0\} = \langle 0 angle. (b) Existence. Let I 
e \{0\}. The set D \coloneqq \{ \deg e : e \in I, \ e 
e 0 \} is a non-empty subset of 
N, so it has a least element n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering; on 
N = \omega it is @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering). Choose a non-zero e \in I with \deg e = n, let a \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(e) 
e 0, and let d \coloneqq a^{-1} e. Then d \in I by (I3), and d is monic of degree n (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f), @thm-degree-of-product (b)). (\supseteq) For h \in F[x], hd \in I by (I3). So \langle d angle \subseteq I. (\subseteq) Let f \in I. Since d 
e 0, @thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a) gives q, r \in F[x] with f = qd + r and \deg r < \deg d = n. Then r = f + (-q)d \in I, by (I3) and (I2). If r 
e 0, then \deg r \in D and \deg r < n, against the choice of n as least. So r = 0, and f = qd \in \langle d angle. Hence I = \langle d angle. Uniqueness. Let d' be monic with I = \langle d' angle. Then d \in \langle d' angle and d' \in \langle d angle (each generator lies in its own ideal), so d' \mid d and d \mid d'. Both are monic, so d = d' by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f). The least-degree description. Let d'' be any monic element of I with \deg d'' = n. The argument of (\supseteq) and (\subseteq) used only that d is a non-zero element of I of degree n; run with d'' in place of d, it gives I = \langle d'' angle, and uniqueness gives d'' = d. This proves the theorem. The answer to the prompt. “Least degree” is used once, in (\subseteq): the remainder r lies in I and has degree below n, so minimality forces r = 0. The minimality is about non-zero elements, which is why r = 0 is the conclusion and not a contradiction. Making d monic plays no part in the existence of a generator: e itself generates I, and so does 2e when 2 
e 0 in F. It is what makes the generator unique, because among the associates of e, all of which generate I, exactly one is monic. An ideal of the form \langle d angle is called principal, hence the name of the theorem. The proof’s move is the one this chapter is built on, and we name it: least degree, then divide. In a set of polynomials closed under the right operations, take a non-zero element d of least degree; divide any element of the set by d; the remainder lies in the set and has smaller degree, so it is 0. It is the polynomial form of “least positive element, then divide” from Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.2. The integer twin is @thm-integer-ideals-principal: every ideal of 
Z is n
Z for exactly one n \in 
N. There “n \ge 0” picked the generator; here “monic” does. In polynomials in two indeterminates the theorem fails (the polynomials with zero constant term are an example, which we state without proof; Exercise A1 asks which step of the proof breaks there, without proving the failure). The greatest common divisor A common divisor of f and g is a polynomial h with h \mid f and h \mid g. Every non-zero constant is one (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (a)). For integers, Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Section 4.2 took the largest common divisor. For polynomials, “largest” can only refer to the degree, and associates have the same degree: x - 1 and 2x - 2 are both common divisors of x^2 - 1 and x^2 + x - 2 in 
Q[x], of the same degree. So the definition asks instead for the property that Bézout’s theorem gave the integer gcd, and fixes one associate by asking it to be monic. The greatest common divisor is the monic common divisor that every common divisor divides. [Greatest Common Divisor of Polynomials] Let F be a field and f, g \in F[x], not both 0. A greatest common divisor of f and g is a monic d \in F[x] such that d \mid f, d \mid g, and h \mid d for every common divisor h of f and g. We set \gcd(0, 0) \coloneqq 0. N, which has a least element n (@fd2:thm-well-ordering). Let e \in I be non-zero of degree n, and d \coloneqq \operatorname{lc}(e)^{-1} e. Then d \in I by (I3), and d is monic of degree n. Every multiple hd lies in I by (I3), so \langle d angle \subseteq I. Conversely, let f \in I, and divide: f = qd + r with \deg r < n (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder (a)). Then r = f + (-q)d \in I by (I3) and (I2). If r 
e 0, it is a non-zero element of I of degree less than n, against the choice of n; so r = 0 and f \in \langle d angle. Hence I = \langle d angle. Uniqueness. If also I = \langle d' angle with d' monic, then d \in \langle d' angle and d' \in \langle d angle, so d and d' divide each other. Then d' = cd for a non-zero constant c (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (f)), and comparing leading coefficients gives c = 1. (b) The ideal \langle f, g angle is not \{0\}, since it contains f and g; let d be its monic generator, from (a). Since f, g \in \langle d angle, d \mid f and d \mid g. Since d \in \langle f, g angle, d = af + bg for some a, b \in F[x]. If h \mid f and h \mid g, then h \mid af + bg = d (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)). So d is a monic common divisor that every common divisor divides: d = \gcd(f, g) by @def-polynomial-gcd. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: a non-zero element of least degree exists, with the well-ordering of 
N cited. - 1: it is made monic, and the monic element is shown to lie in I (absorption). - 3: an arbitrary element of I is divided by d, and the remainder is shown to lie in I. - 2: minimality of the degree forces the remainder to be 0. - 1: uniqueness of the monic generator (by any route: mutual divisibility, or minimality of the degree applied to the difference). - 2: d \mid f, d \mid g, d = af + bg, and “every common divisor divides d” are read off from \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle, and d = \gcd(f, g) is concluded from the definition. Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming that the gcd is a combination of f and g (circular); “d divides f because d has least degree”, with no division step; citing @thm-euclidean-algorithm-polynomials (c) or the gcd clause of @lem-polynomial-gcd-remainder-step for (b) (both are proved from Bézout’s theorem). A second route for (b), the Euclidean algorithm with back-substitution by induction on the number of steps, may use the ideal equality of @lem-polynomial-gcd-remainder-step; it earns the 2 points of (b) when it shows that the monic associate of the last non-zero remainder divides f and g, is a combination of them, and is divisible by every common divisor. Existence in (a) has no second route here. [C2: Scaling the gcd] Let F be a field, f, g \in F[x], and h \in F[x] monic. Prove that \gcd(hf, hg) = h \gcd(f, g). [Hint 1] Compare the ideals \langle hf, hg angle and \langle f, g angle. [Hint 2] Show first that \langle hf, hg angle = \{ hu : u \in \langle f, g angle \}. If f = g = 0, then hf = hg = 0, and both sides are 0: \gcd(0, 0) = 0 = h \cdot 0. Otherwise let d \coloneqq \gcd(f, g), monic, with \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle (@thm-polynomial-bezout (c)). Since h is monic, h 
e 0, and one of hf, hg is non-zero (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors (a)); so @thm-polynomial-bezout applies to (hf, hg) as well. The ideals. For a, b \in F[x], a(hf) + b(hg) = h(af + bg). As a, b range over F[x], af + bg ranges over \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle, so \langle hf, hg angle = \{ h \cdot cd : c \in F[x] \} = \{ c \cdot hd : c \in F[x] \} = \langle hd angle . The generator. hd is monic, since \operatorname{lc}(hd) = \operatorname{lc}(h)\operatorname{lc}(d) = 1 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)). By @thm-polynomial-bezout (c), \langle hf, hg angle = \langle \gcd(hf, hg) angle with \gcd(hf, hg) monic; by the uniqueness in @thm-polynomial-ideals-principal (b), \gcd(hf, hg) = hd = h \gcd(f, g). This is the polynomial twin of @exr-gcd-and-bezout-c2 (\gcd(ka, kb) = k \gcd(a, b) for k > 0), with “monic” in place of “positive”. Without “monic” the formula fails: \gcd(2x, 2) = 1 
e 2 = 2 \gcd(x, 1) in 
Q[x]. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: treats f = g = 0 by the convention, and checks that hf, hg are not both 0 otherwise (no zero divisors in F[x]). - 4: shows \langle hf, hg angle = \langle hd angle, citing \langle f, g angle = \langle d angle. - 2: shows hd is monic. - 2: concludes \gcd(hf, hg) = hd by the uniqueness of the monic generator. Fatal errors (0 for the step): asserting that every common divisor of hf and hg is h times a common divisor of f and g (false: 1 divides x \cdot x and x \cdot (x + 1), and 1 is not x times a polynomial); using factorizations into irreducibles, which this section does not have. A second route (hd = (hf)a + (hg)b is a monic common divisor and a combination, so every common divisor divides it) scores 2 for the zero case, 3 for “monic common divisor and combination”, 3 for “every common divisor divides hd”, 2 for the conclusion by @def-polynomial-gcd. [C3: The gcd of two binomials] Let F be a field. For m, n \in 
N, not both 0, prove that \gcd(x^m - 1, \, x^n - 1) = x^{\gcd(m, n)} - 1 in F[x] (here x^0 - 1 = 0, and \gcd(m, n) is the integer gcd). Compute \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1). Two remarks. For m \ge 1, x^m - 1 is monic of degree m. And for m \ge n \ge 1, by the power laws (@lem-finite-sums-and-powers (c)), x^m - 1 = x^{m-n}(x^n - 1) + (x^{m-n} - 1) , since x^{m-n} x^n - x^{m-n} + x^{m-n} - 1 = x^m - 1. We prove, by @fd1:ax-induction (through @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) on s, the statement P(s): “for all m, n \in 
N, not both 0, with m + n \le s, the displayed formula holds”. P(0) holds vacuously: m + n \le 0 forces m = n = 0. Suppose P(s), and let m + n \le s + 1, not both 0. If m + n \le s, use P(s). Otherwise m + n = s + 1. Case n = 0. Then m \ge 1. The gcd of x^m - 1 and 0 is the monic generator of \langle x^m - 1, 0 angle = \langle x^m - 1 angle (@thm-polynomial-bezout (c)), which is x^m - 1. On the integer side, the common divisors of m and 0 are the divisors of m, and the greatest is m (@fd3:prp-divisibility-rules-integers (a), (e)), so \gcd(m, 0) = m. Both sides are x^m - 1. Case m = 0 is the same, since both gcds are symmetric. Case m, n \ge 1. Both gcds are symmetric, so we may suppose m \ge n. By the identity above and @lem-polynomial-gcd-remainder-step, \gcd(x^m - 1, x^n - 1) = \gcd(x^n - 1, x^{m-n} - 1) . The pair (n, m - n) is not (0, 0), since n \ge 1, and n + (m - n) = m < m + n = s + 1, so P(s) applies to it: the right side is x^{\gcd(n, m - n)} - 1. Finally m = 1 \cdot n + (m - n), so @lem-gcd-remainder-step gives \gcd(m, n) = \gcd(n, m - n). This proves P(s + 1). Since every pair (m, n) has m + n \le s for s = m + n, the formula holds for all m, n. For m = 12, n = 18: \gcd(12, 18) = 6, so \gcd(x^{12} - 1, x^{18} - 1) = x^6 - 1. Each polynomial step is one step (m, n) \mapsto (n, m - n) of the subtractive Euclidean algorithm on the exponents.

title: 5.3 Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization
content:
Irreducible Polynomials and Unique Factorization Over every field, x^4 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1)(x^2 + 1). Over 
Q the last factor cannot be split further; over 
F_5 it can, and x^4 - 1 becomes a product of four factors of degree 1; over 
F_2 all of them coincide, and x^4 - 1 = (x + 1)^4. So the “primes” of F[x] depend on the field F. Once F is fixed, though, every polynomial of positive degree splits into such primes in essentially one way, as every positive integer does in Section 1.2, and for the same reason: a prime that divides a product divides one of the factors. Sections 5.1 and 5.2 supplied the tools: division with remainder (@thm-polynomial-division-remainder), the monic greatest common divisor and its Bézout identity (@thm-polynomial-bezout). This section spends them. Throughout, F is a field, and F[x] is a commutative ring with no zero divisors (@thm-polynomial-ring-laws (a), @cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors); degrees of products add (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), and the units of F[x] are the non-zero constants (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (e)). Irreducible polynomials In 
Z, a prime is a number p \ge 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and p. Two features of that definition need adjusting for polynomials. “Positive” has no meaning in F[x], and its job there was to ignore the units \pm 1; in F[x] the units are the non-zero constants, so we ignore those. And “p \ge 2” kept the units themselves from counting as primes; in F[x] the condition becomes “degree at least 1”. An irreducible polynomial is one that cannot be split into two factors of smaller degree. [Irreducible Polynomial] Let F be a field and p \in F[x]. The polynomial p is irreducible over F if \deg p \ge 1 and, whenever p = gh with g, h \in F[x], one of g, h is a constant. A polynomial of degree at least 1 that is not irreducible over F is reducible over F. In words: the first clause rules out 0 and the non-zero constants; the second says that every way of writing p as a product uses a constant factor. That constant is never 0, since p 
e 0. So p is reducible exactly when p = gh with \deg g \ge 1 and \deg h \ge 1; then \deg g + \deg h = \deg p (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), so both factors have degree strictly less than \deg p. Examples. - Every polynomial of degree 1 is irreducible. If p = gh with \deg p = 1, the degrees of g and h are natural numbers adding up to 1, so one of them is 0. - x^2 + x = x(x + 1) and x^3 = x \cdot x^2 are reducible over every field: each is a product of two factors of degree at least 1. - x^2 + 1 is reducible over 
F_2, where (x + 1)^2 = x^2 + 2x + 1 = x^2 + 1 because 2 = 0. Over 
Q it is irreducible, as the next proposition shows. The polynomial is the same; the field changed, and with it the answer. This is why the definition says “over F”. - If p is irreducible and a \in F is non-zero, then ap is irreducible. First, \deg(ap) = \deg p \ge 1 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)), and a factorization ap = gh gives p = (a^{-1}g)h, so a^{-1}g or h is a constant, and then so is g or h. Associates of irreducibles are irreducible. The constants are kept out by the first clause, and each for a reason. Without it, the polynomial 0 would pass the second clause, since every factorization 0 = gh has g = 0 or h = 0 (@cor-polynomial-no-zero-divisors), a constant. But every polynomial divides 0 (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (a)), so 0 behaves like the integer 0, not like a prime. A non-zero constant a is a unit: it divides everything, and every factorization a = gh has two constant factors, since the degrees add up to 0. If units counted as irreducible, every factorization could be padded with as many of them as we like, just as (1, 2, 2, 3, 5) would pad the factorization of 60 if 1 were prime. The clause \deg p \ge 1 plays the part of the integer condition p \ge 2. For polynomials of degree 2 and 3, irreducibility can be decided by looking for roots. [Irreducibility in Low Degree] Let F be a field and p \in F[x]. 1. If \deg p \ge 2 and p has a root in F, then p is reducible over F. 2. If \deg p \in \{2, 3\}, then p is irreducible over F if and only if p has no root in F. (a) Let c \in F be a root of p. By @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (b), p = (x - c)q for some q \in F[x]. Then \deg q = \deg p - 1 \ge 1 by @thm-degree-of-product (b), and \deg(x - c) = 1, so neither factor is a constant and p is reducible. (b) (\Rightarrow) is (a), read contrapositively. (\Leftarrow) Suppose p is reducible, so p = gh with \deg g, \deg h \ge 1 and \deg g + \deg h = \deg p \in \{2, 3\}. Two natural numbers, each at least 1, with sum 2 or 3: one of them is 1. So p has a factor of degree 1, and @thm-polynomial-remainder-factor (c) gives a root of p in F. For x^2 + 1 over 
Q: for every c \in 
Q, c^2 \ge 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), with 0^2 = 0), so c^2 + 1 \ge 1 > 0 by (b) and (e) of the same proposition. There is no rational root, and (b) makes x^2 + 1 irreducible over 
Q. The same lines work in every ordered field, so x^2 + 1 is irreducible over 
R as well. “No root” does not mean “irreducible” in degree 4 and above. For c \in 
Q, c^4 = (c^2)^2 \ge 0, so c^4 + 4 \ge 4 > 0 (@fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (h)): the polynomial x^4 + 4 has no rational root. Yet x^4 + 4 = (x^2 + 2x + 2)(x^2 - 2x + 2) , as expanding the right side shows: the terms in x^3, x^2 and x cancel. Proposition @prp-irreducible-low-degree (b) is about degrees 2 and 3 only, where every splitting must contain a factor of degree 1; in degree 4 a splitting may be 2 + 2, with no factor of degree 1 and so no root. Is 2x^2 + 4 irreducible over 
Q? Is x^2 + 2 irreducible over 
F_3? Over 
Q, yes: 2x^2 + 4 = 2(x^2 + 2), and x^2 + 2 has no rational root (c^2 + 2 \ge 2 > 0, @fd3:prp-ordered-ring-rules (e), (h)), so it is irreducible by @prp-irreducible-low-degree (b), and so is its associate 2x^2 + 4. The factor 2 is a constant, so 2 \cdot (x^2 + 2) is not a splitting into non-constants. Over 
F_3, no: 1^2 + 2 = 3 = 0, so 1 is a root, and indeed x^2 + 2 = x^2 - 1 = (x - 1)(x + 1) in 
F_3. Euclid’s lemma for polynomials The definition of an irreducible p speaks about the factors of p. Unique factorization needs a statement about the polynomials that p divides. As in 
Z, the bridge is the Bézout identity, and the move is the one of Section 1.2: multiply the Bézout identity. Euclid’s Lemma for Polynomials Let F be a field and f, g, h \in F[x]. If f \mid gh and \gcd(f, g) = 1, then f \mid h. Since \gcd(f, g) = 1, @cor-polynomial-coprime-iff-combination gives a, b \in F[x] with af + bg = 1. Multiplying by h, h = h(af + bg) = (ah)f + b(gh) . Now f \mid f and f \mid gh, so f divides the combination (ah)f + b(gh) (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (c)). Hence f \mid h. The hypothesis \gcd(f, g) = 1 is needed. In 
Q[x], x^2 \mid x \cdot x, but x^2 
mid x, since a divisor of a non-zero polynomial has degree at most its degree (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d)); here \gcd(x^2, x) = x. For an irreducible p, the coprimality comes almost free, exactly as it did for a prime number. [An Irreducible Dividing a Product] Let F be a field and p \in F[x] irreducible over F. 1. For every f \in F[x]: p \mid f or \gcd(p, f) = 1. 2. For all g, h \in F[x]: if p \mid gh, then p \mid g or p \mid h. 3. If (q_1, \dots, q_l) is a list of polynomials in F[x], with l \in 
N, and p \mid q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l, then l \ge 1 and p \mid q_j for some j \in \{1, \dots, l\}. 4. If p and q are monic and irreducible over F and p \mid q, then p = q. Here q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l, also written \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, is the product of a finite list in the commutative ring F[x], given by the recursion of @fd2:def-sum-product as @lem-finite-sums-and-powers (a) reads it: the empty product is 1, and \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j =  igl(\prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j igr) q_{l+1}. For (a), the gcd of p and f is a monic divisor of p, and an irreducible p has only two kinds of divisors: constants and associates of itself. Part (b) is Euclid’s lemma in the coprime case of (a). For (c), peel the last factor off the product and apply (b); induction on the length does the rest. For (d), the cofactor of p in q must be a constant, and comparing leading coefficients makes it 1. (a) Since p 
e 0, the gcd d \coloneqq \gcd(p, f) is monic (@def-polynomial-gcd, @thm-polynomial-bezout (c)). It divides p: write p = du with u \in F[x]. As p is irreducible, d or u is a constant. If d is a constant, it is a monic constant, so d = 1. If u is a constant, then u 
e 0 (as p 
e 0) and d = u^{-1}p; since d \mid f, f = dk = p(u^{-1}k) for some k \in F[x], so p \mid f. (b) Let p \mid gh. By (a), p \mid g or \gcd(p, g) = 1, and in the second case @thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma gives p \mid h. (c) By @fd1:ax-induction (on 
N = \omega, @fd3:cor-omega-identification (b)) we prove, for every l \in 
N, the statement P(l): “for every list (q_1, \dots, q_l) in F[x] with p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j, we have l \ge 1 and p \mid q_j for some j \le l”. Base case P(0). The empty product is 1, and p 
mid 1: otherwise \deg p \le \deg 1 = 0 by @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d), against \deg p \ge 1. So the hypothesis of P(0) never holds, and P(0) is true. Step. Assume P(l), and let p \mid \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j =  igl(\prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j igr) q_{l+1}. By (b), p divides the first factor or p \mid q_{l+1}. In the first case P(l) gives j \le l with p \mid q_j; in the second, take j = l + 1. Either way l + 1 \ge 1, and P(l + 1) holds. (d) Write q = pu with u \in F[x]. As q is irreducible, p or u is a constant, and p is not, since \deg p \ge 1. So u is a non-zero constant, and comparing leading coefficients (@thm-degree-of-product (b)) gives 1 = 1 \cdot u. Hence u = 1 and p = q. Part (b) fails for reducible polynomials: x^2 \mid x \cdot x with x^2 
mid x. Part (d) needs “monic”: x and 2x are irreducible over 
Q, and each divides the other. The same multiplication of a Bézout identity combines two coprime divisors. [Coprime Divisors of a Polynomial] Let F be a field and m, n, h \in F[x] with m \mid h, n \mid h and \gcd(m, n) = 1. Then mn \mid h. Write h = mk with k \in F[x]. Then n \mid mk, and \gcd(n, m) = \gcd(m, n) = 1, since the clauses of @def-polynomial-gcd do not depend on the order of the two polynomials. By @thm-polynomial-euclid-lemma, n \mid k; say k = nt. Then h = m(nt) = (mn)t, so mn \mid h. Without coprimality the conclusion fails: x \mid x twice over, yet x \cdot x = x^2 
mid x. In 
F_2[x], the polynomial x^2 + 1 divides (x + 1)(x + 1), but divides neither factor. Does this contradict @cor-irreducible-divides-product (b)? No. In 
F_2[x], (x + 1)(x + 1) = x^2 + 1, so x^2 + 1 is reducible over 
F_2, and the corollary says nothing about it. (It divides neither factor because each factor has degree 1 < 2, @prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (d).) Factors that cannot be split further The existence half of unique factorization needs a supply of irreducibles: every polynomial of positive degree must have an irreducible factor. In 
Z, the least divisor at least 2 was prime (@lem-least-divisor-prime). For polynomials, size becomes degree, and the “least divisor” becomes a monic divisor of least positive degree. [An Irreducible Factor Exists] Let F be a field and f \in F[x] with \deg f \ge 1. Then f has a monic irreducible divisor in F[x]. Among the monic divisors of positive degree, take one of least degree. A splitting of it into two non-constants would produce a monic divisor of smaller positive degree. Let c be the leading coefficient of f, and let D \coloneqq \{ \deg d : d \in F[x] 	ext{ monic}, \ \deg d \ge 1, \ d \mid f \} \subseteq 
N . The monic associate c^{-1}f has degree \deg f \ge 1 and divides f = c \cdot (c^{-1}f), so D is non-empty. By @fd2:thm-well-ordering (on 
N = \omega it is @fd3:thm-omega-well-ordering), D has a least element n_0; let p be a monic divisor of f of degree n_0. Then \deg p = n_0 \ge 1. Suppose p = gh with \deg g \ge 1 and \deg h \ge 1. Then \deg g = n_0 - \deg h < n_0 (@thm-degree-of-product (b)). Let g_1 be the monic associate of g, so g = \operatorname{lc}(g)\, g_1 and \deg g_1 = \deg g. Then g_1 \mid g, g \mid p and p \mid f, so g_1 \mid f (@prp-polynomial-divisibility-rules (b)), and \deg g_1 \in D is smaller than n_0, against the choice of n_0. So every factorization p = gh has a constant factor, and p is irreducible. This is @lem-least-divisor-prime with degree in place of size; the twin is compared with, not used. Unique factorization Two facts about products of lists. The proof below handles lists of polynomials, and it uses two facts about their products, both proved by induction on the length from the recursion of the product. Let (q_1, \dots, q_l) be a list in F[x], with l \in 
N. 1. If every q_j is non-zero, then \prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j 
e 0, and its degree is \sum_{j=1}^{l} \deg q_j. If every q_j is monic, so is the product. 2. If l \ge 1 and j \in \{1, \dots, l\}, let (q'_1, \dots, q'_{l-1}) be the list with the entry j removed: q'_t \coloneqq q_t for t < j and q'_t \coloneqq q_{t+1} for j \le t \le l - 1. Then \prod_{t=1}^{l} q_t =  igl(\prod_{t=1}^{l-1} q'_t igr) q_j. In particular every entry of a list divides its product. The names (L1), (L2) are used throughout this chapter. (L1). Induction on l. For l = 0 the product is 1, which is monic of degree 0, the empty sum. If the claim holds for l, then \prod_{j=1}^{l+1} q_j =  igl(\prod_{j=1}^{l} q_j igr) q_{l+1} is a product of two non-zero polynomials, so it is non-zero with degree \sum_{j=1}^{l} \deg q_j + \deg q_{l+1} and leading coefficient the product of the two leading coefficients (@thm-degree-of-product (b)); that is 1 \cdot 1 = 1 when both factors are monic. (L2). Induction on l \ge 1, for all j \le l at once. For l = 1, j = 1, the shortened list is empty and both sides are q_1. Suppose the claim holds for lists of length l, and let (q_1, \dots, q_{l+1}) and j \le l + 1 be given. If j = l + 1, the shortened list is (q_1, \dots, q_l) and the claim is the recursion itself. If j \le l, the claim for the list (q_1, \dots, q_l) and the same j gives \prod_{t=1}^{l} q_t =  igl(\prod_{t=1}^{l-1} r_t igr) q_j, where (r_1, \dots, r_{l-1}) is (q_1, \dots, q_l) with entry j removed. The list (q'_1, \dots, q'_l) obtained from (q_1, \dots, q_{l+1}) has the first l - 1 entries r_1, \dots, r_{l-1} and the last entry q'_l = q_{l+1}. So, by the recursion twice and commutativity and associativity in F[x],  egin{aligned} \prod_{t=1}^{l+1} q_t &= \Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{l-1} r_t\Bigr) q_j \, q_{l+1} \ &= \Bigl(\Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{l-1} r_t\Bigr) q_{l+1}\Bigr) q_j = \Bigl(\prod_{t=1}^{l} q'_t\Bigr) q_j . \end{aligned} The last clause of (L2) follows: q_j divides  igl(\prod_{t} q'_t igr) q_j. Everything is now in place. [Unique Factorization of Polynomials] Let F be a field and f \in F[x] with \deg f \ge 1 and leading coefficient c. 1. Existence. There are k \ge 1 and monic polynomials p_1, \dots, p_k, irreducible over F, with f = c \, p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k. 2. Uniqueness. If also f = c' q_1 q_2 \cdots q_l with c' \in F, l \in 
N and monic polynomials q_1, \dots, q_l irreducible over F, then c' = c, l = k, and there is a bijection \sigma \colon \{1, \dots, k\} 	o \{1, \dots, l\} (@fd2:def-bijective) with q_{\sigma(i)} = p_i for every i. In words: every polynomial of positive degree is its leading coefficient times a product of monic irreducibles, and the leading coefficient and the irreducibles, counted with repetition, are determined by f; only their order is free. The bijection \sigma says “the same list, possibly in another order”: it matches each p_i with an equal q_{\sigma(i)}, and each q is used exactly once. Existence. Split off one monic irreducible factor (@lem-polynomial-irreducible-factor); the cofactor has smaller degree, so strong induction on the degree factors it. Uniqueness. Divide by the leading coefficient, so that both products are equal products of monic irreducibles.
